subject: analysis
title: Metric balls, Cauchy sequences, and compact completeness
prompt: For a metric space \(M\) and a Cauchy sequence, prove (a) open balls are open; (b) the sequence is bounded; (c) a convergent subsequence forces convergence of the whole sequence; (d) compact \(M\) is complete.
hints: Use the triangle inequality in each estimate.
Compactness supplies a convergent subsequence of a Cauchy sequence.
solution:
(a) If \(x\in B(a,R)\), set \(\delta=R-d(x,a)>0\). When \(d(y,x)<\delta\), the triangle inequality gives \(d(y,a)<R\). Thus \(B(x,\delta)\subset B(a,R)\), proving openness.

(b) Choose \(N\) so \(d(x_n,x_N)<1\) for \(n\ge N\). A ball centered at \(x_N\) with radius greater than 1 and every one of the finitely many distances \(d(x_j,x_N)\), \(j<N\), contains all terms.

(c) Suppose \(x_{n_k}\to x\). Given \(\varepsilon\), choose \(N\) so late pairs have distance below \(\epsilon/2\). Choose \(k\) with \(n_k\ge N\) and \(d(x_{n_k},x)<\epsilon/2\). Then for every \(n\ge N\), \(d(x_n,x)<\epsilon\) by the triangle inequality.

(d) Every sequence in a compact metric space has a convergent subsequence with limit in \(M\). Apply this to any Cauchy sequence and then use (c). Every Cauchy sequence converges in \(M\), which is completeness.
pitfall: The convergent subsequence's limit must belong to the space when proving completeness.

subject: analysis
title: Exponential limits and a missing constant term
prompt:
Prove (a) \((1+\frac{a}{n})^n\to e^a\); (c) the same limit if \(a_n\to a\); (d) analyze the printed claim: if \(f(0)=f'(0)=0,\ f''(0)=a\), then 
\[
f(\frac{x}{\sqrt n})^n\to e^{\frac{ax^2}{2}}.
\]
hints: Use the derivative of log at one.
In (d), first check whether the base tends to zero or one.
solution:
(a) For sufficiently large \(n\) the base is positive. Since \(\log(1+u)/u\to1\) as \(u\) tends to zero,
\[
 n\log(1+a/n)\longrightarrow a.
\]
Exponentiation gives the limit, with \(a=0\) immediate.

(c) The convergent sequence \(a_n\) is bounded, so \(a_n/n\to0\) and the bases are eventually positive. The same logarithmic estimate gives \(n\log(1+a_n/n)=a_n+o(1)\to a\).

(d) As printed this is false: \(f(0)=0\) implies \(f(x/\sqrt n)\to0\). Its absolute value is eventually at most \(1/2\), so its \(n\)th power tends to zero, not the strictly positive \(e^{ax^2/2}\). Even \(f\) identically zero is a counterexample.

The intended formula has base \(1+f(x/\sqrt n)\), or alternatively assumes \(f(0)=1\) instead of zero. With the printed zero initial value, the existence of \(f''(0)=a\) yields
\[
 f(t)=\tfrac a2t^2+o(t^2).
\]
This follows from \(f'(t)=at+o(t)\) and Cauchy's mean value theorem applied to \(f(t)\) and \(t^2\); no continuous second derivative is required. Thus \(a_n=n f(x/\sqrt n)\to ax^2/2\), and (c) proves
\[
 (1+f(x/\sqrt n))^n\longrightarrow e^{ax^2/2}.
\]
The source labels skip (b); all actually printed parts are covered.
pitfall: An exponential limit requires bases approaching one; a base approaching zero gives a different limit.
note: SOURCE ERROR: printed \(f(0)=0\) with base \(f\), rather than \(1+f\), makes the actual limit zero. Corrected variants are explained. Original subpart labels are (a),(c),(d).

subject: analysis
title: A closed but nonexact radial flux form
prompt:
For 
\[
\omega=\frac{x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}},
\]
 prove (a) smooth and closed on punctured \(\mathbb R^3\); (b) not exact there.
hints: Closedness is the divergence of the corresponding radial field.
An exact form integrates to zero on a closed surface.
solution:
Let \(r=(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{1/2}\). Its denominator is positive on the stated domain, so omega is smooth. The corresponding vector field is \(F=(x,y,z)/r^3\), and
\[
 d\omega=(\operatorname{div}F)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz,\qquad
 \operatorname{div}F=3r^{-3}-3(x^2+y^2+z^2)r^{-5}=0.
\]
Thus omega is closed.

On the outward unit sphere, \(F\) is the outward unit normal. Consequently \(\int_{S^2}\omega=4\pi\). If \(\omega=d\beta\) on the punctured space, restriction to the sphere and Stokes' theorem on the closed manifold \(S^2\) would give
\(\int_{S^2}d\beta=\int_{\partial S^2}\beta=0\), a contradiction. Hence omega is not exact. One cannot apply a flux divergence argument through the whole ball, since \(F\) is undefined at its origin.
pitfall: Closedness is local; the puncture obstructs a global primitive.

subject: analysis
title: A continuous function with all moments zero
prompt:
Using Weierstrass approximation, prove that continuous \(f\) on \([0,1]\) with 
\[
\int_0^1f(x)x^n\,dx=0
\]
 for every nonnegative integer \(n\) is identically zero.
hints: First extend orthogonality from monomials to all polynomials.
Approximate \(f\) itself.
solution:
Linearity gives \(\int_0^1f(x)p(x)\,dx=0\) for every polynomial \(p\). By Weierstrass approximation choose \(p_k\to f\) uniformly. Then
\[
 \left|\int_0^1f^2-\int_0^1fp_k\right|
 \le\|f-p_k\|_\infty\int_0^1|f|\longrightarrow0.
\]
The second integral is zero, so \(\int_0^1f^2=0\). If \(f\) were nonzero at a point, continuity would make \(f^2\) positive on an interval of positive length, contradicting that integral. Thus \(f\) vanishes everywhere.
pitfall: Uniform approximation controls the integral error; pointwise approximation alone would not justify this estimate.

subject: analysis
title: Summation by parts, Dirichlet, and Abel
prompt:
For 
\[
A_n=\sum_{k=0}^na_k:
\]
 (a) prove 
\[
\sum_{n=0}^Na_nb_n=\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}A_n(b_n-b_{n+1})+A_Nb_N;
\]
 (b) prove convergence when \(A_n\) is bounded and \(b_n\) decreases nonnegatively to zero; (c) prove convergence when \(b_n\) decreases and is bounded below and 
\[
\sum a_n
\]
 converges.
hints: Write \(a_n\) as the difference of successive partial sums.
Subtract the limiting value of \(b_n\) in (c).
solution:
(a) Set \(A_{-1}=0\), substitute \(a_n=A_n-A_{n-1}\), and shift the second finite sum:
\[
 \sum_{n=0}^Na_nb_n
 =\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}A_n(b_n-b_{n+1})+A_Nb_N.
\]

(b) If \(|A_n|\le M\), the series on the right converges absolutely, since
\[
 \sum_{n=0}^\infty|A_n(b_n-b_{n+1})|
 \le M\sum_{n=0}^\infty(b_n-b_{n+1})=Mb_0.
\]
Also \(A_Nb_N\to0\). Thus the product series converges.

(c) Monotone bounded \(b_n\) converges to some real \(b\). Put \(c_n=b_n-b\ge0\), which decreases to zero. The convergent series \(\sum a_n\) has bounded partial sums, so (b) proves convergence of \(\sum a_nc_n\). Since \(\sum a_nb_n=\sum a_nc_n+b\sum a_n\), the required series converges too.
pitfall: The weights in (c) may have a negative limit; subtracting it reduces to (b).

subject: analysis
title: Two geometric series in a complex half-plane
prompt:
Determine convergence sets and sums for 
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty(\frac{z}{1+z})^n
\]
 and 
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)(\frac{z}{1+z})^n.
\]
hints: Set \(r\) equal to the common ratio.
Rewrite the absolute-value inequality in terms of the real part of \(z\).
solution:
At \(z=-1\) the expressions are undefined. Else put \(r=z/(1+z)\). The first geometric series converges precisely when \(|r|<1\); for \(|r|\ge1\) its terms do not tend to zero. The second series also converges precisely for \(|r|<1\), by its ratio test inside the disk and the term test outside it. Now
\[
 |z|<|1+z|\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 |z|^2<|z|^2+2\operatorname{Re}z+1
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{Re}z>-1/2.
\]
On that common half-plane their respective sums are
\[
 \frac1{1-r}=1+z,\qquad \frac1{(1-r)^2}=(1+z)^2.
\]
The second identity follows by differentiating the geometric power series within its radius of convergence.
pitfall: There are no convergent boundary points because the terms fail to vanish there.

subject: analysis
title: Oscillation, endpoint derivatives, and critical points
prompt: For \(f(0)=0\), \(f(x)=x^s\sin(\frac{1}{x})\) on \(0<x\le1\), determine \(s\) for boundedness, continuity, existence of \(f'(0)\), existence of \(f''(0)\), and infinitely many critical points.
hints: Test sine maxima for boundedness and first derivatives.
The second derivative at zero uses the difference quotient of \(f'\).
solution:
All endpoint derivatives are right derivatives on this domain.

Boundedness holds iff \(s\ge0\): then \(|f|\le1\), whereas for \(s<0\), sequences with \(\sin(1/x)=1\) give unbounded values. Continuity holds iff \(s>0\), by \(|f(x)|\le x^s\); for \(s=0\) oscillations persist, and for \(s<0\) the function is unbounded near zero.

The first derivative at zero is the limit of \(x^{s-1}\sin(1/x)\), which exists iff \(s>1\) and then equals zero. For \(x>0\),
\[
 f'(x)=s x^{s-1}\sin(1/x)-x^{s-2}\cos(1/x).
\]
For \(s>1\) its endpoint difference quotient is
\[
 \frac{f'(x)-f'(0)}x=s x^{s-2}\sin(1/x)-x^{s-3}\cos(1/x).
\]
It tends to zero if \(s>3\). For \(1<s\le3\), take \(1/x=k\pi\): the sine term vanishes and the cosine term oscillates with magnitude constant or unbounded, so the limit fails. For \(s\le 1\) the first derivative is already absent. Thus \(f''(0)\) exists iff \(s>3\), with value zero.

For every real \(s\) there are infinitely many critical points in \((0,1)\). At \(x_k=1/(k\pi)\), the sign of \(f'(x_k)=-x_k^{s-2}(-1)^k\) alternates. Continuity of \(f'\) on each interval between consecutive \(x_k\) yields a zero in each interval by the intermediate value theorem.
pitfall: A second derivative at zero is not the limit of \(f(x)/x^2\); differentiating the oscillation introduces an extra inverse power.

subject: analysis
title: Uniform convergence, failed derivative convergence, and a powered series
prompt:
For \(f_n(x)=\frac{x}{1+nx^2}\), prove uniform convergence to a differentiable \(f\) on \(\mathbb R\) but failure of derivative convergence everywhere to \(f'\). Determine \(s\) for 
\[
\sum_n(f_n(x))^s
\]
 to converge for every \(x>0\), and show uniform convergence on \(x>0\) when \(s>2\).
hints: Maximize the absolute value of each summand.
At fixed positive \(x\), compare the powered series to a \(p\)-series.
solution:
The maximum absolute value of \(f_n\) is \(1/(2\sqrt n)\), attained at \(x=\pm1/\sqrt n\). Therefore \(f_n\to0\) uniformly on \(\mathbb R\), with differentiable limit \(f=0\).

However,
\[
 f_n'(x)=\frac{1-nx^2}{(1+nx^2)^2}.
\]
At every nonzero \(x\) this tends to zero, while \(f_n'(0)=1\) for all \(n\), so the derivatives do not converge everywhere to \(f'\).

For any fixed \(x>0\), \(n f_n(x)\to1/x\). Thus for real \(s\), \(n^s f_n(x)^s\to x^{-s}>0\). Limit comparison with \(\sum n^{-s}\) proves convergence iff \(s>1\). For \(s>2\),
\[
 0<f_n(x)^s\le2^{-s}n^{-s/2}
\]
for all \(x>0\), and the \(M\)-test proves uniform convergence on that whole domain. In fact it fails uniformly for \(1<s\le2\): at \(x=1/\sqrt N\) and \(N\le n\le2N\), \(f_n(x)\ge1/(3\sqrt N)\), so that tail block has sum at least \(3^{-s}N^{1-s/2}\), which does not tend to zero.
pitfall: Uniform convergence of functions alone does not imply convergence of their derivatives.

subject: analysis
title: Compactness criteria and a nonconvergent enumeration of a compact set
prompt: (a) Give two equivalent metric compactness definitions. (b) Show \(\mathbb N\) with its usual distance is not compact. (c) Show a convergent sequence together with its limit is compact. (d) Give a nonconvergent sequence of distinct terms whose set of terms is compact.
hints: For (c) one open set containing the limit covers the tail.
For (d) enumerate two convergent sequences and include both limit points.
solution:
(a) Compactness means every open cover has a finite subcover. In metric spaces this is equivalent to sequential compactness: every sequence has a subsequence converging to a point of the space. It is also equivalent to completeness plus total boundedness.

(b) The balls \(B(n,1/2)=\{n\}\) form an open cover of \(\mathbb N\) with no finite subcover. Equivalently the sequence 1,2,3,... has no convergent subsequence.

(c) Let \(x_n\to x\). In an open cover of \(\{x\}\cup\{x_n\}\), a member containing \(x\) contains all sufficiently late terms by convergence. Cover the finitely many earlier points with finitely many additional members. This is a finite subcover.

(d) In \(\mathbb R\), start \(y_1=0,y_2=2\), and for \(n\ge1\) put
\(y_{2n+1}=1/n,\ y_{2n+2}=2+1/n\).
All terms are distinct. Their set is the union of two convergent sequences together with their limits, hence compact by (c) and finite-union compactness. But the odd tail tends to zero and the even tail tends to two, so the whole sequence is not convergent.
pitfall: Compactness concerns existence of convergent subsequences, not convergence of every enumeration.

subject: analysis
title: Continuous partial derivatives yield a total derivative
prompt: (a) Define differentiability of \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and relate its partial derivatives to the total derivative. (b) Prove continuous partial derivatives imply differentiability.
hints: Change coordinates one at a time.
Subtract the Jacobian evaluated at the base point from the mean-value expansion.
solution:
(a) Differentiability at a means there exists a linear map \(L\) with
\(f(a+h)=f(a)+Lh+o(\|h\|)\).
Setting \(h=te_j\) shows the \(j\)th column of \(L\) is \(\partial_jf(a)\). Thus \(L\) is the Jacobian with those partial derivatives as columns.

(b) Assume the partial derivatives exist and are continuous in a neighborhood of a. For each scalar component \(f_\ell\), telescope \(f_\ell(a+h)-f_\ell(a)\) by changing the \(n\) coordinates successively. The one-variable mean value theorem writes the \(j\)th change as \(\partial_jf_\ell(\xi_{\ell j})h_j\), where each intermediate point \(\xi_{\ell j}\to a\) as \(h\) tends to zero. Subtracting \(\sum_j\partial_jf_\ell(a)h_j\) leaves
\[
 \sum_j\big(\partial_jf_\ell(\xi_{\ell j})-\partial_jf_\ell(a)\big)h_j.
\]
Its absolute value is bounded by the largest derivative difference times \(\sum_j|h_j|\le\sqrt n\|h\|\). Continuity makes that largest difference tend to zero. There are only finitely many components, so the vector remainder is \(o(\|h\|)\), proving differentiability with derivative the Jacobian.
pitfall: Partial derivatives merely existing at a point do not supply the uniform small-error estimate.

subject: analysis
title: Rank and regions of a spindle surface of revolution
prompt:
For 
\[
f(s,t)=((1+2\cos s)\cos t,(1+2\cos s)\sin t,2\sin s),
\]
 find the maximum derivative rank and its exceptional set \(S\); sketch the image and \(f(S)\); prove the complement has three connected open regions; find the volume of either bounded region.
hints: Compute the orthogonal derivative columns.
Work in the meridian half-plane using cylindrical radius, retaining both signed-radius branches.
solution:
The derivative columns are
\[
 f_s=(-2\sin s\cos t,-2\sin s\sin t,2\cos s),\quad
 f_t=(-(1+2\cos s)\sin t,(1+2\cos s)\cos t,0).
\]
They are orthogonal, with lengths 2 and \(|1+2\cos s|\). The maximum rank is 2, and it fails exactly on
\[
 S=\{(s,t):\cos s=-1/2\}.
\]
There the rank is 1 and \(f(S)=\{(0,0,\sqrt3),(0,0,-\sqrt3)\}\).

Put \(\rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). The image is the surface of revolution whose meridian consists of the right-half-plane arcs
\[
 (\rho-1)^2+z^2=4,\qquad(\rho+1)^2+z^2=4,\qquad \rho\ge0.
\]
These arise from respectively positive and negative signed radius \(1+2\cos s\). The second is an inner arc; their endpoints meet on the axis at \(z=\pm\sqrt3\). This is a spindle surface, with an inner sheet, rather than an ordinary embedded ring torus.

Define \(F_\pm=(\rho\mp1)^2+z^2-4\). Since \(F_-\ge F_+\) for \(\rho\ge0\), the complement partitions into exactly the following three disjoint open sets:
\[
 A=\{F_+<0<F_-\},\qquad B=\{F_-<0\},\qquad C=\{F_+>0\}.
\]
\(B\) is bounded and convex, since its defining inequality is
\(x^2+y^2+z^2+2\sqrt{x^2+y^2}<3\), a strict sublevel of a convex function; hence it is path connected. For \(A\), at each \(|z|<2\) its radial interval is
\[
 |\sqrt{4-z^2}-1|<\rho<1+\sqrt{4-z^2}.
\]
Every such interval is nonempty. Radially move a point to the continuous middle radius \(\max\{1,\sqrt{4-z^2}\}\), then vary \(z\) to zero and rotate the angular coordinate. These paths remain in \(A\), proving path connectedness. For \(C\), first increase |\(z\)| at fixed \(\rho\) until |\(z\)|>2, keeping \(F_+>0\); then move \(\rho\) to 4. At \(\rho =4\) one may move freely between positive and negative heights, and connect through a common plane at \(z=3\). Thus \(C\) is path connected and unbounded. \(A\) and \(B\) are bounded. The three sets exhaust the complement because the excluded equality sets are precisely the image, so these are its three components.

Choosing the bounded region \(A\), its annular cross-section area is
\[
 \pi\big[(1+\sqrt{4-z^2})^2-(\sqrt{4-z^2}-1)^2\big]
 =4\pi\sqrt{4-z^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{Vol}(A)=4\pi\int_{-2}^2\sqrt{4-z^2}\,dz=8\pi^2.
\]
The integral is the area of a semicircle of radius 2. The following meridian sketch is revolved about its vertical axis; the marked axis points are \(f(S)\).
pitfall: The negative signed radius contributes an inner sheet; discarding it changes the number of complementary regions.

subject: analysis
title: Fourier coefficients and reciprocal-square identities
prompt:
For real noninteger a and \(f(x)=e^{iax}\), compute Fourier coefficients and prove 
\[
\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}(n+a)^{-2}=\frac{\pi^2}{\sin^2(\pi a)},
\]
 then 
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty(2n+1)^{-2}=\frac{\pi^2}{8}.
\]
hints: Use the standard period-2pi Fourier basis on [-\(\pi\),\(\pi\)].
Parseval turns the coefficient square sum into a reciprocal-square sum.
solution:
Take the period-\(2\pi\) Fourier expansion of the restriction to \([-\pi,\pi]\). Its complex coefficients are
\[
 c_n=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{i(a-n)x}\,dx
 =\frac{\sin(\pi(a-n))}{\pi(a-n)}
 =\frac{(-1)^n\sin(\pi a)}{\pi(a-n)}.
\]
Parseval's identity applies in \(L^2[-\pi,\pi]\), including the periodic endpoint jump when \(a\) is noninteger. Since \(|f|=1\),
\[
 1=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}|f|^2
 =\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}|c_n|^2
 =\frac{\sin^2(\pi a)}{\pi^2}\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\frac1{(a-n)^2}.
\]
Reindexing by \(n\) to -\(n\) gives the first requested formula. For \(a=1/2\),
\[
 \pi^2=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\frac1{(n+1/2)^2}
 =4\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}\frac1{(2n+1)^2}
 =8\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac1{(2n+1)^2}.
\]
The last equality pairs the positive and negative odd integers. Division gives \(\pi^2/8\). Absolute convergence justifies the pairing and reindexing.
pitfall: A noninteger exponential is not itself 2pi-periodic; Fourier coefficients refer to its restriction and periodic extension.
note: The conventional Fourier interval [-\(\pi\),\(\pi\)] and periodic extension are specified.

subject: linear algebra
title: A polynomial basis dual to three integral functionals
prompt:
On \(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)\), let 
\[
f_1(p)=\int_0^1p,
\]
 
\[
f_2(p)=\int_0^2p,
\]
 
\[
f_3(p)=\int_0^{-1}p.
\]
 Exhibit their dual basis and hence prove they form a basis of \(V^*\).
hints: Keep the sign of the third integral.
Solve for polynomials with prescribed three functional values.
solution:
For \(p=a+bx+cx^2\), the three values are
\[
 a+b/2+c/3,\qquad 2a+2b+8c/3,\qquad -a+b/2-c/3.
\]
Solving for unit functional-value vectors gives
\[
 p_1=1+x-\tfrac32x^2,\qquad
 p_2=-\tfrac16+\tfrac12x^2,\qquad
 p_3=-\tfrac13+x-\tfrac12x^2.
\]
Direct integration verifies \(f_i(p_j)=\delta_{ij}\). The polynomials are independent: applying \(f_i\) to a linear relation recovers its \(i\)th coefficient. They therefore form a basis of the three-dimensional \(V\). Similarly, applying any linear relation among the \(f_i\) to each \(p_j\) proves those functionals independent. Since \(\dim V^*=3\), they are a basis with the displayed dual basis.
pitfall: The third functional integrates from zero to minus one, not from minus one to zero.

subject: linear algebra
title: Schur complement and the misprinted Kronecker determinant exponent
prompt: (a) Factor a block matrix \(C\) with invertible \(C_{11}\) and deduce its determinant formula. (b–\(d\)) For \(A\in M_2(\mathbb C)\), \(B\in M_n(\mathbb C)\), use Schur complements and continuity to analyze the printed \(\det(A\otimes B)=(\det A\det B)^2\).
hints: The Schur complement uses the lower-right block.
A scalar multiplying an \(n\) by \(n\) matrix contributes its \(n\)th power to the determinant.
solution:
(a) Direct block multiplication gives
\[
 C=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\C_{21}C_{11}^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}C_{11}&C_{12}\\0&C_{22}-C_{21}C_{11}^{-1}C_{12}\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first factor is block triangular with determinant one. The second has determinant the product of its diagonal-block determinants. Hence
\[
 \det C=\det C_{11}\det(C_{22}-C_{21}C_{11}^{-1}C_{12}).
\]
The source writes \(C\) in place of \(C_{22}\) inside the final determinant; that expression is dimensionally inconsistent.

(b) If \(a_{11}\ne0\) and \(B\) invertible, the Schur complement of \(a_{11}B\) in \(A\otimes B\) is
\((a_{22}-a_{21}a_{12}/a_{11})B\).
Thus
\[
 \det(A\otimes B)
 =a_{11}^n\det B\,
 (a_{22}-a_{21}a_{12}/a_{11})^n\det B
 =(\det A)^n(\det B)^2.
\]
This is the correct general formula. The printed \((\det A\det B)^2\) is false unless \(n=2\) or additional special data happen to make the powers agree. For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(2,1)\), \(B=I_3\), the actual determinant is 8 and the printed right side is 4.

(c) Keeping \(B\) invertible, replace a zero \(a_{11}\) by a nonzero parameter tending to zero. Determinants are polynomials in entries and hence continuous, so the correct formula persists in the limit.

(d) For arbitrary \(B\) choose complex parameters \(\varepsilon\) tending to zero while avoiding the finitely many values making \(B+\epsilon I\) singular. Apply the formula to these invertible perturbations and pass to the limit. Therefore the corrected formula holds for all \(A\),\(B\).
pitfall: The exponent of det \(A\) is the size of \(B\). The source's exponent two is valid only for \(n=2\).
note: SOURCE ERRORS: Schur complement misprints \(C\) for \(C_22\); the Kronecker formula uses exponent 2 instead of \(n\) on det \(A\). Every subpart is proved for the correct formula.

subject: linear algebra
title: Gram–Schmidt preserving all initial spans
prompt: For a basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_n\) of an inner product space, construct an orthogonal basis \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\) with equal initial spans for every \(k\).
hints: Subtract projections onto the vectors already constructed.
Independence prevents the next residual from vanishing.
solution:
Use the inner-product convention linear in its first argument. Set \(a_1=b_1\), and recursively
\[
 a_k=b_k-\sum_{j<k}\frac{\langle b_k,a_j\rangle}{\langle a_j,a_j\rangle}a_j.
\]
Inductively the earlier vectors are nonzero and mutually orthogonal. Taking inner products with any \(a_i\), \(i<k\), gives \(\langle a_k,a_i\rangle=0\). If \(a_k=0\), then \(b_k\) would lie in the span of earlier a's, which by induction equals the span of \(b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1}\), contradicting that the \(b\)'s form a basis.

The displayed relation and its rearrangement express \(a_k\) in the first \(k\) \(b\)-span and \(b_k\) in the first \(k\) a-span. Induction gives equal initial spans. At \(k=n\) these nonzero orthogonal vectors span \(V\) and form the required basis. Dividing each by its norm would additionally make them orthonormal.
pitfall: Every denominator is nonzero because the input vectors are independent.

subject: linear algebra
title: Mapping nonzero vectors and prescribing coordinates
prompt: Over any field \(F\): (a) find invertible \(A\) with \(Ae_1=\xi\ne0\); (b) find invertible \(C\) taking any nonzero xi to any nonzero eta; (c) find a basis in which a given nonzero vector \(x\) has any prescribed nonzero coordinate vector xi.
hints: Extend a nonzero vector to a basis.
Compose two invertible basis maps.
solution:
(a) Extend xi to a basis of \(F^n\). The matrix \(A\) with those basis vectors as columns is invertible, and its first column gives \(Ae_1=\xi\).

(b) Choose invertible \(A_\xi,A_\eta\) as in (a). Then \(C=A_\eta A_\xi^{-1}\) satisfies \(C\xi=\eta\).

(c) Start with any basis of \(V\) and let eta be the coordinate vector of \(x\), which is nonzero. Choose \(C\) with \(C\xi=\eta\) by (b), and let the new basis consist of the vectors whose old coordinates are the columns of \(C\). In that basis, a vector with new coordinates xi has old coordinates \(C\xi=\eta\), so it is exactly \(x\). This constructs the required basis without restrictions on which coordinates of xi vanish.
pitfall: The prescribed coordinate vector must be nonzero because an invertible coordinate map cannot send zero to a nonzero vector.

subject: linear algebra
title: Eigenvalue, singularity, and determinant equivalence
prompt: (a) Define a characteristic value and vector of \(T\). (b) Prove equivalence of: \(c\) is an eigenvalue, \(T-cI\) is noninvertible, and \(\det(T-cI)=0\).
hints: An eigenvector is a nonzero kernel vector.
Finite-dimensional injectivity and invertibility are equivalent.
solution:
(a) A scalar \(c\) in the field is a characteristic value, or eigenvalue, if there exists a nonzero vector \(v\) with \(Tv=cv\). Such a \(v\) is a characteristic vector, or eigenvector.

(b) The equation is equivalent to \((T-cI)v=0\) for nonzero \(v\), hence to nontrivial kernel of \(T-cI\). In finite dimension a square operator has nontrivial kernel iff it is not invertible, by rank--nullity. Finally, a square matrix is invertible iff its determinant is nonzero. Combining these equivalences proves all three statements. The determinant is independent of the basis, since change of basis is similarity.
pitfall: The zero vector never qualifies as an eigenvector.

subject: linear algebra
title: Commutant subspaces and the simple-spectrum dimension
prompt: For \(K_A=\{B:AB=BA\}\), prove (a) \(K_A\) is a subspace; (b) its members preserve A-eigenspaces; (c) if \(D\) is diagonal with distinct entries, \(K_D\) consists of diagonal matrices; (d) if \(A\) has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues, \(\dim K_A=n\).
hints: Compute A applied to \(Bx\) for an eigenvector \(x\).
Conjugation identifies commutants in two different bases.
solution:
(a) The zero matrix commutes with \(A\), and \(A(rB+sC)=(rB+sC)A\) whenever \(B\),\(C\) commute with \(A\). Thus \(K_A\) is a subspace.

(b) If \(Ax=\lambda x\) and \(AB=BA\), then \(A(Bx)=B(Ax)=\lambda Bx\). Hence \(Bx\) belongs to the same eigenspace, including the possibility \(Bx=0\).

(c) For distinct diagonal entries, each \(D\)-eigenspace is the line spanned by one coordinate vector. Preserving all these lines forces \(B\) diagonal. Conversely every diagonal \(B\) commutes with \(D\).

(d) Distinct eigenvalues give an eigenbasis, so \(A=PDP^{-1}\). The linear isomorphism \(B\mapsto P^{-1}BP\) sends \(K_A\) onto \(K_D\). The latter is the \(n\)-dimensional space of diagonal matrices. Therefore \(\dim K_A=n\).
pitfall: A commuting operator may kill an eigenvector; eigenspace invariance does not require a nonzero image.

subject: linear algebra
title: The product resolvent identity and common eigenvalues
prompt: Prove \(I-BA\) is invertible iff \(I-AB\) is, with \((I-BA)^{-1}=I+B(I-AB)^{-1}A\). Deduce \(AB\) and \(BA\) have the same eigenvalues.
hints: Multiply the proposed inverse on both sides.
Scale A to treat each nonzero spectral parameter.
solution:
Suppose \(I-AB\) is invertible and write \(X=(I-AB)^{-1}\). Its inverse identities give \(X-ABX=I=X-XAB\). Thus
\[
 (I-BA)(I+BXA)
 =I-BA+B(X-ABX)A=I,
\]
and
\[
 (I+BXA)(I-BA)
 =I-BA+B(X-XAB)A=I.
\]
This proves invertibility and the formula. Exchanging \(A\) and \(B\) proves the converse.

For any nonzero complex \(\lambda\), apply this equivalence to \(A/\lambda\) and \(B\). Then \(\lambda I-AB\) is invertible iff \(\lambda I-BA\) is invertible, so their nonzero eigenvalues coincide. Zero is an eigenvalue of either iff its determinant vanishes; \(\det AB=\det A\det B=\det BA\), so zero occurs in both or neither. This proves equality of the eigenvalue sets, after complexification if necessary.
pitfall: The resolvent scaling addresses nonzero eigenvalues; zero needs its own argument.

subject: linear algebra
title: Consistency of four values for a quadratic polynomial
prompt: Prove there exists a real quadratic \(p\) with \(p(-1)=a,p(1)=b,p(3)=c,p(0)=d\) iff \(3a+6b-c-8d=0\).
hints: The first, second, and fourth conditions determine all coefficients.
Evaluate that determined polynomial at three.
solution:
Write \(p(x)=u+vx+wx^2\). The condition at zero gives \(u=d\). The conditions at -1 and 1 give
\[
 v=(b-a)/2,\qquad w=(a+b)/2-d.
\]
Therefore the only possible polynomial is
\[
 p(x)=d+\frac{b-a}{2}x+\left(\frac{a+b}{2}-d\right)x^2.
\]
Its value at 3 is \(d+\tfrac32(b-a)+9((a+b)/2-d)=3a+6b-8d\). Hence necessity is \(c=3a+6b-8d\), exactly the displayed relation. Conversely, when this relation holds the displayed polynomial satisfies all four values, proving sufficiency and uniqueness.
pitfall: Four prescribed values are generally overdetermined for a three-dimensional polynomial space.

subject: linear algebra
title: Strict off-diagonal principal-minor positivity
prompt: For real symmetric positive definite \(A\) and \(i<j\), prove \(a_{ii}a_{jj}-a_{ij}^2>0\).
hints: Restrict the quadratic form to two coordinate directions.
Choose a vector that eliminates the cross term.
solution:
Positive definiteness gives \(a_{ii}=e_i^TAe_i>0\). Choose
\(v=-(a_{ij}/a_{ii})e_i+e_j\), which is nonzero since \(i\) and \(j\) are distinct. Its quadratic form is
\[
 v^TAv=a_{jj}-a_{ij}^2/a_{ii}>0.
\]
Multiplying by \(a_{ii}>0\) gives \(a_{ii}a_{jj}-a_{ij}^2>0\). Equivalently, the two-coordinate principal restriction is positive definite and therefore has positive determinant. The distinct-index condition printed in this exam excludes the equality case on the diagonal.
pitfall: A positive diagonal alone is insufficient; the full positive quadratic form supplies the strict inequality.

subject: linear algebra
title: A polynomial integral operator: range and kernel
prompt:
On \(\mathcal P_3(\mathbb R)\), 
\[
Tp(x)=\int_0^1(x-y)^2p(y)\,dy.
\]
 Prove linearity, find its standard-basis matrix, and find bases of range and kernel.
hints: Expand the kernel polynomial into its three moments.
The degree-three shifted Legendre polynomial is orthogonal to all degree-two polynomials.
solution:
Linearity follows from linearity of the integral. Expanding,
\[
 Tp(x)=x^2\int_0^1p(y)\,dy-2x\int_0^1yp(y)\,dy+\int_0^1y^2p(y)\,dy,
\]
so \(T\) maps into \(\mathcal P_2\subset\mathcal P_3\). On the ordered basis \(1,x,x^2,x^3\), its matrix is
\[
 [T]=\begin{pmatrix}
 1/3&1/4&1/5&1/6\\
 -1&-2/3&-1/2&-2/5\\
 1&1/2&1/3&1/4\\
 0&0&0&0
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The moment map \(\mathcal P_2\to\mathbb R^3\), \(p\mapsto(\int p,\int yp,\int y^2p)\), is injective: if all moments vanish, then \(\int p^2=0\), because \(p\) is a linear combination of \(1,y,y^2\), so \(p=0\). Equal dimensions make it bijective. The displayed expansion then shows \(T\) has rank 3, with range exactly \(\mathcal P_2\), basis \(1,x,x^2\).

Rank--nullity gives a one-dimensional kernel. The polynomial
\[
 q(x)=20x^3-30x^2+12x-1
\]
has zero moments against \(1,x,x^2\), as direct integration verifies:
\(5-10+6-1=0\),
\(4-15/2+4-1/2=0\),
and \(10/3-6+3-1/3=0\).
Thus \(Tq=0\), and \(q\) is nonzero, so \(\{q\}\) is a kernel basis.
pitfall: The range has degree at most two even though the ambient space has degree at most three.

subject: linear algebra
title: Rank-one dichotomy
prompt: For rank-one \(T\) on a finite-dimensional real vector space, prove it is diagonalizable or nilpotent, but not both.
hints: Write Tx as a functional times a fixed range vector.
The scalar \(f(u)\) separates the cases.
solution:
Choose nonzero \(u\) spanning the range and a nonzero linear functional \(f\) such that \(Tx=f(x)u\). Then
\[
 T^2=f(u)T.
\]
If \(f(u)=0\), \(T\) is a nonzero square-zero operator, hence nilpotent. A diagonalizable nilpotent operator would be zero, so this case is not diagonalizable.

If \(f(u)\ne0\), the space decomposes as \(\ker f\oplus\operatorname{span}\{u\}\), since every \(x\) is
\[
 x=\left(x-\frac{f(x)}{f(u)}u\right)+\frac{f(x)}{f(u)}u.
\]
\(T\) acts as zero on the first summand and as the nonzero scalar \(f(u)\) on the second. A basis adapted to the decomposition diagonalizes \(T\), and the nonzero eigenvalue prevents nilpotence. The two cases are exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
pitfall: The nonzero rank assumption rules out the zero operator exception.

subject: linear algebra
title: A normal square of a nonnormal matrix
prompt: Give a \(2\times2\) matrix A whose square is normal but \(A\) is not, proving both assertions.
hints: A nonzero square-zero matrix has a normal zero square.
Compute its two Gram products.
solution:
Take
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It satisfies \(A^2=0\), and the zero matrix is normal because both products with its adjoint are zero. But
\[
 AA^*=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 A^*A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
They are unequal, so \(A\) is not normal. This example works over the real field with transpose or the complex field with Hermitian adjoint.
pitfall: Normality of a polynomial in A does not imply normality of \(A\).

subject: analysis
title: Continuity and endpoint limits of a positive series
prompt:
For 
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{1+n^2x},
\]
 \(x>0\), prove continuity, \(f(x)\to\infty\) as \(x\) tends to zero from above, and \(f(x)\to0\) as \(x\) tends to infinity.
hints: Away from zero, compare to a convergent \(p\)-series.
For divergence use arbitrarily large finite partial sums.
solution:
On a compact interval \([a,b]\subset(0,\infty)\), each continuous summand is at most \(1/(an^2)\). The \(M\)-test gives uniform convergence there, hence continuity at every positive \(x\).

For the first limit, fix any \(L>0\) and choose an integer \(N\)>2L. As \(x\) tends to zero, the first \(N\) summands tend to one, so their sum tends to \(N\). Thus for sufficiently small \(x\) the partial sum, and hence \(f(x)\), exceeds \(L\). This proves divergence to \(+\infty\).

Finally,
\[
 0\le f(x)\le\frac1x\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n^2},
\]
whose right side tends to zero as \(x\) tends to infinity. The squeeze theorem proves the second limit.
pitfall: An infinite termwise limit cannot be summed without justification; finite partial sums prove divergence safely.

subject: analysis
title: Compactness of bounded-velocity ODE solutions
prompt: Let \(f_n\) be uniformly bounded on \([0,1]\times\mathbb R\), and let \(y_n\) solve \(y_n'(t)=f_n(t,y_n(t))\), \(y_n(0)=0\). Prove a subsequence converges uniformly.
hints: Every solution has the same derivative bound.
Apply Arzelà–Ascoli to the solutions.
solution:
Let \(M\) be a common bound for all \(|f_n(t,y)|\). The differential equation gives \(|y_n'(t)|\le M\). The mean value theorem therefore yields
\[
 |y_n(t)-y_n(s)|\le M|t-s|,\qquad |y_n(t)|\le Mt\le M.
\]
Thus the solutions are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on \([0,1]\). Arzela--Ascoli provides a subsequence converging uniformly to a continuous function. For an absolutely continuous interpretation of solutions, the same estimates follow by integrating the almost-everywhere derivative bound. Existence of the given solutions is assumed, rather than deduced from boundedness of the right sides.
pitfall: Uniform boundedness of \(f_n\) does not itself prove existence or uniqueness of an ODE solution.

subject: analysis
title: Volume under an invertible linear map
prompt:
Find the volume of the image of the unit ball in \(\mathbb R^3\) under 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&5&-4\\0&-1&3\\0&0&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
hints: A linear map scales volume by the absolute determinant.
The matrix is triangular.
solution:
Since \(A\) is triangular, \(\det A=2(-1)3=-6\), so it is invertible. Its derivative is A at every point, and the change-of-variables theorem gives
\[
 \operatorname{Vol}(A(B))=\int_B|\det A|\,dx
 =6\operatorname{Vol}(B)=6\cdot\frac{4\pi}{3}=8\pi.
\]
The sign of the determinant records orientation reversal but does not change the positive volume. Whether the source ball is open or closed does not affect volume, since its sphere boundary has measure zero.
pitfall: Use the absolute determinant, not the signed determinant.

subject: analysis
title: No injective continuously differentiable map from the plane to a line
prompt: Use the implicit function theorem to prove no \(C^1\) map \(\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is one-to-one.
hints: A nonzero partial derivative produces a level curve.
If all derivatives vanish, the map is constant.
solution:
Let \(f\) be \(C^1\). If \(
abla f(p)
e0\) at some \(p\), one partial derivative is nonzero. The implicit function theorem expresses the level set \(f=f(p)\) near \(p\) as a graph over an open interval in the other coordinate. This graph contains more than one point, all with the same image, so \(f\) is not injective.

Otherwise \(
abla f\) is zero everywhere. For any \(p\),\(q\), the function \(t\mapsto f(p+t(q-p))\) on \([0,1]\) has derivative \(
abla f(p+t(q-p))\cdot(q-p)=0\). The mean value theorem gives \(f(p)=f(q)\). Thus \(f\) is constant, again not injective. These alternatives exhaust all possibilities.
pitfall: A rank argument alone is insufficient; a derivative may vanish at an isolated point of an injective function. The level-curve argument uses a nonzero derivative anywhere.

subject: analysis
title: Directional derivatives need not form a total derivative
prompt: (a) Define differentiability of \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) at \(p\). (b) Decide whether directional derivatives in every direction imply differentiability.
hints: The total derivative is one linear map controlling all small increments.
Construct a homogeneous rational function with nonlinear directional derivatives.
solution:
(a) Differentiability at \(p\) means there is a linear map \(L:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) with
\[
 \lim_{h\to0}\frac{|f(p+h)-f(p)-Lh|}{\|h\|}=0.
\]
This \(L\) is the derivative.

(b) False. Define \(f(0,0)=0\) and \(f(x,y)=x^3/(x^2+y^2)\) elsewhere. It is continuous at zero since \(|f(x,y)|\le|x|\). For any nonzero direction \(v=(a,b)\),
\[
 \frac{f(tv)-f(0)}t=\frac{a^3}{a^2+b^2}
\]
for all \(t\ne0\), so every two-sided directional derivative exists. The coordinate derivatives are 1 and 0; hence a total derivative, if it existed, would be \(L(x,y)=x\). Along \(h=(t,t)\), however, \(f(h)=t/2\) and
\[
 \frac{|f(h)-Lh|}{\|h\|}=\frac1{2\sqrt2},
\]
so the required limit is not zero.
pitfall: Even continuity plus every directional derivative is insufficient; the directional data need not be linear.

subject: analysis
title: Green's first identity and harmonic uniqueness
prompt: For \(g,h\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)\), a bounded smooth domain \(\Omega\), and \(F=g\nabla h\), (a) derive Green's first identity by divergence; (b) show harmonic \(h\) with zero boundary values vanishes.
hints: Expand the divergence by the product rule.
Set \(g\) equal to \(h\) to obtain a nonnegative energy integral.
solution:
(a) The product rule gives
\(\operatorname{div}(g\nabla h)=\nabla g\cdot\nabla h+g\Delta h\).
The divergence theorem therefore yields
\[
 \int_\Omega(g\Delta h+\nabla g\cdot\nabla h)\,dV
 =\int_{\partial\Omega}g\,\nabla h\cdot n\,dA.
\]

(b) Choose \(g=h\). Harmonicity makes \(h\Delta h=0\), and \(h=0\) on the boundary makes the boundary integrand zero. Thus \(\int_\Omega|\nabla h|^2=0\). Continuity and nonnegativity imply \(\nabla h=0\) at every point. Hence \(h\) is constant on the connected domain. Its boundary values force that constant to be zero. If domain were used for a possibly disconnected open set, the same reasoning applies on each bounded component.
pitfall: The energy method avoids any appeal to a maximum principle.

subject: analysis
title: Local uniform convergence of translated peaks
prompt:
Prove 
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{1+(x-n)^2}
\]
 defines a continuous function on \(\mathbb R\).
hints: Bound \(x\) on a compact interval.
Far enough along the series, the distance from \(n\) grows at least like \(n/2\).
solution:
Fix \(R>0\) and restrict \(|x|\le R\). For \(n>2R\), \(|x-n|\ge n-R>n/2\), and
\[
 \frac1{1+(x-n)^2}\le\frac4{n^2}.
\]
The majorant series converges, so the tail converges uniformly by the \(M\)-test. The finitely many earlier terms are continuous. Thus the whole series converges uniformly on [-\(R\),\(R\)] and its sum is continuous there. Every real point belongs to such an interval, proving continuity on \(\mathbb R\).
pitfall: These peaks do not have uniformly small maxima on the whole line; compact-interval bounds are the right approach.
note: Canonical April 1–4 are supplement questions; 5–10 are appended final questions.

subject: analysis
title: Persistence of an interior maximum requires a boundary gap
prompt: For continuous \(f\),\(g\) on compact \(K\subset\mathbb R^n\), the maximum of \(f\) occurs at an interior point. Analyze the claim that \(f+\epsilon g\) has an interior maximum for all sufficiently small positive \(\varepsilon\).
hints: An interior maximum may be tied with a boundary maximum.
A strict gap between the boundary and the global maximum gives the intended estimate.
solution:
The literal claim is false. Take \(K=[0,1]\), \(f\) identically zero and \(g(x)=x\). Every interior point maximizes \(f\), but for every \(\epsilon>0\), \(f+\epsilon g=\epsilon x\) has its unique maximum at the boundary point 1.

A sufficient corrected hypothesis is
\[
 M=\max_Kf>\max_{\partial K}f=m.
\]
This holds, for example, if \(f\) has a unique global maximizer and it is interior. Put \(\delta=M-m>0\), let \(p\) be an interior maximizer, and set \(G=\max_K|g|\). For a boundary point \(x\),
\[
 (f+\epsilon g)(p)-(f+\epsilon g)(x)\ge\delta-2\epsilon G.
\]
If \(G=0\) this is positive for all \(\varepsilon\); otherwise take \(0<\epsilon<\delta/(2G)\). Compactness ensures an attained maximum of the perturbed function, and the positive gap excludes every boundary point, so it is interior.
pitfall: The word occurs does not mean occurs only there; tied boundary maxima invalidate the assertion.
note: SOURCE ERROR: an interior maximizing point alone is insufficient. A strict boundary gap gives the valid corrected theorem.

subject: analysis
title: Countable intersections and continuous images
prompt: Decide: (a) countable intersections of open intervals are open; (b) continuous \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) maps bounded sets to bounded sets; (c) such \(f\) maps closed sets to closed sets.
hints: For (a) shrink intervals to a point.
For (b) contain the set in a compact interval.
solution:
(a) False: \(\bigcap_{j=1}^\infty(-1/j,1/j)=\{0\}\), which is not open.

(b) True. Any bounded \(E\) lies in some compact interval [-\(R\),\(R\)]. Continuity makes \(f([-R,R])\) compact and therefore bounded; its subset \(f(E)\) is bounded too.

(c) False. The set \(E\) equal to \(\mathbb R\) is closed, but for \(f(x)=e^x\) its image is \((0,\infty)\), not closed. Compact sets, rather than arbitrary closed sets, have compact and hence closed images under continuous real-valued maps.
pitfall: Boundedness of the domain set is helpful here because \(f\) is defined continuously on the entire real line.
note: April supplement problem 3.

subject: analysis
title: Equality from all moments
prompt:
For continuous \(f\),\(g\) on \([0,1]\), assume 
\[
\int_0^1x^nf(x)\,dx=\int_0^1x^ng(x)\,dx
\]
 for every nonnegative integer \(n\). Prove \(f=g\).
hints: Their difference is orthogonal to every polynomial.
Approximate that difference uniformly by polynomials.
solution:
Let \(h=f-g\). By linearity, \(\int_0^1p(x)h(x)\,dx=0\) for every polynomial \(p\). The Weierstrass approximation theorem gives polynomials \(p_k\) converging uniformly to \(h\). Consequently
\[
 \left|\int_0^1h^2-\int_0^1p_kh\right|
 \le\|h-p_k\|_\infty\int_0^1|h|\longrightarrow0.
\]
The second integral is zero for every \(k\), so \(\int_0^1h^2=0\). Since \(h^2\) is continuous and nonnegative, any positive value would yield a positive integral on a small interval. Thus \(h=0\) everywhere and \(f=g\).
pitfall: The \(n=0\) moment is included and is needed for arbitrary polynomial combinations.
note: April supplement problem 4.

subject: analysis
title: A square map and an inconsistent inverse point
prompt: For \(f(x,y)=(x^2-y^2,2xy)\), (a) compute \(Df(1,1)\); (b) the source says a local inverse \(g\) satisfies \(g(2,0)=(1,1)\) and asks \(Dg(2,0)\). Analyze and correct this.
hints: First evaluate \(f\) at the proposed inverse output.
Invert the Jacobian at the matching point.
solution:
(a)
\[
 Df(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}2x&-2y\\2y&2x\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Df(1,1)=\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its determinant is 8, so the inverse function theorem applies near \((1,1)\).

(b) The stated local inverse cannot exist: \(f(1,1)=(0,2)\), whereas the identity \(f(g(2,0))=(2,0)\) would demand otherwise. Correcting the input to \((0,2)\), the branch through \((1,1)\) has
\[
 Dg(0,2)=Df(1,1)^{-1}
 =\frac14\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If instead one retains the input \((2,0)\), its actual real preimages are \((\sqrt2,0)\) and \((-\sqrt2,0)\). The derivatives of the corresponding inverse branches at \((2,0)\) are respectively \(I/(2\sqrt2)\) and \(-I/(2\sqrt2)\). None of those branches takes \((2,0)\) to \((1,1)\).
pitfall: The inverse derivative formula must use a point and its actual preimage.
note: SOURCE ERROR: \(f(1,1)\)=\((0,2)\), not \((2,0)\). Both possible consistent interpretations are calculated.

subject: analysis
title: Derivative along a parabolic path
prompt:
For differentiable \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\), express 
\[
\left.\frac d{dt}f(t,t^2)\right|_{t=1}
\]
 using its partial derivatives at \((1,1)\).
hints: Differentiate the path before applying the derivative of \(f\).
Use the multivariable chain rule.
solution:
The path \(\gamma(t)=(t,t^2)\) is differentiable, with \(\gamma(1)=(1,1)\) and \(\gamma'(1)=(1,2)\). The chain rule gives
\[
 \left.\frac d{dt}f(t,t^2)\right|_{t=1}
 =Df(1,1)\gamma'(1)
 =f_x(1,1)+2f_y(1,1).
\]
The second coefficient is 2 because the derivative of \(t^2\) at \(t=1\) is 2, rather than the value of the coordinate itself.
pitfall: The velocity of the path, not its position, supplies the coefficients.
note: Canonical 6 is appended final problem 2.

subject: analysis
title: An everywhere nonsingular derivative makes a map open
prompt: If \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2\) is \(C^1\) and \(Df\) is invertible everywhere, prove \(f(U)\) is open for every open \(U\).
hints: Use a local inverse neighborhood inside \(U\) at each point.
The image is a union of open image neighborhoods.
solution: Take any \(y\in f(U)\), so \(y=f(x)\) for some \(x\) in \(U\). By the inverse function theorem, \(f\) restricts to a diffeomorphism from an open neighborhood \(V\) of \(x\) onto an open neighborhood \(W\) of \(y\). Since \(U\) is open, shrink \(V\), if needed, to an open neighborhood \(V'\subset U\cap V\). A homeomorphism maps open subsets of \(V\) to open subsets of \(W\), so \(f(V')\) is an open neighborhood of \(y\) contained in \(f(U)\). Every point of \(f(U)\) therefore has an open neighborhood contained in it, proving openness. Global injectivity is not required.
pitfall: Local invertibility does not imply one global inverse, but it does suffice for openness.
note: Canonical 7 is appended final problem 3.

subject: analysis
title: An exponential integral over a parallelogram
hints: Use the two edge vectors as coordinates.
The exponent separates in those coordinates.
solution:
Parametrize \(P\) by
\[
 (x,y)=u(-1,2)+v(2,3)=(-u+2v,2u+3v),\qquad 0\le u,v\le1.
\]
The determinant is \((-1)3-2\cdot2=-7\), so the area factor is 7. Also \(x+y=u+5v\). Thus
\[
 \int_Pe^{x+y}\,dx\,dy
 =7\int_0^1\int_0^1e^{u+5v}\,du\,dv
 =\frac75(e-1)(e^5-1).
\]
The fourth vertex is the sum of the two edge vectors, confirming that the unit square maps to the given parallelogram.
pitfall: Use the absolute Jacobian even though the chosen edge ordering reverses orientation.
note: Canonical 8 is appended final problem 4.

subject: analysis
title: Closed forms, exact forms, and pullback to a ball
prompt: (a) Define closed and exact differential forms. (b) Show every continuous 1-form on \(\mathbb R\) is exact. (c) For a closed \(k\)-form omega on \(E\) and \(\Phi:B\to E\), \(B\) the unit ball, show its pullback is exact, with the appropriate degree and regularity conventions.
hints: In one dimension use the fundamental theorem of calculus.
Use the radial homotopy on the ball for positive-degree forms.
solution:
(a) A differentiable \(k\)-form omega is closed when \(d\omega=0\). It is exact when \(\omega=d\beta\) for some \((k-1)\)-form \(\beta\). Exact differentiable forms are closed because \(d^2=0\).

(b) Write the continuous 1-form as \(a(x)\,dx\). Set \(F(x)=\int_0^xa(t)\,dt\). The fundamental theorem of calculus gives \(F'=a\), hence \(dF=a(x)\,dx\).

(c) In the usual smooth setting with \(k\ge1\), exterior differentiation commutes with pullback, so \(\eta=\Phi^*\omega\) is closed. On a ball define the radial homotopy operator by
\[
 (H\eta)_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})
 =\int_0^1t^{k-1}\eta_{tx}(x,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})\,dt.
\]
The homotopy identity is \(dH\eta+Hd\eta=\eta\) for positive-degree forms: apply the product and chain rules to the dilation pullbacks \(r_t^*\eta\), integrate their \(t\)-derivative from 0 to 1, and note the pullback at the constant map \(r_0\) vanishes for positive degree. Since \(d\eta=0\), \(\eta=d(H\eta)\), proving exactness. This is the Poincare lemma on a star-shaped domain.

The source states only a \(C^1\) map \(\Phi\) and a form on a subset \(E\). For the classical \(C^1\)-coefficient identity \(d(\Phi^*\omega)=\Phi^*(d\omega)\), assume sufficient regularity, for example \(\Phi\) smooth (or \(C^2\)) and omega \(C^1\) on a neighborhood of its image. A merely \(C^1\) pullback can have only continuous coefficients; the same homotopy argument gives exactness in the weak exterior-derivative formulation, but calling it classically closed requires a regularity convention. Also \(k=0\) is excluded: a nonzero constant closed 0-form is not exact.

Here is a precise justification of the weak formulation for the printed \(C^1\) map. Assume omega has \(C^1\) coefficients and is closed on an open neighborhood of \(E\) (or is the restriction of such a form). On any closed concentric subball of radius less than one, approximate \(\Phi\) in the \(C^1\) norm by smooth maps \(\Phi_j\), using convolution on a slightly larger subball. The compact image lies a positive distance from the complement of the neighborhood, so the approximants also have image in that neighborhood for large \(j\). Their pullbacks \(\eta_j=\Phi_j^*\omega\) converge uniformly to eta. The classical homotopy identity gives \(d(H\eta_j)=\eta_j\), since \(d\omega=0\). The integral formula for \(H\) implies \(H\eta_j\to H\eta\) uniformly too. Exterior differentiation is continuous under distributional convergence (integrate against compactly supported test forms), so \(d(H\eta)=\eta\) in distributions. The same globally defined \(H\) works on every subball, proving weak exactness on \(B\). For \(k=1\), the primitive is a continuous function with continuous distributional gradient eta; hence it is \(C^1\), giving classical exactness even for the printed \(C^1\) map. For higher \(k\) this argument provides a continuous primitive with the stated weak exterior derivative; additional coefficient regularity is needed if exactness is defined to require a \(C^1\) primitive.
pitfall: The Poincare lemma requires positive degree; pullback regularity must support the meaning of exterior differentiation.
note: Classical form proof assumes \(k\ge 1\) and sufficient regularity; the printed \(C^1\) map may require weak derivatives. Canonical 9 is appended final problem 5.

subject: analysis
title: Sphere area and ball volume by Stokes
prompt:
For the unit sphere \(S\) and ball \(B\) in \(\mathbb R^n\), with 
\[
\sigma_n=\int_S\sum_i(-1)^{i-1}x_i\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n,
\]
 express the volume of \(B\) using Stokes' theorem.
hints: Differentiate the displayed (\(n-1\))-form.
Each of its \(n\) terms contributes the volume form with positive sign.
solution:
Let
\[
 \omega=\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^{i-1}x_i\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n.
\]
The hat denotes omission. Exterior differentiation gives
\[
 d\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n(-1)^{i-1}dx_i\wedge dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\widehat{dx_i}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n
 =n\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_n.
\]
Moving \(dx_i\) past \(i-1\) factors cancels its sign. With the standard orientation of \(B\) and its outward boundary orientation, Stokes gives
\[
 \sigma_n=\int_S\omega=\int_Bd\omega=n\operatorname{Vol}(B).
\]
Therefore \(\operatorname{Vol}(B)=\sigma_n/n\). On the unit sphere the radial unit vector is the outward normal, so the restriction of omega is exactly the oriented area form, consistent with the given area interpretation.
pitfall: The omitted differential is essential; a full \(n\)-form would not integrate as sphere area.
note: Canonical 10 is appended final problem 6.

subject: linear algebra
title: The adjoint of an inverse
prompt: For an invertible operator \(T\) on a complex inner product space, prove \(T^*\) is invertible and \((T^*)^{-1}=(T^{-1})^*\).
hints: Take adjoints of both inverse identities.
The adjoint reverses multiplication order.
solution:
Assuming the indicated adjoints exist (automatic in finite dimension), take adjoints of \(TT^{-1}=I\) and \(T^{-1}T=I\). The product rule for adjoints yields
\[
 (T^{-1})^*T^*=I,\qquad T^*(T^{-1})^*=I.
\]
Thus \((T^{-1})^*\) is both a left and a right inverse of \(T^*\), proving invertibility and the asserted equality. The product rule itself follows immediately from the defining identity of the adjoint applied successively to two factors.
pitfall: Taking an adjoint reverses the order of the factors.

subject: linear algebra
title: Cyclicity of trace and similarity invariance
prompt:
Over any field, prove (a) 
\[
\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA);
\]
 (b) similar matrices have equal traces.
hints: Write trace as a double sum.
Apply the identity to the factors of a similarity.
solution:
(a) Using entrywise multiplication,
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_i\sum_ja_{ij}b_{ji}
 =\sum_j\sum_ib_{ji}a_{ij}=\operatorname{tr}(BA).
\]
Only commutativity of the underlying field and finiteness of the sums are used.

(b) If \(B=S^{-1}AS\), then
\[
 \operatorname{tr}B=\operatorname{tr}\big((S^{-1}A)S\big)
 =\operatorname{tr}\big(S(S^{-1}A)\big)=\operatorname{tr}A.
\]
Thus trace is independent of the basis of a linear operator.
pitfall: Cyclic rearrangement of a product is allowed; arbitrary rearrangement of several factors is not.

subject: linear algebra
title: A real invariant line or plane
prompt: Prove every operator on a nonzero finite-dimensional real vector space has an invariant subspace of dimension one or two.
hints: Complexify and take an eigenvector.
A nonreal conjugate eigenpair yields a real plane.
solution:
Complexify the space and operator. The characteristic polynomial has a complex root \(\lambda\) and a nonzero complex eigenvector.

If \(\lambda\) is real, writing the eigenvector as \(u\)+iv shows both \(u\) and \(v\) satisfy the real eigenvector equation, and at least one is nonzero. Its span is an invariant real line.

If \(\lambda=\alpha+i\beta\) with \(\beta\ne0\), write the eigenvector as \(u\)+iv. Then
\[
 Tu=\alpha u-\beta v,\qquad Tv=\beta u+\alpha v.
\]
The real vectors \(u\),\(v\) are independent: dependence would make \(u\)+iv a complex scalar multiple of a nonzero real vector \(w\), forcing \(Tw=\lambda w\), impossible for nonreal \(\lambda\) and real Tw. Thus their span is a two-dimensional real invariant subspace.

The assertion requires \(V\) nonzero; a zero-dimensional space has no such subspace.
pitfall: A real operator need not have a real eigenvalue, so the invariant-plane alternative is essential.
note: Nonzero dimension is required.

subject: linear algebra
title: Product minimal polynomials can differ in either direction
prompt: If \(p(AB)=0\), (a) prove \(q(t)=tp(t)\) annihilates \(BA\). (b) Analyze the printed conclusion: either \(m_{BA}=m_{AB}\) or \(m_{AB}=t\,m_{BA}\).
hints: Relate powers of \(BA\) to \(B\) times powers of \(AB\) times \(A\).
Apply the result in both orders and compare irreducible exponents.
solution:
(a) For \(j\ge0\), \(B(AB)^jA=(BA)^{j+1}\). Thus if \(p(t)=\sum_jc_jt^j\),
\[
 q(BA)=\sum_jc_j(BA)^{j+1}=Bp(AB)A=0.
\]

(b) Minimal polynomials divide every annihilating polynomial (divide by the minimal polynomial and use minimality of the remainder). Applying (a) in both orders gives
\[
 m_{BA}\mid t\,m_{AB},\qquad m_{AB}\mid t\,m_{BA}.
\]
All nonzero-root factors consequently have identical exponents. The powers of \(t\) can differ by at most one. The correct alternatives are
\[
 m_{BA}=m_{AB},\quad m_{AB}=t\,m_{BA},\quad\text{or }m_{BA}=t\,m_{AB}.
\]
The printed two-option conclusion omits the third possibility. For
\(A=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\),
we have \(AB=0\), \(BA=B\ne0\), and \(B^2=0\). Therefore \(m_{AB}=t\), \(m_{BA}=t^2\), violating both printed alternatives but satisfying the corrected third one.
pitfall: The extra zero Jordan-chain length can occur on either product; there is no fixed direction without additional hypotheses.
note: SOURCE ERROR: the two listed alternatives omit \(m_BA=t\) \(m_AB\). Both divisibility statements and a counterexample are supplied.

subject: linear algebra
title: Decay of powers and the finite-dimensional hypothesis
prompt: For a complex operator \(T\), prove all eigenvalues have modulus below one iff \(T^kx\to0\) for every \(x\).
hints: Necessity follows on an eigenvector.
Sufficiency uses finite Jordan blocks and exponential domination of polynomials.
solution:
In finite dimension, necessity is immediate: for \(Tv=\lambda v\), \(v\ne0\), \(T^kv=\lambda^kv\to0\) forces \(|\lambda|<1\).

For sufficiency put \(T\) in Jordan form. A block \(J=\lambda I+N\), \(N^r=0\), has
\[
 J^k=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\binom{k}{j}\lambda^{k-j}N^j
\]
for \(k\ge r\). If \(0<|\lambda|<1\), each coefficient tends to zero because a fixed polynomial in \(k\) times a geometric factor below one tends to zero. For \(\lambda=0\), the block power is eventually zero. Every block therefore tends to zero, and a fixed change of basis implies \(T^k\to0\), hence \(T^kx\to0\) for every \(x\).

The source does not explicitly say \(V\) is finite-dimensional in this question. Without that hypothesis the eigenvalue criterion fails: the right shift on \(\ell^2\) has no eigenvalues, so the listed condition is vacuous, but every power preserves the norm of a nonzero vector. The intended matrix/finite-dimensional interpretation is necessary.
pitfall: Eigenvalues alone do not govern powers of a general infinite-dimensional operator.
note: The eigenvalue criterion assumes finite dimension; the literal unrestricted version fails for the unilateral right shift.

subject: linear algebra
title: Self-adjointness from real quadratic forms and normal projections
prompt: (a) Define self-adjointness. (b) Prove \(T\) is self-adjoint iff \(\langle Tx,x\rangle\) is real for every \(x\) in a complex inner product space. (c) For \(T^2=T\), prove self-adjointness iff \(TT^*=T^*T\).
hints: Use the Hermitian imaginary part for (b).
For (c) compare kernels of a normal operator and its adjoint.
solution:
(a) \(T\) is self-adjoint when \(T=T^*\), equivalently \(\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle\) for all \(x\),\(y\).

(b) Self-adjointness makes \(\langle Tx,x\rangle\) equal to its conjugate, hence real. Conversely, put \(K=(T-T^*)/(2i)\), a self-adjoint operator. Reality of the quadratic form of \(T\) implies \(\langle Kx,x\rangle=0\) for every \(x\). Polarization, obtained by substituting \(x+y\) and \(x\)+\(iy\) into this zero quadratic form, gives \(\langle Kx,y\rangle=0\) for every \(x\),\(y\). Taking \(y=Kx\) yields \(K=0\), hence \(T=T^*\).

(c) A self-adjoint operator is normal. Conversely, normality gives \(\|Tx\|^2=\|T^*x\|^2\), so \(\ker T=\ker T^*\). If \(u=Ty\) is in the range and \(v\in\ker T\), then \(\langle u,v\rangle=\langle y,T^*v\rangle=0\). Idempotence decomposes every \(x\) as \(Tx+(I-T)x\), with the first term in the range and the second in the kernel. The decomposition is therefore orthogonal, making \(T\) the orthogonal projection onto its range. An orthogonal projection is self-adjoint: decomposing both \(x\) and \(y\), \(\langle Tx,y\rangle=\langle Tx,Ty\rangle=\langle x,Ty\rangle\).
pitfall: Reality of quadratic forms characterizes self-adjointness over a complex space; a real-space quadratic form alone would not detect the skew-symmetric part.

subject: linear algebra
title: Trace pairing represents every matrix functional
prompt:
Over any field: (i) prove trace is linear and 
\[
\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\operatorname{tr}(BA);
\]
 (ii) for \(f_B(A)=\operatorname{tr}(B^TA)\), prove linearity and \(f_B(E_{ij})=b_{ij}\); (iii) represent every linear functional uniquely this way.
hints: Expand the trace pairing in entries.
A functional is determined by its values on the matrix-unit basis.
solution:
(i) The diagonal sum is linear. Also
\(\operatorname{tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}b_{ji}=\operatorname{tr}(BA)\).

(ii) Entry expansion gives
\[
 f_B(A)=\operatorname{tr}(B^TA)=\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}a_{ij}.
\]
This is linear in \(A\) and evaluates to \(b_{ij}\) on \(E_{ij}\).

(iii) Given any linear functional \(f\), define \(B\) by \(b_{ij}=f(E_{ij})\). Since \(A=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}E_{ij}\), linearity gives \(f(A)=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}b_{ij}=f_B(A)\). Uniqueness follows because the values on all \(E_{ij}\) recover every entry of \(B\). The use of transpose rather than conjugate transpose makes this a bilinear representation valid over any field.
pitfall: The pairing is algebraic, not a Hermitian inner product; no conjugation is intended.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: An idempotent and its algebraic dual
prompt: If \(V=\ker P\oplus\ker(I-P)\), prove \(P^2=P\). Define the dual space and dual operator, show \((P^*)^2=P^*\), and deduce the analogous kernel decomposition of \(V^*\).
hints: Compute \(P\) on the two summands.
The algebraic dual operator acts by composition.
solution:
Write \(x=u+v\), with \(Pu=0\) and \(Pv=v\). Then \(Px=v\) and \(P^2x=Pv=v=Px\), proving idempotence.

The algebraic dual is \(V^*=\{\ell:V\to\mathbb R:\ell\text{ linear}\}\), and \(P^*\ell=\ell\circ P\). Thus
\[
 (P^*)^2\ell=\ell\circ P^2=\ell\circ P=P^*\ell.
\]
For any idempotent \(Q\), each \(z\) has the decomposition \(z=(z-Qz)+Qz\), with the first term in \(\ker Q\) and the second in \(\ker(I-Q)\). Their intersection is zero, since \(Qz=0\) and \(Qz=z\) imply \(z=0\). Applying this to \(Q=P^*\) gives
\[
 V^*=\ker P^*\oplus\ker(I-P^*).
\]
pitfall: Here the star denotes the algebraic dual map, not an inner-product adjoint.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: Roots of the minimal polynomial and a defective example
prompt: Define the minimal and characteristic polynomials, state Cayley–Hamilton, prove they have the same roots, and give an example with \(\chi_T(t)=t^4-t^3\), \(m_T(t)=t^3-t^2\). Is it diagonalizable?
hints: Minimality excludes a removable non-eigenvalue factor.
Use a size-two zero Jordan block.
solution:
The minimal polynomial is the unique monic polynomial of least degree annihilating \(T\); the characteristic polynomial is \(\chi_T(t)=\det(tI-T)\) in any basis. Cayley--Hamilton states \(\chi_T(T)=0\).

A root \(\lambda\) of the characteristic polynomial is an eigenvalue: if \(Tv=\lambda v\) with \(v\ne0\), then \(0=m_T(T)v=m_T(\lambda)v\), so \(m_T(\lambda)=0\). Conversely, if \(m_T(t)=(t-\lambda)q(t)\) but \(\lambda\) were not an eigenvalue, \(T-\lambda I\) would be invertible. The identity \((T-\lambda I)q(T)=0\) would then imply \(q(T)=0\), contradicting minimal degree. Thus the two polynomials have exactly the same roots.

Take
\[
 T=J_2(0)\oplus[0]\oplus[1].
\]
Its characteristic polynomial is \(t^3(t-1)=t^4-t^3\), and its minimal polynomial is \(t^2(t-1)=t^3-t^2\). The size-two zero block makes it nondiagonalizable; equivalently its minimal polynomial has a repeated root.
pitfall: Equal root sets do not mean equal multiplicities.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: Best approximation by orthonormal coordinates
prompt:
For orthonormal \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real inner product space, let \(a_i=\langle x,v_i\rangle\), 
\[
s=\sum_i a_iv_i,
\]
 and 
\[
t=\sum_i b_iv_i.
\]
 (i) Prove \(\|x-s\|\le\|x-t\|\), with equality iff \(a_i=b_i\). (ii) Prove independence. (iii) Deduce \(x=s\).
hints: The residual is orthogonal to the chosen vectors.
Use Pythagoras, then the dimension count.
solution:
For each \(j\), \(\langle x-s,v_j\rangle=\langle x,v_j\rangle-a_j=0\). Hence \(x-s\) is orthogonal to \(s-t\), and Pythagoras gives
\[
 \|x-t\|^2=\|x-s\|^2+\|s-t\|^2
 =\|x-s\|^2+\sum_i(a_i-b_i)^2.
\]
This proves the inequality and its equality characterization.

If \(\sum_ic_iv_i=0\), taking the inner product with \(v_j\) gives \(c_j=0\), so the vectors are independent. Since there are \(n\) of them in dimension \(n\), they form a basis. In particular \(x\) is some candidate \(t\) in (i). Then \(\|x-s\|\le\|x-x\|=0\), yielding \(x=s\) and the orthonormal coordinate expansion.
pitfall: The best-approximation argument works for an incomplete orthonormal set too; \(x=s\) additionally uses that the set is a basis.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: Eight true–false statements with explanations
prompt: Decide: (a) products of positive definite matrices are positive definite; (b) \(I+N\) has a square root for nilpotent real \(N\); (c) triangularizability iff the minimal polynomial splits into linear factors; (d) every operator has a cyclic vector; (e) a monic companion matrix has determinant equal to the constant coefficient; (f) equal quadratic norms imply equal inner products; (g) \(S^{\perp\perp}=S\) in finite dimension; (h) \(A\) is never similar to \(A+I\).
hints: Check symmetry as well as eigenvalues in (a).
Use polarization for (f) and the companion characteristic polynomial for (e).
solution:
(a) False with the standard Hermitian positive definition. Take \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\), both positive definite. Their product \(\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) is not symmetric and hence not positive definite in that sense.

(b) True. If \(N^r=0\), let \(S=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\binom{1/2}{j}N^j\). The formal binomial identity modulo \(t^r\) gives \(S^2=I+N\); all coefficients are real.

(c) True over the chosen field. Upper triangular form implies the minimal polynomial divides a split characteristic polynomial. Conversely, a split annihilating polynomial gives an eigenvector over that field (otherwise every linear factor evaluated at \(T\) would be invertible). On the quotient by its invariant line the minimal polynomial still divides a split polynomial. Induction constructs an invariant flag and a triangular basis.

(d) False. On a two-dimensional space the identity has \(\operatorname{span}\{v,Tv,T^2v,\ldots\}=\operatorname{span}\{v\}\), never the whole space.

(e) False in general. For a monic degree-\(n\) polynomial with constant coefficient \(c_0\), the companion characteristic polynomial is that polynomial, so \(\det P=(-1)^nc_0\). Degree one with \(c_0=1\) gives determinant -1.

(f) True. The real polarization identity recovers inner products from \(\|v+w\|^2-\|v-w\|^2\); in a complex space the additional tests \(v\)+\(iw\) and \(v\)-\(iw\) recover the imaginary part. Thus equality of all squared norms implies equality of both inner products.

(g) True. Orthogonal decomposition \(V=S\oplus S^\perp\) yields \(\dim S^\perp=\dim V-\dim S\); inclusion \(S\subset S^{\perp\perp}\) and equal dimensions give equality.

(h) True in positive dimension over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\): trace changes by \(n\), while similarity preserves trace. If arbitrary positive-characteristic fields were allowed, the assertion would need qualification: over \(\mathbb F_p\), diagonal matrices listing all \(p\) field elements are similar to their identity shifts by a permutation.
pitfall: Several claims depend on the field and on the standard Hermitian meaning of positivity.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: Rank-one operators: diagonalizable or nilpotent
prompt: If \(T\) has rank one in finite dimension, prove it is diagonalizable or nilpotent, but not both.
hints: Represent \(T\) as a vector times a functional.
Its square is a scalar multiple of itself.
solution:
Since the range is a line, write \(Tx=f(x)u\) for nonzero \(u\) and a nonzero linear functional \(f\). Set \(c=f(u)\). Then \(T^2x=f(x)f(u)u=cTx\), so \(T^2=cT\).

If \(c=0\), \(T\) is nilpotent of index two because rank one ensures \(T\) is nonzero. It cannot be diagonalizable: a diagonalizable nilpotent operator is zero.

If \(c\) is nonzero, the polynomial \(t(t-c)\) annihilates \(T\) and has distinct roots. More directly, \(V=\ker f\oplus\operatorname{span}\{u\}\), with eigenvalues 0 on the first and \(c\) on the second. Thus \(T\) is diagonalizable and not nilpotent. This includes the one-dimensional case, where the first summand is zero.
pitfall: Rank one excludes the zero operator, which otherwise would be both diagonalizable and nilpotent.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: Classifying three-dimensional nilpotents by minimal polynomial
prompt: Prove two nilpotent \(3\times3\) matrices are similar iff their minimal polynomials agree.
hints: List the partitions of three.
The largest Jordan block is the nilpotence index.
solution:
Similarity preserves the minimal polynomial, proving necessity. For sufficiency, a nilpotent matrix has Jordan blocks only at zero. The partitions of dimension three are exactly
\[
 3,\qquad 2+1,\qquad1+1+1.
\]
The corresponding forms are \(J_3(0)\), \(J_2(0)\oplus[0]\), and \(0_3\), with minimal polynomials \(t^3,t^2,t\) respectively. Each possible minimal polynomial therefore determines exactly one Jordan form and hence one similarity class. The result is special to this dimension: in dimension four \(J_2(0)\oplus J_2(0)\) and \(J_2(0)\oplus[0]\oplus[0]\) have the same minimal polynomial but are not similar.
pitfall: A largest block size does not determine the entire partition in higher dimensions.
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: Realizing a prescribed minimal polynomial
prompt: Give a matrix whose minimal polynomial is \(t^2(t-1)\).
hints: Use separate blocks for the roots zero and one.
The zero root needs a size-two block.
solution:
Take
\[
 A=J_2(0)\oplus[1]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
On its first block the least monic annihilator is \(t^2\), because the block is nonzero but its square vanishes. On the second block the least monic annihilator is \(t-1\). A polynomial annihilates a direct sum exactly when it annihilates each block, so the minimal polynomial is their least common multiple, \(t^2(t-1)\), as required.
pitfall: A scalar zero block alone would only supply one factor of \(t\).
note: The PDF actually contains four supplement problems and twelve appended final problems, despite the cover's ten-question instruction. Canonical 1–4 are supplement; 5–16 are final 1–12.

subject: linear algebra
title: A positive matrix has a positive square root
prompt: Prove every positive matrix is the square of a positive matrix.
hints: Use an orthonormal eigenbasis.
Take nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues.
solution:
Under the Hermitian positive convention, the spectral theorem gives \(A=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^*\), with all \(\lambda_j>0\) for positive definite \(A\), or \(\lambda_j\ge0\) for positive semidefinite \(A\). Define
\[
 B=U\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt{\lambda_1},\ldots,\sqrt{\lambda_n})U^*.
\]
It is Hermitian and has the corresponding positive or nonnegative eigenvalues, so it is positive in the same sense as \(A\). Multiplication gives \(B^2=A\). For real symmetric \(A\), \(U\) may be chosen real orthogonal, producing a real symmetric positive square root.
pitfall: Entrywise positive matrices are a different notion; the spectral argument uses Hermitian positivity.
note: Canonical 9 is appended final problem 5.

subject: linear algebra
title: The commutant of a simple-spectrum operator consists of polynomials
prompt: If \(T\) has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues on an \(n\)-dimensional space, prove every commuting operator \(S\) is a polynomial in \(T\).
hints: Each one-dimensional eigenspace is invariant under \(S\).
Interpolate \(S\)'s eigenvalues as a polynomial in those of \(T\).
solution:
The \(n\) eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\) form a basis. If \(ST=TS\), then for \(Tv_i=\lambda_iv_i\), \(T(Sv_i)=S(Tv_i)=\lambda_iSv_i\). Hence \(S\) preserves each one-dimensional eigenspace, so \(Sv_i=\mu_iv_i\).

The Lagrange interpolation polynomial
\[
 p(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n\mu_i
 \prod_{j\ne i}\frac{t-\lambda_j}{\lambda_i-\lambda_j}
\]
has degree at most \(n-1\) and satisfies \(p(\lambda_i)=\mu_i\). Thus \(p(T)v_i=\mu_iv_i=Sv_i\) on a basis, proving \(S=p(T)\). The eigenvalues must lie in the field over which this basis and polynomial are requested.
pitfall: A common eigenbasis makes the interpolation argument possible; distinct eigenvalues are doing more than proving commutation.
note: Canonical 10 is appended final problem 6.

subject: linear algebra
title: Range of the adjoint as a kernel complement
prompt:
On a finite-dimensional inner product space, prove 
\[
\operatorname{range}T^*=(\ker T)^\perp.
\]
hints: Use the defining adjoint identity for inclusion.
Then compare dimensions.
solution:
If \(u=T^*y\) and \(x\in\ker T\), then \(\langle x,u\rangle=\langle Tx,y\rangle=0\), so \(\operatorname{range}T^*\subset(\ker T)^\perp\).

Moreover \(y\in\ker T^*\) iff \(\langle Tx,y\rangle=0\) for every \(x\), so \(\ker T^*=(\operatorname{range}T)^\perp\). In finite dimension this implies
\[
 \operatorname{rank}T^*=\dim V-\dim\ker T^*
 =\dim\operatorname{range}T=\operatorname{rank}T.
\]
Rank--nullity then gives \(\dim(\ker T)^\perp=\operatorname{rank}T=\operatorname{rank}T^*\). Inclusion and equal dimensions establish the desired equality.
pitfall: The source has range of \(T\)-star; replacing it by range of \(T\) would be false for a general operator.
note: Canonical 11 is appended final problem 7.

subject: linear algebra
title: Orthogonality of distinct normal eigenvectors
prompt: If \(T\) is normal, prove eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
hints: A normal operator and its adjoint have matched conjugate eigenvectors.
Apply the adjoint identity to two eigenvectors.
solution:
For a normal operator, \(T-\lambda I\) is normal too, and its norm equality
\(\|(T-\lambda I)x\|=\|(T^*-\overline\lambda I)x\|\)
shows that \(Tv=\lambda v\) implies \(T^*v=\overline\lambda v\). Use the convention \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^*y\). If \(Tv=\lambda v\), \(Tw=\mu w\), then
\[
 \mu\langle v,w\rangle=\langle v,Tw\rangle
 =\langle T^*v,w\rangle
 =\lambda\langle v,w\rangle.
\]
For \(\lambda\ne\mu\), this forces \(\langle v,w\rangle=0\). Thus distinct eigenspaces are mutually orthogonal, without needing to assume diagonalizability beforehand.
pitfall: The conjugation from the adjoint eigenvalue is canceled by conjugate-linearity in the first argument.
note: Canonical 12 is appended final problem 8.

subject: linear algebra
title: The orthogonal complement of odd continuous functions
prompt:
In \(C([-2,2],\mathbb R)\) with 
\[
\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{-2}^2fg,
\]
 find the orthogonal complement of the subspace \(W\) of odd functions.
hints: Split a function into its even and odd parts.
Test a candidate orthogonal function against its own odd part.
solution:
Every even continuous function is orthogonal to every odd continuous function, because their product is odd and has integral zero on \([-2,2]\).

Conversely, suppose \(f\) belongs to \(W^\perp\). Decompose
\[
 f=f_e+f_o,\qquad f_e(t)=\frac{f(t)+f(-t)}2,\quad
 f_o(t)=\frac{f(t)-f(-t)}2.
\]
Both parts are continuous, and \(f_o\in W\). Therefore
\[
 0=\langle f,f_o\rangle=\langle f_e,f_o\rangle+\langle f_o,f_o\rangle
 =\int_{-2}^2f_o(t)^2\,dt.
\]
Continuity and nonnegativity imply \(f_o=0\), so \(f\) is even. Thus \(W^\perp\) is exactly the even continuous functions.
pitfall: This inner product space is not complete in its integral norm, but the explicit even–odd decomposition suffices.
note: Canonical 13 is appended final problem 9.

subject: linear algebra
title: An explicit commuting semisimple–nilpotent decomposition
prompt:
For 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1&-1\\2&2&-1\\2&2&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
 find in the standard basis a diagonalizable \(D\) and nilpotent \(N\) with \(A=D+N\) and \(DN=ND\).
hints: Its characteristic polynomial is \((t-1)(t-2)^2\).
Use the polynomial spectral projection onto eigenvalue one.
solution:
The characteristic polynomial is \((t-1)(t-2)^2\). Cayley--Hamilton gives \((A-I)(A-2I)^2=0\). Define
\[
 P=(A-2I)^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1&0\\0&0&0\\2&-2&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Direct multiplication gives \(P^2=P\). Set \(D=2I-P\) and \(N=A-D\), obtaining
\[
 D=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&2&0\\-2&2&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 N=\begin{pmatrix}2&0&-1\\2&0&-1\\4&0&-2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
An idempotent \(P\) is diagonalizable with eigenvalues zero and one, so \(D\) is diagonalizable with eigenvalues 2 and 1. Directly \(N^2=0\), proving nilpotence. Both \(D\) and \(N\) are polynomials in \(A\), so they commute. The displayed matrices sum to \(A\) and verify every requested property in the standard basis.
pitfall: The diagonalizable part is not required to be a diagonal matrix in the standard basis.
note: Canonical 14 is appended final problem 10.

subject: linear algebra
title: A block determinant with commuting blocks
prompt:
For pairwise commuting complex \(n\times n\) matrices \(A\),\(B\),\(C\),\(D\) and 
\[
E=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix},
\]
 prove \(\det E=\det(AD-BC)\).
hints: Construct a common invariant flag for all four matrices.
Interleave the two copies of that flag.
solution:
A commuting family of complex matrices can be simultaneously triangularized. To prove this, successively restrict to a nonzero eigenspace of each family member: commutation makes every such eigenspace invariant under the remaining members, so a common eigenvector exists. Quotient by its invariant line and induct on dimension to obtain a common invariant flag.
