Apply the same change of basis to all four blocks, producing upper triangular matrices with diagonals \(a_i,b_i,c_i,d_i\). This conjugates \(E\) and leaves its determinant unchanged. Interleave the two coordinate copies in the order first-coordinate-in-each-copy, then second-coordinate-in-each-copy, and so on. The resulting matrix is block upper triangular with diagonal blocks
\(\begin{pmatrix}a_i&b_i\\c_i&d_i\end{pmatrix}\).
Hence
\[
 \det E=\prod_i(a_id_i-b_ic_i).
\]
Meanwhile \(AD-BC\) is upper triangular with those same diagonal entries, so its determinant equals that product. This proof covers singular blocks without requiring any inverse.
pitfall: A Schur-complement proof that assumes \(A\) invertible needs an additional limiting argument for singular \(A\).
note: Canonical 15 is appended final problem 11.

subject: linear algebra
title: Power decay despite repeated eigenvalues
prompt: On a finite-dimensional complex space, prove \(T^mx\to0\) for every \(x\) iff every distinct eigenvalue has modulus less than one.
hints: Necessity follows from an eigenvector.
Jordan nilpotent parts add only fixed-degree polynomial factors.
solution:
If \(Tv=\lambda v\) with \(v\) nonzero and the powers kill every vector in the limit, then \(\lambda^mv=T^mv\to0\), so \(|\lambda|<1\).

Conversely, assume this bound for every eigenvalue and use Jordan form. On a size-\(r\) block \(J=\lambda I+N\), \(N^r=0\), for sufficiently large \(m\),
\[
 J^m=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\binom mj\lambda^{m-j}N^j.
\]
For nonzero \(\lambda\) each coefficient tends to zero, since \(\binom mj\) grows polynomially and \(|\lambda|^m\) decays geometrically. When \(\lambda\) is zero the block is nilpotent and its powers eventually vanish. Thus every block tends to zero. Conjugating by a fixed basis change preserves convergence, so \(T^m\to0\) and hence \(T^mx\to0\) for all \(x\).
pitfall: The list of distinct eigenvalues need not have length \(n\), and \(T\) need not be diagonalizable.
note: Canonical 16 is appended final problem 12.

subject: analysis
title: Summable increments imply convergence
prompt: If \(x_n\in\mathbb R^m\) and \(|x_{n+1}-x_n|\le\frac{1}{n^2+n}\), prove convergence.
hints: Bound the distance between two late terms by a telescoping sum.
Use completeness.
solution:
For \(k>n\), the triangle inequality and \(1/(j(j+1))=1/j-1/(j+1)\) give
\[
 |x_k-x_n|\le\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}|x_{j+1}-x_j|
 \le\sum_{j=n}^{k-1}\left(\frac1j-\frac1{j+1}\right)
 =\frac1n-\frac1k\le\frac1n.
\]
Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose \(N\) with \(1/N<\epsilon\). Any \(k\),\(n\) at least \(N\) then have distance less than \(\epsilon\). Thus the sequence is Cauchy, and completeness of \(\mathbb R^m\) implies it converges.
pitfall: Small increments alone do not suffice; their summability supplies the Cauchy bound.

subject: analysis
title: A triangular local inverse
prompt: For \(f\in C^1(\mathbb R)\), set \(g(x,y)=(f(x),xf(x)-y)\). (a) Show local invertibility at \((x_0,y_0)\) when \(f'(x_0)\ne0\). (b) Find the inverse.
hints: Compute the Jacobian determinant.
Recover \(x\) from the first output coordinate, then \(y\).
solution:
(a) The derivative is
\[
 Dg(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}f'(x)&0\\f(x)+xf'(x)&-1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad\det Dg(x,y)=-f'(x).
\]
At \((x_0,y_0)\) this is nonzero, and \(g\) is \(C^1\), so the inverse function theorem provides a local \(C^1\) inverse.

(b) Let \(h\) be the local inverse branch of \(f\) near \(x_0\). If \((u,v)=g(x,y)\), then \(x=h(u)\) and \(y=xu-v\). Therefore
\[
 g^{-1}(u,v)=(h(u),u h(u)-v)
\]
on the corresponding neighborhood. Substitution verifies both inverse identities. No global inverse follows merely from \(f'(x_0)\ne0\); for example \(f(x)=x^2\) has such points but is globally noninjective.
pitfall: Use the correct local branch of the scalar inverse.

subject: analysis
title: Closed ranges, boundedness, and nonuniform convergence
prompt: Prove or refute: (a) the set of terms of a convergent real sequence is closed; (b) a uniformly continuous function on \((0,1)\) is bounded; (c) continuous functions converging pointwise on a compact set to a continuous limit converge uniformly.
hints: A sequence's limit need not be one of its terms.
For (c) use peaks that move toward zero.
solution:
(a) False. The sequence \(1/n\) converges to zero, but its set of terms does not contain zero and is not closed. Adding the limit would make the set closed.

(b) True. Choose \(\delta>0\) so \(|f(x)-f(y)|<1\) whenever \(|x-y|<\delta\). Choose finitely many points in \((0,1)\) whose \(\delta\)-balls cover \((0,1)\). Each \(x\) is within \(\delta\) of one of them, so \(|f(x)|\le1+\max_j|f(x_j)|\). Hence \(f\) is bounded.

(c) False. On \([0,1]\) let \(f_n(x)=\max\{1-|nx-2|,0\}\) for \(n\ge3\). These continuous triangular peaks have height one at \(2/n\) and support contained in \([1/n,3/n]\). For each fixed \(x\) they eventually vanish, including \(x=0\). Thus the pointwise limit is the continuous zero function, but \(\sup_x|f_n(x)|=1\) for every \(n\).
pitfall: Dini's theorem needs monotonicity in addition to compactness and a continuous limit.

subject: analysis
title: An everywhere-convergent integrated exponential series
prompt:
For 
\[
f(x)=\int_0^{x^2}e^{-\frac{t^2}{2}}\,dt,
\]
 find its power series for all real \(x\) and its first two nonzero coefficients.
hints: Expand the exponential on bounded \(t\)-intervals.
Integrate each term and then substitute \(x^2\).
solution:
The exponential series gives
\[
 e^{-t^2/2}=\sum_{j=0}^\infty\frac{(-1)^jt^{2j}}{2^jj!}.
\]
On every bounded \(t\)-interval this converges absolutely and uniformly by the \(M\)-test. Thus integration term by term is valid:
\[
 f(x)=\sum_{j=0}^\infty
 \frac{(-1)^j x^{4j+2}}{2^jj!(2j+1)}
 =x^2-\frac{x^6}{6}+\frac{x^{10}}{40}-\cdots.
\]
For each fixed real \(x\) the required \(t\)-interval is bounded, so this represents \(f\) for every \(x\). The ratio test also gives infinite radius of convergence for this \(x\)-series. The first nonzero coefficients are \(a_2=1\) and \(a_6=-1/6\).
pitfall: The upper endpoint is \(x^2\), so the exponents are 4j+2.

subject: analysis
title: Continuous persistence of a simple polynomial root
prompt: A monic real polynomial has a simple real root \(x_0\). Show sufficiently small changes of its lower coefficients preserve a real root that depends continuously on those coefficients.
hints: Treat the coefficients as parameters.
Differentiate the polynomial equation with respect to the root variable.
solution:
Write \(a=(a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1})\) and
\[
 F(x,a)=x^N+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}a_jx^j.
\]
This function is smooth in all its real variables. At the original coefficient vector \(\bar a\), \(F(x_0,\bar a)=0\), and simplicity means \(\partial_xF(x_0,\bar a)=p'(x_0)\ne0\). The implicit function theorem therefore supplies a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar a\) and a \(C^1\), hence continuous, real function \(\phi:U\to\mathbb R\) with \(\phi(\bar a)=x_0\) and \(F(\phi(a),a)=0\). In particular all sufficiently small coefficient perturbations have this root. The theorem also gives uniqueness within a fixed small neighborhood of \(x_0\).
pitfall: A multiple root need not persist as a real root under perturbation.

subject: analysis
title: A logarithmic integral with two regimes
prompt:
For \(0<\alpha\le1\), evaluate 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1n\log(1+(\frac{x}{n})^\alpha)\,dx.
\]
hints: Compare the logarithm to its argument for small nonnegative inputs.
Distinguish \(\alpha\) equal to one from \(\alpha\) less than one.
solution:
For \(0\le u\le1\), \(u/2\le\log(1+u)\le u\). With \(u=(x/n)^\alpha\), integration gives
\[
 \frac{n^{1-\alpha}}{2(\alpha+1)}
 \le\int_0^1n\log(1+(x/n)^\alpha)\,dx
 \le\frac{n^{1-\alpha}}{\alpha+1}.
\]
For \(0<\alpha<1\) the lower bound tends to \(+\infty\), so the requested limit is \(+\infty\). For \(\alpha=1\), the sharper estimate \(0\le u-\log(1+u)\le u^2/2\) gives
\[
 0\le x-n\log(1+x/n)\le x^2/(2n).
\]
This is uniform on \([0,1]\), so the integral tends to \(\int_0^1x\,dx=1/2\).
pitfall: The prefactor \(n\) does not balance \(n\) to the power \(\alpha\) unless \(\alpha\) equals one.

subject: analysis
title: Positive attained distance to a compact set
prompt: For compact A in a metric space and \(y\notin A\), prove \(\inf_{x\in A}d(x,y)=d(x^*,y)>0\) for some \(x^*\in A\).
hints: The distance function is continuous.
A zero attained distance would put \(y\) in \(A\).
solution: Assume \(A\) is nonempty, as required for an attaining point. The triangle inequality gives \(|d(x,y)-d(z,y)|\le d(x,z)\), so \(x\mapsto d(x,y)\) is continuous on \(A\). It attains a minimum at some \(x^*\in A\) by compactness. If this minimum were zero, definiteness of the metric would imply \(x^*=y\), contradicting \(y\notin A\). Thus the attained infimum is strictly positive. For empty \(A\) the assertion of such an \(x^*\) is false, so that case must be excluded.
pitfall: Closedness alone does not guarantee attainment in a general metric space.
note: Nonempty \(A\) is necessary. April supplement problems 1–4 are canonical 1–4; appended final problems 1–6 are canonical 5–10.

subject: analysis
title: Monotone convergence and a summably small subsequence
prompt: (a) If \(x_n\le y_n\), \(x_n\le x_{n+1}\), and \(y_{n+1}\le y_n\), prove \(x_n\) converges. (b) If \(a_n\ge0\) and \(a_n\to0\), find a subsequence with sum less than any prescribed \(\epsilon>0\).
hints: For (a) use the first upper bound.
For (b) prescribe geometric upper bounds.
solution:
(a) The sequence \(x_n\) is increasing and satisfies \(x_n\le y_n\le y_1\). Hence it is bounded above and converges by monotone convergence; its limit is \(\sup_n x_n\). No assertion that the two sequences have the same limit is needed.

(b) Recursively choose indices \(n_k>n_{k-1}\) so that \(a_{n_k}<\epsilon\,2^{-k-1}\), possible because \(a_n\to0\). With \(b_k=a_{n_k}\),
\[
 0\le\sum_{k=1}^\infty b_k
 \le\sum_{k=1}^\infty\epsilon\,2^{-k-1}
 =\epsilon/2<\epsilon.
\]
The indices are strictly increasing, so this is a genuine subsequence.
pitfall: Convergence to zero does not make the original series summable; selecting a sparse subsequence does.
note: April supplement problem 2.

subject: analysis
title: Continuity of an exponentially weighted parameter series
prompt:
Prove 
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{n^x}{2^n}
\]
 is continuous on \(\mathbb R\).
hints: Work on a bounded \(x\)-interval.
Exponential decay dominates any fixed polynomial power.
solution: Fix \(R>0\). For \(|x|\le R\) and \(n\ge1\), \(0<n^x/2^n\le n^R/2^n\). The majorant series converges, since the ratio of successive terms tends to \(1/2<1\). The \(M\)-test therefore yields uniform convergence on [-\(R\),\(R\)]. Each term \(n^x/2^n=\exp(x\log n)/2^n\) is continuous in \(x\), so the sum is continuous on this interval. Since \(R\) is arbitrary, \(f\) is continuous at every real \(x\). Uniform convergence on all of \(\mathbb R\) is neither required nor true for this argument.
pitfall: Local uniform convergence is sufficient for continuity on the whole real line.
note: April supplement problem 3.

subject: analysis
title: Compactness of primitives and a weighted geometric sum
prompt:
(a) For uniformly bounded integrable \(f_n\) on \([a,b]\), show 
\[
F_n(x)=\int_a^xf_n(t)\,dt
\]
 has a uniformly convergent subsequence. (b) Evaluate 
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{n+1}{2^n}.
\]
hints: The primitives have a common Lipschitz bound.
Differentiate the geometric series inside its radius.
solution:
(a) Let \(|f_n|\le M\). Then \(|F_n(x)|\le M(b-a)\), and
\[
 |F_n(x)-F_n(y)|\le M|x-y|.
\]
Thus the continuous functions \(F_n\) are uniformly bounded and equicontinuous on the compact interval. Arzela--Ascoli gives a subsequence converging uniformly there to a continuous function.

(b) For \(|r|<1\), termwise differentiation of \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty r^{n+1}=r/(1-r)\) gives
\[
 \sum_{n=0}^\infty(n+1)r^n=\frac1{(1-r)^2}.
\]
At \(r=1/2\) the sum is 4.
pitfall: The integrands themselves need not be continuous or equicontinuous; integration supplies the needed regularity.
note: April supplement problem 4.

subject: analysis
title: Local inverse derivatives and quadratic perturbations
prompt: For \(f(x,y)=(\sin(x+y),x-y+e^{xy})\): (a) prove local invertibility near zero; (b) compute \(Df^{-1}(0,1)\); (c) if \(\|g(x,y)\|\le M\|(x,y)\|^2\), prove \(D(f+g)(0,0)=Df(0,0)\).
hints: Evaluate the Jacobian at the preimage of \((0,1)\).
The perturbation has derivative zero at the origin.
solution:
(a) We have \(f(0,0)=(0,1)\) and
\[
 Df(0,0)=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \det Df(0,0)=-2.
\]
The map is smooth, so the inverse function theorem gives a local smooth inverse.

(b) Differentiate the inverse identity:
\[
 Df^{-1}(0,1)=Df(0,0)^{-1}
 =\frac12\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

(c) The bound forces \(g(0)=0\), and for \(z\) tending to zero,
\[
 \frac{\|g(z)-g(0)-0z\|}{\|z\|}\le M\|z\|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus \(g\) is differentiable at zero with derivative zero, even if no other regularity of \(g\) is known. Adding derivatives gives \(D(f+g)(0)=Df(0)\).
pitfall: Part (c) proves differentiability at the origin; it does not assert a continuously differentiable perturbation nearby.
note: Canonical 5 is the appended final problem 1.

subject: analysis
title: A constrained maximum and the missing endpoint condition
prompt: If \(f,g\in C^1(\mathbb R^2)\), a curve \(S\) lies in \(g=c\), and \(g_y\ne0\) on \(S\), derive the relation between \(f_x,f_y,g_x,g_y\) at a maximum of \(f\) on \(S\).
hints: Write the level set locally as a graph.
Check that the maximum is interior on a two-sided curve arc.
solution:
At a point \((x_0,y_0)\) with \(g_y\ne0\), the implicit function theorem expresses the level set locally as \(y=\phi(x)\), with
\[
 \phi'(x_0)=-g_x(x_0,y_0)/g_y(x_0,y_0).
\]
If \(S\) contains this arc on both sides of \(x_0\), a maximum of \(f\) on \(S\) implies the differentiable function \(x\mapsto f(x,\phi(x))\) has derivative zero. The chain rule gives
\[
 0=f_x+f_y\phi',\qquad f_x=\frac{f_y g_x}{g_y}
\]
at the maximizing point.

As literally stated for an arbitrary curve \(S\), an endpoint maximum need not satisfy this relation. For example, \(S=\{(x,0):-1\le x\le0\}\), \(g(x,y)=y\), and \(f(x,y)=x\). The maximum is at \((0,0)\), with \(g_y=1\), but the proposed relation would say \(1=0\). The conclusion requires an interior point of a regular two-sided level arc, or the corresponding no-boundary convention for \(S\).
pitfall: A constrained endpoint maximum does not force vanishing tangential derivative.
note: SOURCE QUALIFICATION: the maximum must be interior along a two-sided regular level arc. Canonical 6 is appended final problem 2.

subject: analysis
title: A boundary-layer limit and reversed integration order
prompt:
Evaluate (a) 
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1\frac{1+x}{1+e^{-nx}}\,dx;
\]
 (b) 
\[
\int_0^9\int_{\sqrt y}^3\cos(x^3)\,dx\,dy.
\]
hints: For (a) bound the error from \(1+x\) directly.
For (b) describe the region using \(x\) first.
solution:
(a) The difference from \(1+x\) is nonnegative and bounded by \(2e^{-nx}\):
\[
 0\le (1+x)-\frac{1+x}{1+e^{-nx}}
 =\frac{(1+x)e^{-nx}}{1+e^{-nx}}\le2e^{-nx}.
\]
Its integral is at most \(2(1-e^{-n})/n\to0\). Therefore the limit is \(\int_0^1(1+x)\,dx=3/2\). This avoids needing uniform convergence at the endpoint zero.

(b) The region is \(0\le x\le3,\ 0\le y\le x^2\). Continuity allows reversing the order:
\[
 \int_0^3\int_0^{x^2}\cos(x^3)\,dy\,dx
 =\int_0^3x^2\cos(x^3)\,dx
 =\frac13\sin27.
\]
pitfall: The original inner integral has no convenient elementary antiderivative; changing order introduces exactly the needed factor.
note: Canonical 7 is the appended final problem 3.

subject: analysis
title: The tail Cauchy property of an improper integral
prompt:
If \(f\) is locally Riemann integrable on \([a,\infty)\) and its improper integral is finite, prove that sufficiently late 
\[
\left|\int_{t_1}^{t_2}f\right|
\]
 is less than any prescribed \(\varepsilon\).
hints: Use the convergence of the primitive at infinity.
Write a tail interval as a difference of two primitive values.
solution:
Let \(F(t)=\int_a^tf(x)\,dx\), and let \(L=\lim_{t\to\infty}F(t)\), which exists and is finite by hypothesis. Given \(\epsilon>0\), choose \(T>\max\{a,0\}\) so that \(|F(t)-L|<\epsilon/2\) for all \(t\ge T\). For any \(t_1,t_2\ge T\), additivity of the integral, with the usual signed-interval convention, gives
\[
 \left|\int_{t_1}^{t_2}f(x)\,dx\right|
 =|F(t_2)-F(t_1)|
 \le|F(t_2)-L|+|F(t_1)-L|<\epsilon.
\]
No absolute convergence is required.
pitfall: A finite improper integral can be conditionally convergent; the assertion bounds signed tails.
note: Canonical 8 is the appended final problem 4.

subject: analysis
title: Zero ball averages and a harmonicity criterion
prompt:
Let \(u\in C^2(V)\), with \(V\) open, nonempty and bounded in \(\mathbb R^2\). (a) If its integral over every ball contained in \(V\) is zero, prove \(u=0\). (b) Prove \(\Delta u=0\) iff 
\[
\oint_{\partial E}(u_x\,dy-u_y\,dx)=0
\]
 for all appropriate regions \(E\) in \(V\) with piecewise smooth boundary.
hints: Continuity prevents a nonzero function from having zero integrals over all small balls.
Apply Green's theorem to the one-form.
solution:
(a) Suppose \(u(p)>0\) at some \(p\). Continuity and openness give a small ball \(B_\delta(p)\subset V\) on which \(u\ge u(p)/2>0\), so its integral is positive, a contradiction. The same argument applied to -\(u\) rules out \(u(p)<0\). Thus \(u\) vanishes everywhere.

(b) Take bounded regions with \(\overline E\subset V\) and positively oriented piecewise smooth boundary, including the appropriate opposite orientations on hole boundaries. Green's theorem gives
\[
 \oint_{\partial E}(u_x\,dy-u_y\,dx)
 =\iint_E(u_{xx}+u_{yy})\,dx\,dy.
\]
If \(u\) is harmonic the right side is zero. Conversely, the hypothesized zero boundary integrals give zero integrals of the continuous function \(\Delta u\) over every sufficiently small closed-inside-\(V\) disk. Part (a)'s sign argument applied to \(\Delta u\) gives \(\Delta u=0\).

The boundary must lie where the derivatives are defined; the natural test regions are compactly contained in \(V\). Merely saying \(E\subset V\) permits a boundary outside \(V\) and an undefined integral.
pitfall: Boundary orientation and the availability of derivatives on the boundary are part of Green's hypotheses.
note: The test-region closure is taken inside \(V\) so boundary derivatives exist. Canonical 9 is appended final problem 5.

subject: analysis
title: Ellipse orientations and circulation by Stokes
prompt:
Let \(R\) be bounded by \(x^2-y^2+2z^2=4\), \(y=2\) and \(y=0\). (a) Positively orient and parametrize the intersection ellipses \(C_1\) at \(y=2\) and \(C_2\) at \(y=0\) relative to the outward normals of \(R\). (b) Evaluate 
\[
\oint_{C_1}F\cdot T\,ds,
\]
 where \(F=(xe^y,x+e^y,y(x+\cos z))\).
hints: The outward normals of the two caps point in opposite directions.
Use the planar top disk for Stokes' theorem.
solution:
The bounded region is \(0\le y\le2,\ x^2+2z^2\le4+y^2\). Its top and bottom cap normals are respectively \(+e_y\) and \(-e_y\). Positively oriented parametrizations, for \(0\le t\le2\pi\), are
\[
 C_1(t)=(2\sqrt2\cos t,\,2,\,-2\sin t),\qquad
 C_2(t)=(2\cos t,\,0,\,\sqrt2\sin t).
\]
For instance the top disk coordinates in the +\(x\) and -\(z\) directions have cross product +\(y\), verifying its orientation.

The curl is
\[
 \nabla\times F=(x+\cos z,\,-y,\,1-xe^y).
\]
Use the top elliptical disk \(D\) with normal \(+e_y\). Its area is \(\pi(2\sqrt2)(2)=4\sqrt2\pi\), and the curl's normal component on \(y=2\) is -2. Stokes' theorem gives
\[
 \oint_{C_1}F\cdot T\,ds=\iint_D(-2)\,dS=-8\sqrt2\pi.
\]
Direct parametrization gives the same sign: the non-exact surviving term is \(2x\,dz\), whose integral with the top parametrization is \(-8\sqrt2\pi\).
pitfall: Viewing an ellipse in the xz-plane can reverse orientation: +\(x\) crossed with +\(z\) points toward -\(y\).
note: Canonical 10 is the appended final problem 6.

subject: linear algebra
title: Riesz representation from an orthonormal basis
prompt: Prove from first principles that every linear functional \(\ell\) on a finite-dimensional inner product space is uniquely \(\ell(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\).
hints: Specify the complex inner-product convention.
Choose the coordinates of \(y\) in an orthonormal basis.
solution:
Use the convention that the inner product is linear in its first argument. In an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), define
\[
 y=\sum_{j=1}^m\overline{\ell(e_j)}e_j.
\]
For \(x=\sum_jx_je_j\), we obtain \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_jx_j\ell(e_j)=\ell(x)\). Over the real field the conjugation is omitted. If \(y\) and \(z\) both represent the functional, then \(\langle x,y-z\rangle=0\) for every \(x\). Taking \(x=y-z\) shows \(\|y-z\|^2=0\), proving uniqueness. This also covers the zero-dimensional space by empty sums.
pitfall: For a complex space, the conjugation depends on which argument is linear.

subject: linear algebra
title: Kernel containment forces proportional functionals
prompt: (A) If \(f(\alpha)\ne0\), write every \(\beta=c\alpha+\gamma\) with \(f(\gamma)=0\). (B) If \(\ker f\subset\ker g\), prove \(g\) is a scalar multiple of \(f\).
hints: Apply \(f\) to identify \(c\).
Treat the zero functional separately.
solution:
(A) Set \(c=f(\beta)/f(\alpha)\) and \(\gamma=\beta-c\alpha\). Then \(f(\gamma)=f(\beta)-cf(\alpha)=0\), as desired.

(B) If \(f\) is zero, its kernel is all of \(V\), so the assumed containment gives \(g=0\), which is a scalar multiple of \(f\). Otherwise select \(\alpha\) with \(f(\alpha)\ne0\). Apply (A) to any \(\beta\). Since \(g(\gamma)=0\),
\[
 g(\beta)=cg(\alpha)=\frac{g(\alpha)}{f(\alpha)}\,f(\beta).
\]
The scalar is independent of \(\beta\), proving proportionality. Neither argument actually requires finite dimension.
pitfall: Do not divide by a functional value until the nonzero-functional case has been established.

subject: linear algebra
title: Five claims about orthogonality, projections, and powers
prompt: Decide: (a) a complex orthogonal matrix is unitary; (b) every projection is diagonalizable; (c) the inverse of an invertible normal matrix is normal; (d) unit-circle eigenvalues imply bounded powers; (e) a real symmetric matrix has a minimal polynomial with distinct linear factors.
hints: Complex orthogonality uses transpose, whereas unitarity uses adjoint.
A Jordan block on the unit circle can grow polynomially.
solution:
(a) False when orthogonal means \(A^TA=I\) over \(\mathbb C\). Take
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}5/3&4i/3\\-4i/3&5/3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Direct multiplication gives \(A^TA=I\), but the squared Hermitian norm of its first column is \(41/9\ne1\), so \(A^*A\ne I\).

(b) True for a projection \(P^2=P\). Every \(x\) splits as \(Px+(x-Px)\), in the range and kernel respectively, whose intersection is zero. Their bases diagonalize \(P\) with eigenvalues 1 and 0.

(c) True. Unitary diagonalization \(A=UDU^*\) for a normal invertible \(A\) gives \(A^{-1}=UD^{-1}U^*\), again normal.

(d) False. \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) has only eigenvalue 1, but \(A^k=\begin{pmatrix}1&k\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is unbounded.

(e) True. Orthogonal diagonalization of a real symmetric matrix shows that its minimal polynomial is the product of \(t-\lambda\) over its distinct real eigenvalues, each occurring once.
pitfall: Projection means an idempotent here and need not be orthogonal; it is still diagonalizable.

subject: linear algebra
title: Positive definiteness and the zero-vector qualification
prompt: For real symmetric \(A\), prove \(x^TAx>0\) for all \(x\) iff every eigenvalue is positive.
hints: The literal phrase for all \(x\) includes zero.
Prove the standard version using an eigenbasis.
solution:
The intended quantifier is every nonzero \(x\); at \(x=0\) the quadratic form is always zero. For the corrected assertion, if \(A\) is positive definite and \(Av=\lambda v\), with \(v\ne0\), then \(0<v^TAv=\lambda\|v\|^2\), forcing \(\lambda>0\). Conversely, the spectral theorem gives \(A=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_j)Q^T\), so
\[
 x^TAx=\sum_j\lambda_j(Q^Tx)_j^2>0
\]
for nonzero \(x\) when all \(\lambda_j>0\). The literal all-\(x\) claim is false even for \(A=I\); the standard nonzero-vector version is proved above.
pitfall: Strict positivity of a quadratic form always excludes the zero vector.
note: SOURCE QUALIFICATION: replace 'for all \(x'\) by 'for all nonzero \(x'\).

subject: linear algebra
title: Trace and determinant count algebraic multiplicities
prompt: Prove the trace of a complex matrix is the sum of its eigenvalues, and its determinant their product.
hints: Triangularize by similarity.
Keep algebraic multiplicities in both lists.
solution:
Over \(\mathbb C\), \(A\) is similar to an upper triangular matrix \(T\), for instance by Schur triangularization. Its characteristic polynomial is \(\prod_{j=1}^n(t-t_{jj})\); hence its diagonal entries are exactly the eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\), with algebraic multiplicity. Trace is invariant under similarity by \(\operatorname{tr}(XY)=\operatorname{tr}(YX)\), and determinant is invariant by multiplicativity. Therefore
\[
 \operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}T=\sum_j\lambda_j,\qquad
 \det A=\det T=\prod_j\lambda_j.
\]
Diagonalizability is not needed.
pitfall: A defective eigenvalue is counted according to its algebraic multiplicity, not its eigenspace dimension.

subject: linear algebra
title: A real block for a conjugate eigenpair
prompt:
(A) If a real matrix has eigenvector \(u+iv\) for \(\alpha+i\beta\), \(\beta\ne0\), prove \(u\),\(v\) are independent. (B) In dimension two find \(P\) giving block 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\-\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}.
\]
 (C) Do so for 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&-4\\2&5\end{pmatrix}.
\]
hints: Equate real and imaginary parts.
Use \(u\) and \(v\) as the columns of \(P\).
solution:
The eigenvector equation gives
\[
 Au=\alpha u-\beta v,\qquad Av=\beta u+\alpha v.
\]
If \(u\) and \(v\) were dependent, there would be a nonzero real vector \(w\) and real scalars a,\(b\), not both zero, such that \(u=aw,v=bw\). Then \(u+iv=(a+ib)w\), and cancelling its nonzero scalar would give \(Aw=(\alpha+i\beta)w\), impossible because Aw is real and \(\beta w\ne0\). Thus \(u\),\(v\) are independent.

In dimension two \(P=[u\ v]\) is invertible, and the displayed equations give the required block \(P^{-1}AP=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\\-\beta&\alpha\end{pmatrix}\).

For the example, the characteristic polynomial is \(t^2-6t+13\), with roots \(3\pm2i\). For \(3+2i\) take the eigenvector \((2,-1-i)^T\). Thus
\[
 P=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 P^{-1}AP=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\-2&3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
pitfall: The sign in the real block depends on whether the second basis vector is \(v\) or -\(v\).

subject: linear algebra
title: Row-stochastic products and a missing entry condition
prompt: For nonnegative real matrices with every row sum one, prove products have the same property. Analyze the assertion that \(A\) is stochastic iff \(Ae=e\), where \(e\) is the all-ones vector.
hints: The vector equation states only the row sums.
Check positivity separately.
solution:
If \(A\) and \(B\) are row-stochastic, every product entry \((AB)_{ij}=\sum_ka_{ik}b_{kj}\) is nonnegative. Also \(Ae=e\) and \(Be=e\), so \(ABe=Ae=e\); the product has row sums one.

For a matrix already assumed entrywise nonnegative, \(Ae=e\) is exactly the row-sum requirement and is equivalent to being stochastic. For an arbitrary real matrix it is insufficient: \(\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}e=e\), but the negative entry prevents stochasticity. Thus the printed equivalence must retain the nonnegative-entry assumption.
pitfall: A linear equation for row sums cannot enforce entrywise nonnegativity.
note: SOURCE QUALIFICATION: \(Ae=e\) characterizes row-stochastic matrices only among entrywise nonnegative matrices.

subject: linear algebra
title: A scalar matrix plus an all-ones matrix
prompt: For \(A\) with diagonal \(x+y\) and off-diagonal \(x\), prove \(\det A=y^{n-1}(nx+y)\), and find its inverse when it exists.
hints: Write \(A=yI+xJ\), with \(J^2\) equal to nJ.
Separate the all-ones direction from its complement.
solution:
Over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\), let \(J\) be the all-ones matrix. On \(\operatorname{span}\{e\}\), \(J\) acts as \(n\); on the subspace of coordinate sum zero it acts as zero. Thus \(A=yI+xJ\) has eigenvalues \(y+nx\) once and \(y\) with multiplicity \(n-1\). Consequently
\[
 \det A=y^{n-1}(y+nx).
\]
For \(n\ge2\), invertibility is equivalent to \(y\ne0\) and \(y+nx\ne0\). Using \(J^2=nJ\), multiplication verifies
\[
 A^{-1}=\frac1yI-\frac{x}{y(y+nx)}J.
\]
It has the requested same form, with diagonal \(1/y-x/[y(y+nx)]\) and off-diagonal \(-x/[y(y+nx)]\).

For \(n=1\), \(A\) is simply [\(x+y\)], and its inverse is [1/(\(x+y\))] whenever \(x+y\ne0\), including \(y=0\). The determinant formula remains valid with the factor \(y^0\) understood as 1.
pitfall: The usual inverse formula divides by \(y\) and therefore needs a separate one-dimensional case.

subject: linear algebra
title: An inner product induced by a positive matrix
prompt: For a positive definite complex matrix \(A\), (a) prove its diagonal entries are real and positive; (b) show \((x,y)_A=(x,Ay)\) defines an inner product.
hints: Use the standard basis to read the diagonal.
Hermitian symmetry of A supplies conjugate symmetry.
solution:
Use positive definite in the standard Hermitian sense and the base inner product \((x,y)=x^*y\), conjugate-linear in its first argument. Then \(A=A^*\) and \(x^*Ax>0\) for nonzero \(x\).

(a) \(a_{ii}=e_i^*Ae_i>0\), so each diagonal entry is real and strictly positive.

(b) The form \((x,y)_A=x^*Ay\) is conjugate-linear in \(x\) and linear in \(y\). Also
\[
 \overline{(y,x)_A}=\overline{y^*Ax}=x^*A^*y=x^*Ay=(x,y)_A.
\]
Finally \((x,x)_A=x^*Ax>0\) for nonzero \(x\). These are exactly the inner-product axioms. With the alternative convention linear in the first argument, the stated formula works equally well after the corresponding conjugations.
pitfall: Positive definite for complex matrices includes Hermitian symmetry.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: The Hermitian part controls real parts of eigenvalues
prompt:
(a) If \(A+A^*\) is positive definite, prove every eigenvalue of \(A\) has positive real part. (b) Apply this to 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}2&-9&2\\10&1&-5\\1&4&3\end{pmatrix}
\]
 without computing eigenvalues.
hints: Evaluate A plus its adjoint on an eigenvector.
Check principal minors of the real symmetric sum.
solution:
(a) If \(Av=\lambda v\) and \(v\ne0\), then
\[
 v^*(A+A^*)v=2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda)\|v\|^2>0.
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda>0\).

(b) For the displayed real matrix,
\[
 A+A^T=\begin{pmatrix}4&1&3\\1&2&-1\\3&-1&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its leading principal minors are 4, 7, and 14, all positive. Sylvester's criterion therefore proves it is positive definite, and (a) proves all eigenvalues of A have positive real parts. In particular none is zero.
pitfall: \(A\) need not be Hermitian; its Hermitian part is the positive definite matrix.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Exponential of a triangular matrix with a Jordan coupling
prompt:
Find \(e^{tA}\) for 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\0&1&1\\0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
hints: Solve the upper triangular matrix differential equation.
The repeated eigenvalue introduces factors of \(t\).
solution:
Let \(E(t)=e^{tA}\). It is the unique solution of \(E'=AE,\ E(0)=I\). Triangularity gives diagonal entries \(e^t,e^t,e^{-t}\). For the entry \(v=E_{23}\), \(v'=v+e^{-t}\), \(v(0)=0\), so \(v=(e^t-e^{-t})/2\). The entry \(E_{12}\) is \(te^t\). For \(u=E_{13}\),
\[
 u'=u+v+e^{-t},\qquad
 (e^{-t}u)'=\tfrac12+\tfrac12e^{-2t}.
\]
Integrating from zero gives \(u=\tfrac12te^t+\tfrac14(e^t-e^{-t})\). Therefore
\[
 e^{tA}=\begin{pmatrix}
 e^t&te^t&\tfrac12te^t+\tfrac14(e^t-e^{-t})\\
 0&e^t&\tfrac12(e^t-e^{-t})\\
 0&0&e^{-t}
 \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The displayed formula has value \(I\) at zero and differentiation verifies \(E'=AE\).
pitfall: The \((1,3)\) entry receives both direct and indirect contributions.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Skew-Hermitian spectral properties
prompt: If \(A^*=-A\), prove its eigenvalues have zero real parts and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are orthogonal.
hints: The quadratic form is purely imaginary.
Use the adjoint equation between two eigenvectors.
solution:
If \(Av=\lambda v\), then \(\overline{v^*Av}=v^*A^*v=-v^*Av\), so \(v^*Av=\lambda\|v\|^2\) is purely imaginary. Hence \(\operatorname{Re}\lambda=0\).

Let \(Av=\lambda v\), \(Aw=\mu w\). Since \(A^*=-A\),
\[
 v^*Aw=\mu v^*w,\qquad
 v^*Aw=-(Av)^*w=-\overline\lambda v^*w=\lambda v^*w.
\]
Thus \((\mu-\lambda)v^*w=0\); for distinct eigenvalues this forces \(v^*w=0\). This is orthogonality in the Hermitian inner product.
pitfall: Conjugation in the adjoint identity is essential for the orthogonality argument.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Derivative of a simple eigenvalue
prompt:
For a real matrix \(A\) and a simple eigenvalue \(\lambda\) with \(Av=\lambda v\), \(A^Tw=\lambda w\), prove 
\[
\frac{\partial\lambda}{\partial a_{ij}}=\frac{w_iv_j}{w^Tv},
\]
 using differentiable local eigenvectors.
hints: Differentiate the right eigenvector equation.
Multiply by the left eigenvector to cancel the derivative of \(v\).
solution:
Simplicity means algebraic multiplicity one; local eigenvalue and eigenvector branches are differentiable as granted. First \(w^Tv\ne0\). Indeed \(\operatorname{range}(A-\lambda I)=\ker w^T\): both have dimension \(n-1\), and inclusion follows from the left eigenvector equation. If \(w^Tv=0\), then \(v=(A-\lambda I)z\) for some \(z\), producing a length-two Jordan chain and contradicting simplicity.

Differentiate \(Av=\lambda v\) in the real parameter \(a_{ij}\). Since \(\partial A/\partial a_{ij}=E_{ij}\),
\[
 E_{ij}v+A v'=\lambda'v+\lambda v'.
\]
Multiplying on the left by \(w^T\) cancels the two terms containing \(v'\), giving
\(\lambda'w^Tv=w^TE_{ij}v=w_iv_j\).
Division proves the formula. It is invariant under nonzero rescalings of \(v\) and \(w\). Complex simple eigenvalues of a real matrix use the same bilinear transpose identity with complex \(v\),\(w\).
pitfall: A merely geometrically simple eigenvalue can have zero left-right pairing; algebraic simplicity is needed.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: A reciprocal Rayleigh quotient maximum
prompt:
For positive definite A prove 
\[
\lambda_{\max}(A)=\max_{x^*Ax=1}\frac{1}{x^*x}.
\]
hints: Bound the quadratic form by the top eigenvalue.
Scale a unit top eigenvector.
solution: By the Hermitian spectral theorem, \(x^*Ax\le\lambda_{\max}\|x\|^2\). On the constraint \(x^*Ax=1\), \(x\) is nonzero, and this yields \(1/\|x\|^2\le\lambda_{\max}\). If \(u\) is a unit eigenvector for \(\lambda_{\max}>0\), choose \(x=u/\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}\). Then \(x^*Ax=1\) and \(1/(x^*x)=\lambda_{\max}\), so this upper bound is attained and is the desired maximum.
pitfall: Normalizing by the ordinary norm does not itself impose the quadratic constraint.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Spectral square root and logarithm of a positive matrix
prompt:
For 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&5\end{pmatrix},
\]
 (a) find eigenvalues/eigenvectors; (b) find the unique positive definite square root; (c) find \(B\) with \(e^B=A\).
hints: The eigenvalues are 1 and 6.
Apply the desired scalar functions to an orthonormal eigenbasis.
solution:
The characteristic polynomial is \(t^2-7t+6=(t-1)(t-6)\). Unit eigenvectors are \(q_1=(-2,1)^T/\sqrt5\) for 1 and \(q_6=(1,2)^T/\sqrt5\) for 6. Hence \(A=q_1q_1^T+6q_6q_6^T\).

Its positive definite square root is
\[
 S=q_1q_1^T+\sqrt6q_6q_6^T
 =\frac15\begin{pmatrix}4+\sqrt6&2(\sqrt6-1)\\2(\sqrt6-1)&1+4\sqrt6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It is positive definite and \(S^2=A\). For uniqueness, any positive definite square root \(R\) commutes with A because \(R^2=A\). Thus it preserves each of these one-dimensional eigenspaces, and its positive eigenvalues there must be 1 and \(\sqrt6\), determining \(R=S\).

A logarithm is
\[
 B=(\log6)q_6q_6^T=\frac{\log6}{5}\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are 0 and \(\log6\) on the same eigenspaces, so exponentiating gives \(A\).
pitfall: The uniqueness assertion concerns the positive definite square root; other square roots can exist.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Strict spectral stability from connected Gershgorin bounds
prompt:
For \(a,b,c,d>0\), \(s=a+b+c+d\), consider

\[

 A=\begin{pmatrix}-1-s&a&b&c&0&d\\a&-s&b&c&d&0\\b&c&-s&d&0&a\\c&d&0&-s&a&b\\d&0&a&b&-s&c\\0&a&b&c&d&-s-1\end{pmatrix}.

\]

Prove every eigenvalue has negative real part and \(A\) is invertible.
hints: Gershgorin bounds give nonpositive real parts.
Exclude zero using a maximum-modulus eigenvector coordinate and positive connections.
solution:
The off-diagonal row sum is \(s\) in every row. The first and last Gershgorin disks have center \(-s-1\) and radius \(s\) and lie in \(\operatorname{Re}z\le-1\). The other disks have center -\(s\) and radius \(s\) and lie in \(\operatorname{Re}z\le0\), touching the imaginary axis only at zero. Thus any eigenvalue with nonnegative real part would have to be zero.

Suppose \(Av=0\), \(v\ne0\), and choose \(k\) with \(|v_k|=M=\max_j|v_j|>0\). If \(k\) is 1 or 6, its row equation gives \((s+1)M\le sM\), impossible. If \(k\) is 2,3,4 or 5, its equation gives
\[
 sM=\left|\sum_{j\ne k}a_{kj}v_j\right|\le\sum_{j\ne k}a_{kj}|v_j|\le sM.
\]
Equality forces every coordinate with positive coefficient in that row to have modulus \(M\). In each of rows 2–5 the coefficient of \(v_1\) is respectively a,\(b\),\(c\),\(d\), all strictly positive, so \(|v_1|=M\). The first-row contradiction applies again. Thus zero is not an eigenvalue. Combining with the disks proves strict negative real parts and invertibility.
pitfall: Ordinary Gershgorin disks alone only give a closed left half-plane; the positive connections exclude the boundary case.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Positive probability matrices and the false converse
prompt: A probability matrix has strictly positive entries and column sums one. A probability vector has strictly positive entries summing to one. (a) Prove products are probability matrices. (b) Bound the spectral radius by one. (c) Analyze the claimed converse: preserving every probability vector implies a probability matrix.
hints: Use the induced 1-norm for the spectral bound.
The identity preserves strictly positive vectors but has zero entries.
solution:
(a) Every entry of \(AB\) is a sum of strictly positive products and is strictly positive. With \(e\) the all-ones vector, \(e^TA=e^T\) and \(e^TB=e^T\), so \(e^TAB=e^T\): the column sums remain one.

(b) Because the entries are nonnegative and columns sum to one, the induced norm is \(\|A\|_1=\max_j\sum_i|a_{ij}|=1\). For any complex eigenvector, \(|\lambda|\|v\|_1=\|Av\|_1\le\|v\|_1\), hence \(|\lambda|\le1\). In fact 1 is an eigenvalue since \(A^Te=e\), so the spectral radius is exactly one.

(c) False for the stated strictly positive convention: \(I_n\), for \(n\ge2\), preserves every strictly positive probability vector but has zero off-diagonal entries. The exact conclusion is that \(A\) is entrywise nonnegative, has column sums one, and has no zero row. To see necessity, approach each standard basis vector by interior probability vectors; their images converge to the corresponding column, proving nonnegativity and column sum one. A zero row would give a zero image coordinate for every input and is impossible. Conversely, nonnegative entries and a nonzero entry in each row make \(Av\) strictly positive for every strictly positive \(v\), while column sums preserve its total sum.
pitfall: Preservation of the interior of the simplex permits zero matrix entries.
note: SOURCE ERROR: the strict-positive converse is false; \(I_n\) is a counterexample. The exact nonnegative/no-zero-row characterization is proved. Canonical 9 is Part \(I\) problem 9.

subject: linear algebra
title: An inverse as a polynomial in the matrix
prompt:
For an invertible \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), prove 
\[
A^{-1}=c_0I+c_1A+\cdots+c_{n-1}A^{n-1}.
\]
hints: Use the nonzero constant coefficient of the characteristic polynomial.
Multiply Cayley–Hamilton by the inverse.
solution:
Write the characteristic polynomial as \(p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^n b_jt^j\), where \(b_n=1\). Invertibility gives \(b_0=(-1)^n\det A\ne0\). Cayley--Hamilton says \(p(A)=0\). Multiplying by \(A^{-1}\) and solving gives
\[
 A^{-1}=-\frac1{b_0}\sum_{j=1}^n b_jA^{j-1}.
\]
Thus the requested coefficients are \(c_k=-b_{k+1}/b_0\), for \(0\le k\le n-1\). This is a polynomial in A of degree at most \(n-1\). The sum formula includes \(n=1\) without negative powers: it gives \(A^{-1}=-I/b_0\), the inverse of the scalar matrix with characteristic polynomial \(t+b_0\).
pitfall: The nonzero constant coefficient is what permits solving for the inverse.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Three functionals and their dual polynomial basis
prompt:
On \(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R)\) let \(\sigma_1(p)=p(0)\), 
\[
\sigma_2(p)=\int_0^1p(t)\,dt,
\]
 \(\sigma_3(p)=p'(1)\). Prove these form a dual-space basis and find the corresponding basis in \(\mathcal P_2\).
hints: Write their values on 1,\(t\),\(t^2\).
Solve for polynomials whose functional values are unit coordinate vectors.
solution:
For \(p=a+bt+ct^2\), the functional values are \(a,\ a+b/2+c/3,\ b+2c\). Their matrix in the coefficient basis is
\[
 M=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\1&1/2&1/3\\0&1&2\end{pmatrix},\qquad \det M=2/3\ne0.
\]
Hence the functionals are linearly independent and form a basis of the three-dimensional dual space. Solving \(M(a,b,c)^T=e_j\) gives
\[
 p_1=1-3t+\tfrac32t^2,\qquad
 p_2=3t-\tfrac32t^2,\qquad
 p_3=-\tfrac12t+\tfrac34t^2.
\]
Substitution checks \(\sigma_i(p_j)=\delta_{ij}\), so these polynomials form the requested basis of \(V\).
pitfall: Do not confuse the matrix's rows, which represent functionals, with the columns of its inverse, which represent the dual vectors.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: An explicit common eigenbasis
prompt:
For 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
 
\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-2\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
 verify commutation and simultaneously diagonalize. Explain why commuting matrices with distinct eigenvalues admit a common eigenbasis.
hints: An operator commuting with A preserves every A-eigenspace.
Choose the eigenvectors of A first.
solution:
Direct multiplication gives
\[
 AB=BA=\begin{pmatrix}-4&-4\\2&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Eigenvectors of A are \(v_2=(-2,1)^T\) for eigenvalue 2 and \(v_1=(-1,1)^T\) for eigenvalue 1. They satisfy \(Bv_2=-v_2\) and \(Bv_1=0\). Thus
\[
 P=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
 P^{-1}AP=\operatorname{diag}(2,1),\quad
 P^{-1}BP=\operatorname{diag}(-1,0).
\]
The general argument is that \(AB=BA\) implies \(B\) preserves each A-eigenspace. When \(A\) has distinct eigenvalues over the field under consideration, its eigenspaces are one-dimensional and supply a basis. \(B\) acts by a scalar on each, so that basis diagonalizes both. Distinct eigenvalues for \(B\) are not additionally necessary.
pitfall: Commutation alone gives triangularization, but without diagonalizability it need not give diagonalization.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: Jordan forms from minimum and characteristic polynomials
prompt: For a complex matrix with minimal polynomial \(t^2(t-2)(t^2+2t+2)^2\) and characteristic polynomial \(t^2(t-2)^2(t^2+2t+2)^3\): (a) find Jordan form; (b) give real Jordan form; (c) trace and determinant; (d) describe the intersection of kernel and range.
hints: The characteristic polynomial gives block-size sums; the minimal polynomial gives the largest sizes.
The size-two zero block has a nonzero vector in both kernel and range.
solution:
The eigenvalues are \(0,2,-1+i,-1-i\). The zero multiplicity is 2 with largest block 2, so its part is \(J_2(0)\). Eigenvalue 2 has multiplicity 2 with largest block 1, so it has two scalar blocks. Each nonreal eigenvalue has multiplicity 3 with largest block 2, forcing block sizes 2 and 1. Thus the complex Jordan form is
\[
 J_2(0)\oplus[2]\oplus[2]\oplus J_2(-1+i)\oplus[-1+i]
 \oplus J_2(-1-i)\oplus[-1-i].
\]

Set \(C=\begin{pmatrix}-1&-1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}\). A real representative is
\[
 J_2(0)\oplus[2]\oplus[2]\oplus
 \begin{pmatrix}C&I_2\\0&C\end{pmatrix}\oplus C.
\]
For a real A this is its real Jordan form under real similarity. Since the question only assumes A complex, this is a real matrix in its complex similarity class; a real-basis change for an arbitrary complex \(A\) is not promised.

Counting algebraic multiplicities gives \(\operatorname{tr}A=2\cdot2+3(-1+i)+3(-1-i)=-2\), and \(\det A=0\).

The nonzero eigenvalue blocks are invertible and contribute nothing to the kernel. In \(J_2(0)\), the first coordinate vector is both killed and the image of the second. Thus \(\ker A\cap\operatorname{range}A\) has dimension one, in particular contains a nonzero vector.
pitfall: The block-size partition is forced here; trace counts every multiplicity. All subspaces contain zero, so part (d) asks about nontrivial intersection.
note: Part II problem 4; 'real Jordan form' requires clarification since \(A\) is only specified complex.

subject: linear algebra
title: Properties of the commutant
prompt: For fixed complex A let \(V_0(A)=\{B:AB=BA\}\). Prove (a) it is a subspace; (b) invertible \(B\) in it has its inverse in it; (c) if \(A^T=A\), it is closed under transpose; (d) if \(A\) is diagonal with distinct diagonal entries, it consists precisely of diagonal matrices.
hints: Commutation is a homogeneous linear equation.
Compute the \((i,j)\) entry for a diagonal \(A\).
solution:
(a) The zero matrix commutes with \(A\), and if \(B\),\(C\) do, then
\(A(rB+sC)=rBA+sCA=(rB+sC)A\).
Thus the set is a vector subspace.

(b) From \(AB=BA\), multiply on the left and right by \(B^{-1}\) to obtain \(B^{-1}A=AB^{-1}\).

(c) Transposing the equation gives \(B^TA^T=A^TB^T\). If \(A^T=A\), this says \(B^TA=AB^T\), so \(B^T\) belongs to the commutant.

(d) For \(A=\operatorname{diag}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_n)\),
\[
 (AB-BA)_{ij}=(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)b_{ij}.
\]
Distinct diagonal entries force \(b_{ij}=0\) for \(i\ne j\). Conversely, all diagonal \(B\) commute with \(A\). This characterizes the set exactly.
pitfall: In part (c) symmetry is transpose symmetry, which is distinct from Hermitian symmetry over \(C\).
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: linear algebra
title: An operator preserving every subspace is scalar
prompt: If a linear operator \(T\) on a finite-dimensional vector space leaves every subspace invariant, prove it is a scalar multiple of the identity.
hints: Every line is invariant.
Compare the eigenvalue scalars on two basis vectors using their sum.
solution:
If \(V\) is zero-dimensional, \(T\) is zero and the claim holds. Otherwise choose a basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\). Invariance of each line implies \(Te_j=\lambda_je_j\). For distinct \(i\),\(j\), the line spanned by \(e_i+e_j\) is also invariant, so
\[
 \lambda_ie_i+\lambda_je_j=T(e_i+e_j)=c(e_i+e_j)
\]
for some scalar \(c\). Independence of \(e_i,e_j\) gives \(\lambda_i=\lambda_j=c\). Thus all basis scalars are equal to a single \(\lambda\), and \(T=\lambda I\). In dimension one the line argument alone suffices. The proof works over any field.
pitfall: Preserving coordinate lines alone only proves diagonal form; preserving their sums forces equal diagonal entries.
note: Part \(I\) numbers 1–9 are canonical 1–9; Part II numbers 1–6 are canonical 10–15.

subject: analysis
title: An alternating contraction recurrence
prompt: Let \(a_0=1\), \(a_n=1+\frac{1}{1+a_{n-1}}\) for \(n\ge1\). Prove \(a_n\ge1\), convergence, and calculate the limit.
hints: The recurrence keeps the sequence in a compact interval.
The defining map is a contraction there, even though the sequence is not monotone.
solution:
Induction gives \(a_n\ge1\): the denominator is positive and the added reciprocal is positive. It also gives \(a_n\le3/2\) for \(n\ge1\). On \(I=[1,3/2]\), \(F(t)=1+1/(1+t)\) maps \(I\) into itself and \(|F'(t)|=1/(1+t)^2\le1/4\). Hence it is a contraction on the complete interval, so its iterates converge to its unique fixed point \(L\). Solving
\[
 L=1+\frac1{1+L}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad L^2=2
\]
and using \(L\ge1\) yields \(L=\sqrt2\). One can prove convergence without quoting the fixed-point theorem: \(|a_{n+1}-a_n|\le(1/4)|a_n-a_{n-1}|\); summing this geometric bound makes the sequence Cauchy, then passing to the continuous recurrence gives the same limit.
pitfall: The map is decreasing, so the iterates oscillate; do not claim the full sequence is monotone.

subject: analysis
title: A convergent subsequence and failure of compactness
prompt: (i) Find distinct positive integers \(n_k\) for which \(\sin n_k\) converges. (ii) For noncompact \(A\subset\mathbb R\), construct decreasing closed \(F_k\) meeting A but with \(A\cap\bigcap_kF_k=\varnothing\).
hints: The sine values lie in a compact interval.
Noncompactness in Euclidean space means either unboundedness or failure to be closed.
solution:
(i) The bounded sequence \((\sin n)_{n\ge1}\) has a convergent subsequence by Bolzano--Weierstrass. Its strictly increasing indices \(n_k\) are the desired distinct positive integers.

(ii) If \(A\) is unbounded, take \(F_k=\{x:|x|\ge k\}\). These are decreasing closed sets, each meeting \(A\), and their intersection is empty. If \(A\) is bounded but noncompact, Heine--Borel implies it is not closed. Choose \(b\in\overline A\setminus A\) and take \(F_k=[b-1/k,b+1/k]\). Every \(F_k\) meets \(A\), their intersection is \(\{b\}\), and its intersection with \(A\) is empty. The identical construction works in \(\mathbb R^n\), replacing intervals by closed balls.
pitfall: The intersection of the \(F\) sets may be nonempty; only its intersection with \(A\) is required to vanish.

subject: analysis
title: When unions of connected sets remain connected
prompt: For connected \(A_n\) in a metric space, prove connectedness of their union if (i) all share a point, or (ii) \(A_n\cap A_{n+1}\ne\varnothing\). (iii) Does merely requiring each set to meet some other set suffice?
hints: A connected set lies entirely on one side of any separation.
For successive intersections, take connected finite initial unions.
solution:
(i) Suppose the union had a separation into disjoint nonempty relatively open sets \(U,V\). A common point belongs to one side, say \(U\). Each \(A_n\), being connected and containing that point, lies entirely in \(U\): otherwise its intersections with \(U,V\) would separate it. Thus the union could not meet \(V\), contradiction.

(ii) By induction the finite union \(B_k=A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_k\) is connected, since the previous union and \(A_{k+1}\) meet in at least \(A_k\cap A_{k+1}\). All \(B_k\) contain a point of nonempty \(A_1\), so (i) makes their union connected.

(iii) No. In \(\mathbb R\), take \(A_1=A_2=[0,1]\) and \(A_n=[2,3]\) for \(n\ge3\). Each set meets another distinct indexed set, but the union \([0,1]\cup[2,3]\) is disconnected. Intersections must link all the pieces, not just furnish isolated clusters.
pitfall: Meeting some other set is weaker than an intersection chain joining the entire family.

subject: analysis
title: Continuous partial derivatives imply differentiability
prompt: Using the definition, prove a real function on \(\mathbb R^n\) with all continuous first partial derivatives is differentiable.
hints: Break the increment into coordinate steps.
Apply the one-variable mean value theorem on each step and estimate the remainder.
solution:
Fix \(a\) and let \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_n)\). Put \(a^{(j)}=a+(h_1,\ldots,h_j,0,\ldots,0)\). Telescoping and the scalar mean value theorem on each coordinate segment give
\[
 f(a+h)-f(a)=\sum_{j=1}^n f_j(\xi_j)h_j,
\]
where \(\xi_j\) lies on the \(j\)-th segment and \(|\xi_j-a|\le|h|\); if \(h_j=0\), that term is zero and no intermediate point is needed. Subtract \(Lh=\sum_j f_j(a)h_j\). Define \(\omega(h)=\max_j\sup_{|z-a|\le|h|}|f_j(z)-f_j(a)|\). Continuity of the finitely many partials makes \(\omega(h)\to0\). Thus
\[
 |f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh|
 \le\omega(h)\sum_j|h_j|\le\sqrt n\,\omega(h)|h|.
\]
Dividing by \(|h|\) gives the defining little-\(o\) condition. Therefore \(Df(a)h=\nabla f(a)\cdot h\).
pitfall: Existence of partial derivatives alone does not control the points on the coordinate segments; continuity supplies the common small remainder.

subject: analysis
title: Coercivity, minimizing sequences, and surjectivity of the gradient
prompt: For differentiable real \(f\) on \(\mathbb R^n\) with \(f(x)\to\infty\) as \(|x|\to\infty\), let \(m=\inf f\). Prove (i) every minimizing sequence has a convergent subsequence; (ii) \(m\) is finite and a critical point exists; (iii) if \(\frac{f(x)}{|x|}\to\infty\), then for every \(y\), \(f(x)-y\cdot x\to\infty\) and \(\nabla f(z)=y\) for some \(z\).
hints: A sublevel set containing the tail of a minimizing sequence is bounded.
Subtracting a linear function preserves coercivity under superlinear growth.
solution:
(i) The infimum satisfies \(m\le f(0)\), though it might initially be regarded as \(-\infty\). If \(f(x_k)\to m\), then eventually \(f(x_k)\le f(0)+1\), even in the \(-\infty\) case. Coercivity puts these terms in a fixed closed ball; the finite initial segment does not affect boundedness. Bolzano--Weierstrass yields a convergent subsequence \(x_{k_j}\to z\).

(ii) Continuity gives \(f(x_{k_j})\to f(z)\), finite. A minimizing sequence exists by the definition of infimum (using values below \(-k\) if it were \(-\infty\)), so (i) excludes \(m=-\infty\), and gives \(f(z)=m\). At this global minimum, differentiability and Fermat's theorem give \(\nabla f(z)=0\). Alternatively, a lower bound follows by minimizing on a large ball and bounding \(f\) below outside it.

(iii) For fixed \(y\),
\[
 f(x)-y\cdot x\ge |x|\left(\frac{f(x)}{|x|}-|y|\right)\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
The function \(g(x)=f(x)-y\cdot x\) is differentiable and coercive, so by (ii) it has a minimizer \(z\) with \(\nabla g(z)=0\), that is \(\nabla f(z)=y\). No uniqueness follows without convexity.
pitfall: Do not assume the infimum is finite before proving it; the minimizing-sequence argument also excludes negative infinity.

subject: analysis
title: Support and total integral of a convolution
prompt:
Continuous \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) vanishes off \([0,1]\). Set 
\[
g(x)=\int_0^1f(t)f(x-t)\,dt.
\]
 Prove continuity, support in \([0,2]\), 
\[
\int_0^2f(x-t)\,dx=\int_0^1f
\]
 for \(t\in[0,1]\), and 
\[
\int_0^2g=(\int_0^1f)^2.
\]
hints: The integrand is continuous on every relevant compact rectangle.
Substitute \(x\) minus \(t\), then use the support assumption.
solution:
(i) For each \(x\) the continuous \(t\)-integrand has a finite Riemann integral. On a compact neighborhood of any fixed \(x\), \((x,t)\mapsto f(t)f(x-t)\) is uniformly continuous, so its change under a small change in \(x\) is uniformly small in \(t\). Integrating proves continuity of \(g\).

(ii) If \(x<0\), then \(x-t<0\) for all \(t\in[0,1]\); if \(x>2\), then \(x-t>1\) for all such \(t\). Thus the integrand vanishes, proving the support assertion.

(iii) Substitution gives \(\int_0^2 f(x-t)\,dx=\int_{-t}^{2-t}f(s)\,ds\). For \(0\le t\le1\), the interval contains \([0,1]\); outside that interval \(f\) is zero. Hence this equals \(\int_0^1f(s)\,ds\).

(iv) The integrand is continuous on \([0,2]\times[0,1]\), so iterated Riemann integrals can be interchanged:
\[
 \int_0^2g(x)\,dx=\int_0^1f(t)\left(\int_0^2f(x-t)\,dx\right)dt
 =\left(\int_0^1f\right)^2.
\]
pitfall: The support of the convolution is the sum of the two support intervals; verify this before shortening the translated integral.

subject: analysis
title: Positive Hessian, coercivity, and a global gradient inverse
prompt: For \(C^2\) \(f\) with \(D^2f(x)[h,h]>0\) for \(h\ne0\), solve all final-paper parts (i)–(ix): strict tangent inequality, uniqueness of critical points, existence under coercivity, linear tilts, gradient surjectivity under superlinear growth, and the system for \(f(u,v)=u^2+\sin u\sin v+v^2\).
hints: Use Taylor's integral remainder along a segment.
Minimize a linearly tilted function to prescribe the gradient.
solution:
(i) For \(y\ne x\), let \(h=y-x\). Taylor's integral formula gives
\[
 f(y)-f(x)-Df(x)h=\int_0^1(1-t)D^2f(x+th)[h,h]\,dt>0.
\]
The integrand is positive on \(0\le t<1\), proving the strict tangent inequality.

(ii) If the derivative vanished at distinct \(x\),\(y\), applying (i) in both directions would give \(f(y)>f(x)\) and \(f(x)>f(y)\), impossible.

(iii) Suppose also \(f(x)\to\infty\) at infinity. Choose \(R\) large enough that outside the ball \(f\) exceeds \(f(0)+1\). Continuity gives a minimum on the compact closed ball, so \(f\) is bounded below and the minimum there is also global. In the requested minimizing-sequence approach, its eventually bounded sublevel set supplies a convergent subsequence, and continuity attains the infimum.

(iv) Fermat's theorem gives a critical point at the minimizer; (ii) makes it unique.

(v) For fixed \(z\), \(g(x)=f(x)-z\cdot x\) is \(C^2\) and has \(D^2g=D^2f\), still positive definite.

(vi) Under \(f(x)/|x|\to\infty\), \(g(x)\ge |x|(f(x)/|x|-|z|)\to\infty\).

(vii) Apply (iii),(iv) to \(g\). Its unique critical point satisfies \(\nabla f(x)=z\). This proves bijectivity of the gradient onto \(\mathbb R^n\); the superlinear condition also implies the coercivity needed there.

(viii) For the specified two-variable function,
\[
 H=\begin{pmatrix}2-\sin u\sin v&\cos u\cos v\\\cos u\cos v&2-\sin u\sin v\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its eigenvalues are \(2+\cos(u+v)\) and \(2-\cos(u-v)\), both in \([1,3]\). Therefore its trace is positive, its determinant is at least one (in particular nonzero), and \(h^THh>0\) for every nonzero \(h\). Positivity of the trace and mere nonvanishing of a determinant would not suffice for a general symmetric matrix; here we have proved its determinant positive and both eigenvalues positive.

(ix) \(f(u,v)\ge u^2+v^2-1\), so \(f(u,v)/\sqrt{u^2+v^2}\to\infty\). Part (vii) now says for every \((b,c)\), the equations
\[
 2u+\cos u\sin v=b,\qquad 2v+\sin u\cos v=c
\]
have exactly one solution.
pitfall: Positive Hessian does not alone imply surjectivity of the gradient; the growth hypothesis supplies existence for every linear tilt.
note: The linked PDF includes this nine-part final problem on pages 1–2, followed by three separately numbered prelim questions on page 3. Internal numbers 1–4 distinguish these four problem groups.

subject: analysis
title: A lower distance bound controls the inverse derivative
prompt: Prelim 1: (a) if differentiable \(f\) has singular \(Df(x)\), find \(x_k\to x\) with \(\frac{|f(x_k)-f(x)|}{|x_k-x|}\to0\); (b) a local upper Lipschitz bound implies \(|Df(x_0)h|\le M|h|\); (c),(d) if \(|f(y)-f(x)|\ge\alpha|y-x|\), show invertibility of every derivative and \(|Df(x)^{-1}h|\le\frac{|h|}{\alpha}\), using the inverse theorem when \(f\) is \(C^1\).
hints: Follow a nonzero kernel direction in (a).
The local inverse inherits the reciprocal Lipschitz bound.
solution:
(a) A singular square linear map has a nonzero kernel vector \(v\). Set \(x_k=x+v/k\). Differentiability gives \(f(x+h)-f(x)=Df(x)h+o(|h|)\); along these increments the linear term is zero, yielding the stated ratio limit.

(b) For fixed \(h\), divide the bound \(|f(x_0+th)-f(x_0)|\le M|t|\,|h|\) by \(|t|\) and let \(t\to0\). Differentiability gives \(|Df(x_0)h|\le M|h|\), which implies the requested weaker \((M+\varepsilon)|h|\) inequality for every \(\varepsilon>0\). For \(h=0\) the conclusion is immediate.

(c) The lower distance bound makes every nonzero increment ratio at least \(\alpha>0\), contradicting (a) if any derivative were singular. Thus all derivatives are invertible. Direct differentiation also gives \(|Df(x)v|\ge\alpha|v|\).

(d) If \(f\) is \(C^1\), the inverse function theorem provides a local inverse \(g\) near \(f(x)\), with \(Dg(f(x))=Df(x)^{-1}\). The original lower bound gives \(|g(a)-g(b)|\le|a-b|/\alpha\) for points in that inverse neighborhood. Apply (b) to \(g\) with \(M=1/\alpha\) to obtain \(|Df(x)^{-1}h|\le|h|/\alpha\). No assumption that \(f\) is globally onto is needed.
pitfall: The inverse function theorem gives local inverse neighborhoods; applying a derivative bound to an undefined global inverse is unnecessary.
note: Internal problem 2 corresponds to printed Prelim 1.

subject: analysis
title: Stone--Weierstrass for functions vanishing at one point
prompt: Prelim 2: on compact metric \(M\) with fixed \(x_*\), prove evaluation is continuous; \(C_*(M)=\{f:f(x_*)=0\}\) is a closed algebra; adjoining constants to a subalgebra \(A\subset C_*(M)\) preserves point separation; and a point-separating \(A\) is dense in \(C_*(M)\).
hints: Evaluation is bounded by the uniform norm.
Approximate using A plus constants, then use the vanishing value to make the constant small.
solution:
(a) \(|f(x_*)-g(x_*)|\le\|f-g\|_\infty\), so evaluation is a continuous linear map.

(b) Its zero preimage is closed. Sums, scalar multiples, and products of functions vanishing at \(x_*\) still vanish there, so \(C_*(M)\) is an algebra, generally without the constant unit.

(c) For \(B=\{p+c:p\in A,c\in\mathbb R\}\), closure under addition and scalar multiplication is immediate, and
\[
 (p+c)(q+d)=(pq+dp+cq)+cd\in B.
\]
It contains constants. If A separates points, so does \(B\). Conversely, a difference \((p+c)(x)-(p+c)(y)\) equals \(p(x)-p(y)\), so any separation by \(B\) is already by \(A\).

(d) The real Stone--Weierstrass theorem makes \(B\) dense in \(C(M)\). For \(f\in C_*(M)\) and tolerance \(\eta>0\), choose \(p+c\in B\) with \(\|f-(p+c)\|_\infty<\eta/2\). Evaluation at \(x_*\), where \(f\) and \(p\) vanish, gives \(|c|<\eta/2\). Therefore \(\|f-p\|_\infty<\eta\), proving density of A in \(C_*(M)\).
pitfall: A itself does not contain the constant unit, so apply Stone--Weierstrass after adjoining constants and then remove the small constant.
note: Internal problem 3 corresponds to printed Prelim 2.

subject: analysis
title: A proper submersion is onto
prompt: Prelim 3: for \(C^1\) \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), prove (i) surjective derivative everywhere implies open image; (ii) compact preimages of compact sets imply closed image; (iii) surjective derivatives and \(|f(x)|\to\infty\) as \(|x|\to\infty\) imply \(f\) onto.
hints: For unequal dimensions restrict to a complement of the derivative kernel.
Lift a convergent target sequence into the compact preimage of its closure.
solution:
(i) Fix \(x\). Surjectivity of \(Df(x)\) provides an \(m\)-dimensional linear subspace \(E\) on which the derivative is an isomorphism onto \(\mathbb R^m\): choose preimages of a target basis. Restrict \(f\) to the affine slice \(x+E\), and identify \(E\) with \(\mathbb R^m\). The inverse function theorem says the image of a small neighborhood in this slice contains a neighborhood of \(f(x)\). Thus each point of the full image is interior, and the image is open.

(ii) If \(y_k=f(x_k)\to y\), the set \(K=\{y,y_1,y_2,\ldots\}\) is compact. By hypothesis \(f^{-1}(K)\) is compact and contains every \(x_k\). Choose a convergent subsequence with limit \(x\) in this preimage; continuity gives \(f(x)=y\). The image contains limits of all its convergent sequences, hence is closed in the metric target.

(iii) For compact \(K\), its boundedness and the growth assumption make \(f^{-1}(K)\) bounded. Continuity makes it closed, so Heine--Borel makes it compact. Parts (i),(ii) make the nonempty image both open and closed in connected \(\mathbb R^m\), hence the entire target.
pitfall: When \(n\) and \(m\) differ, the full derivative is not a square isomorphism; use an \(m\)-dimensional slice for the inverse theorem.
note: Internal problem 4 corresponds to printed Prelim 3.

subject: analysis
title: Cesàro averages preserve limits but conceal oscillation
prompt:
For 
\[
y_n=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^nx_j,
\]
 (a) prove \(x_n\to x\) implies \(y_n\to x\); (b) give a divergent sequence whose averages converge.
hints: Split off a fixed finite initial segment.
Alternating values cancel in averages.
solution:
(a) Given \(\varepsilon>0\), take \(N\) so that \(|x_j-x|<\varepsilon\) for \(j>N\). For \(n>N\),
\[
 |y_n-x|\le\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^N|x_j-x|+\frac{n-N}{n}\varepsilon.
\]
The finite numerator in the first term is constant, so its quotient tends to zero. Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves the limit.

(b) Take \(x_j=(-1)^j\). Its even and odd subsequences have different limits, but its partial sums have absolute value at most one, so \(|y_n|\le1/n\to0\). Adding a constant gives any desired limiting average.
pitfall: Convergence of arithmetic averages does not imply convergence of the original sequence.

subject: analysis
title: Factoring a function vanishing on an axis
prompt:
For \(C^2\) \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) with \(f(0,y)=0\), (a) show \(f=xg\), 
\[
g(x,y)=\int_0^1f_x(tx,y)\,dt;
\]
 (b) prove \(g\) is \(C^1\), \(g(0,y)=f_x(0,y)\), \(g_y(0,y)=f_{xy}(0,y)\); (c) describe the local zero set when \(f_x(0,0)\ne0\), and when \(f_x(0,0)=0\), \(f_{xy}(0,0)\ne0\).
hints: Integrate in the \(x\) direction.
The second case applies the implicit function theorem to \(g\), not to \(f\).
solution:
(a) The fundamental theorem gives \(f(x,y)-f(0,y)=x\int_0^1f_x(tx,y)\,dt\), proving the factorization even at \(x=0\).

(b) On compact neighborhoods the integrand and its parameter derivatives are continuous and uniformly controlled, allowing differentiation under the finite integral:
\[
 g_x(x,y)=\int_0^1t f_{xx}(tx,y)\,dt,\qquad
 g_y(x,y)=\int_0^1f_{xy}(tx,y)\,dt.
\]
The same compact uniform-continuity argument makes these partials continuous. At \(x=0\) the formulas give \(g(0,y)=f_x(0,y)\), \(g_y(0,y)=f_{xy}(0,y)\).

(c) If \(f_x(0,0)\ne0\), continuity keeps \(g\) nonzero near zero, so \(f=xg=0\) there exactly when \(x=0\). If instead \(f_x(0,0)=0\) and \(f_{xy}(0,0)\ne0\), then \(g(0,0)=0\) and \(g_y(0,0)\ne0\). The implicit function theorem makes the zeros of \(g\) near zero a \(C^1\) graph \(y=\psi(x)\), with \(\psi(0)=0\). Consequently the zeros of \(f\) are the union of the vertical axis and this graph. Its tangent vector is \((1,\psi'(0))\), so it is not vertical; explicitly \(\psi'(0)=-f_{xx}(0,0)/(2f_{xy}(0,0))\).
pitfall: In the second case the gradient of \(f\) at zero may vanish, so apply the implicit theorem to the factored function \(g\).

subject: analysis
title: Closed sets detecting a noncompact subset
prompt: For noncompact \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\), construct decreasing closed \(F_k\) each meeting \(A\), with \(A\cap\bigcap_kF_k=\varnothing\).
hints: Separate unboundedness from nonclosedness.
Use either outer regions or shrinking balls about a missing limit point.
solution: Heine--Borel says \(A\) is either unbounded or not closed. In the unbounded case take \(F_k=\{x:|x|\ge k\}\). Each meets \(A\), the sets are closed and decreasing, and their intersection is empty. If \(A\) is bounded and nonclosed, choose \(b\in\overline A\setminus A\) and put \(F_k=\{x:|x-b|\le1/k\}\). Each meets A because \(b\) is in its closure. These are decreasing closed sets with intersection \(\{b\}\), which does not meet \(A\). This handles every noncompact subset.
pitfall: Closedness of \(F\) is ambient closedness in Euclidean space; A itself need not be closed.

subject: analysis
title: Integral convergence on a fixed polynomial space becomes uniform
prompt: For \(X=C([0,1],\mathbb R)\), (a) justify the uniform and integral norms are well defined; (b) prove uniform convergence implies integral-norm convergence and give a converse counterexample; (c) for fixed degree bound \(k\), show integral-norm convergence of polynomials to continuous \(x\) implies \(x\) is a polynomial of that degree and convergence is uniform.
hints: Compactness supplies a maximum and integrability.
On a finite-dimensional polynomial space all norms are equivalent.
solution:
(a) Continuity on the compact interval supplies a finite maximum of the absolute value, and \(|x|\) is continuous and Riemann integrable, so both formulas give finite real values.

(b) \(\|x_n-x\|_1\le\|x_n-x\|_\infty\), since the interval has length one. Conversely \(x_n(t)=t^n\) has \(\|x_n\|_1=1/(n+1)\to0\) but \(\|x_n\|_\infty=1\), so convergence to zero is not uniform.

(c) To spell out norm equivalence, write \(p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^k a_jt^j\). On the compact coefficient sphere \(|a|_2=1\), the continuous positive function \(a\mapsto\int_0^1|p(t)|\,dt\) has a positive minimum \(c\): a nonzero polynomial cannot have zero absolute integral. Continuity here follows from \(\|p_a-p_b\|_1\le\sum_j|a_j-b_j|\). Thus \(\|p\|_1\ge c|a|_2\), while \(\|p\|_\infty\le\sqrt{k+1}|a|_2\). An integral-norm Cauchy polynomial sequence therefore has Cauchy coefficients and converges coefficientwise to \(p\) in the same polynomial space, uniformly as well. Since it was also converging to \(x\) in integral norm, \(\|x-p\|_1=0\). Continuity implies \(x=p\) pointwise. Hence \(x\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k\) and the convergence is uniform.
pitfall: The degree bound must stay fixed; polynomials of increasing degree can have small integral norm but a persistent peak.

subject: analysis
title: Uniform convergence with moving integration endpoints
prompt:
For continuous \(f_n\to f\) uniformly on \([0,1]\), and \(0<x_n\le1\), \(x_n\to1\), prove 
\[
\int_0^{x_n}f_n\to\int_0^1f.
\]
 Does pointwise convergence suffice?
hints: Separate the integrand error from the short missing interval.
Use a shrinking spike away from the moving endpoint for a counterexample.
solution:
The uniform limit is continuous and bounded. Then
\[
 \left|\int_0^{x_n}f_n-\int_0^1f\right|
 \le x_n\|f_n-f\|_\infty+(1-x_n)\|f\|_\infty\longrightarrow0.
\]
Pointwise convergence alone is insufficient. For \(n\ge2\), let \(f_n\) be a triangular continuous spike supported on \([0,2/n]\), zero at both endpoints, and height \(n\) at \(1/n\). More explicitly use \(n^2t\) on \([0,1/n]\), \(n^2(2/n-t)\) on \([1/n,2/n]\), and zero afterwards. For every fixed \(t\) the functions tend to zero, including \(t=0\), yet their integrals equal the triangle area one. Taking \(x_n=1\) satisfies the endpoint condition but the integrals fail to approach the zero integral of the pointwise limit.
pitfall: Control of the endpoint does not compensate for uncontrolled spikes in the integrand.

subject: analysis
title: Equal temperatures at opposite circle points
prompt: For continuous temperature on a spherical surface, prove any nondegenerate circular section has two diametrically opposed points with equal temperature.
hints: Subtract the temperature at the opposite point.
The difference changes sign after a half-turn.
solution:
Parametrize the section circle continuously by \(\gamma(\theta)\), with opposite point \(\gamma(\theta+\pi)\). Let
\[
 h(\theta)=T(\gamma(\theta))-T(\gamma(\theta+\pi)).
\]
It is continuous and \(h(\theta+\pi)=-h(\theta)\), using the circle's \(2\pi\)-periodicity. If \(h(0)=0\), the initial pair works. Otherwise \(h(0)\) and \(h(\pi)\) have opposite signs, so the intermediate value theorem supplies a zero between them. The corresponding opposite points have equal temperatures. This needs no advanced sphere theorem; continuity along the circle suffices.
pitfall: Use diametrically opposed points of the section circle; they need not be antipodal points of the whole sphere.

subject: linear algebra
title: Matrix powers vanish exactly inside the spectral unit disk
prompt: (a) If the minimal polynomial is \((t-\lambda)^r\), show a Jordan basis gives \(\lambda I+N\) with nilpotent \(N\). (b) Prove \(U^mv\to0\) for all \(v\) iff \(|\lambda|<1\). (c) Extend to an operator with several eigenvalues using primary decomposition.
hints: Expand powers of a scalar plus a nilpotent matrix.
A fixed polynomial in \(m\) times a decaying geometric factor still tends to zero.
solution:
(a) Every Jordan block has eigenvalue \(\lambda\), and subtracting \(\lambda I\) leaves a block diagonal nilpotent matrix \(N\), with \(N^r=0\).

(b) If \(\lambda=0\), powers eventually vanish. If \(0<|\lambda|<1\), for \(m\ge r\) the binomial theorem gives
\[
 (\lambda I+N)^m=\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}\binom mj\lambda^{m-j}N^j.
\]
For each fixed \(j\) the scalar coefficient tends to zero, because a fixed-degree polynomial in \(m\) is dominated by geometric decay. The finite sum therefore tends to zero in any matrix norm, hence on each vector. Conversely, a nonzero eigenvector satisfies \(U^mv=\lambda^mv\); convergence to zero forces \(|\lambda|<1\).

(c) In the primary decomposition \(V=\bigoplus W_i\), each restriction has just the eigenvalue \(\lambda_i\) and a nilpotent scalar perturbation. Part (b) makes its powers vanish iff \(|\lambda_i|<1\). Decomposing any vector into the finitely many primary components gives sufficiency, and eigenvectors in each component give necessity. Thus convergence of all powers is equivalent to spectral radius less than one.
pitfall: The nilpotent terms introduce polynomial factors; geometric decay dominates them only when the eigenvalue modulus is strictly below one.

subject: linear algebra
title: A block determinant for triangular or commuting blocks
prompt:
For 
\[
E=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}
\]
 with square complex blocks, prove \(\det E=\det(AD-BC)\) when (a) all blocks are diagonal, (b) all are upper triangular, (c) they commute pairwise.
hints: Interleave the two sets of coordinate vectors.
Commuting complex matrices admit a common invariant flag.
solution:
(a) Permuting rows and columns by the same permutation to order coordinates as first-block 1, second-block 1, first-block 2, second-block 2, and so on, makes \(E\) a direct sum of \(2\times2\) matrices. Its determinant is \(\prod_i(a_id_i-b_ic_i)=\det(AD-BC)\).

(b) The same interleaving makes \(E\) block upper triangular with \(2\times2\) diagonal blocks \(\begin{pmatrix}a_{ii}&b_{ii}\\c_{ii}&d_{ii}\end{pmatrix}\). Thus its determinant is \(\prod_i(a_{ii}d_{ii}-b_{ii}c_{ii})\). Since \(AD-BC\) is upper triangular with exactly these diagonal entries, its determinant agrees.

(c) Pairwise commuting complex matrices can be simultaneously upper triangularized. To justify this, successively restrict to eigenspaces of the first, second, and subsequent operators; commutation preserves these nonzero eigenspaces, yielding a common eigenvector. Its line is invariant. The induced operators on the quotient still commute, so induction builds a common invariant flag and an adapted basis making all operators upper triangular. A simultaneous similarity by \(S\) on the blocks corresponds to similarity by \(\operatorname{diag}(S,S)\) on \(E\), and changes \(AD-BC\) by the same \(S\) similarity. Determinants are unchanged, so part (b) applies. No block need be invertible.
pitfall: The formula is false for arbitrary noncommuting blocks; the triangular or commuting structure supplies the proof.

subject: linear algebra
title: What characteristic and minimal polynomials determine
prompt: (a) Find Jordan form for \(\chi_M=(t-4)^3(t+6)^2\), \(m_M=(t-4)^2(t+6)\). (b) Do equal characteristic and minimal polynomials imply similarity? (c) What if the minimal polynomial also equals the characteristic polynomial?
hints: At each eigenvalue the largest Jordan block is specified by the minimal polynomial.
Several smaller blocks can vary unless there is just one block per eigenvalue.
solution:
(a) At 4 the total size is three and the largest block size two, so the partition is \(2+1\). At \(-6\) the total size is two and the largest block size one, so the partition is \(1+1\). Hence
\[
 J_M=J_2(4)\oplus[4]\oplus[-6]\oplus[-6].
\]

(b) No. Take \(A=J_2(0)\oplus J_2(0)\) and \(B=J_2(0)\oplus[0]\oplus[0]\). Both have characteristic polynomial \(t^4\) and minimal polynomial \(t^2\), but ranks two and one, respectively. Rank is similarity invariant, so they are not similar.

(c) Yes over \(\mathbb C\). For every eigenvalue, equality of the characteristic and minimal polynomial exponents means the largest Jordan block already has size equal to the full algebraic multiplicity. Hence there is exactly one block at that eigenvalue. The common polynomial therefore uniquely specifies all Jordan blocks, and the two matrices are similar. The printed reference to part 2 is understood as the preceding subpart (b).
pitfall: The minimal polynomial records the largest block, not the full partition of each algebraic multiplicity.

subject: linear algebra
title: Products and eigenvalues of orthogonal matrices
prompt: (a) Prove the product of orthogonal matrices is orthogonal. (b) Prove every complex eigenvalue of a real orthogonal matrix has modulus one.
hints: Transpose the product in reverse order.
The real matrix also preserves the Hermitian norm on its complexification.
solution:
(a) If \(O_1^TO_1=O_2^TO_2=I\), then
\[
 (O_1O_2)^T(O_1O_2)=O_2^TO_1^TO_1O_2=I.
\]
Thus the product is orthogonal.

(b) For a nonzero complex eigenvector \(Ov=\lambda v\), a real orthogonal \(O\) has \(O^*O=O^TO=I\), so \(\|Ov\|_2=\|v\|_2\). The eigenvalue equation gives \(|\lambda|\|v\|_2=\|v\|_2\), hence \(|\lambda|=1\). This includes nonreal eigenvalues; real eigenvalues must specifically be \(1\) or \(-1\).
pitfall: Orthogonal matrices may have nonreal eigenvalues, so the modulus statement is stronger than simply checking real eigenvectors.

subject: linear algebra
title: Composition ranks and an onto factor
prompt:
For endomorphisms \(S\),\(T\) of finite dimensional \(V\), prove (a) 
\[
\operatorname{rank}ST\le\operatorname{rank}T;
\]
 (b) 
\[
\operatorname{rank}TS\le\operatorname{rank}T;
\]
 (c) onto \(S\) makes both ranks equal to that of \(T\).
hints: The image of \(ST\) is the image of range \(T\) under \(S\).
Onto in finite equal dimensions also means injective.
solution:
(a) \(\operatorname{range}(ST)=S(\operatorname{range}T)\); a linear map cannot increase the dimension of a subspace, proving the first inequality. Equivalently \(\ker T\subset\ker ST\), and rank--nullity gives the same result.

(b) \(\operatorname{range}(TS)\subset\operatorname{range}T\), proving the second.

(c) If \(S\) is onto, \(\operatorname{range}(TS)=T(V)=\operatorname{range}T\). Since \(S\) is an endomorphism of a finite dimensional space, rank--nullity also makes it injective. Thus its restriction to \(\operatorname{range}T\) is injective, so \(\dim S(\operatorname{range}T)=\dim\operatorname{range}T\). Both ranks equal \(\operatorname{rank}T\).
pitfall: The equality for \(ST\) uses injectivity of \(S\), derived here from finite-dimensional surjectivity.

subject: linear algebra
title: Positive eigenvalues and the largest matrix entry
