prompt: For real symmetric \(M\), (a) prove \(M>0\) iff all eigenvalues are positive; (b) prove its largest entry is on the diagonal.
hints: Use an orthonormal eigenbasis.
The positive inner product defined by \(M\) bounds off-diagonal entries.
solution:
(a) If \(M\) is positive definite and \(Mv=\lambda v\), then \(0<v^TMv=\lambda|v|^2\), so \(\lambda>0\). Conversely, orthogonal diagonalization \(M=Q\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_i)Q^T\) gives
\[
 x^TMx=\sum_i\lambda_i(Q^Tx)_i^2>0
\]
for nonzero \(x\) if all eigenvalues are positive.

(b) Each diagonal entry \(m_{ii}=e_i^TMe_i>0\). Cauchy--Schwarz in the \(M\)-inner product gives \(|m_{ij}|\le\sqrt{m_{ii}m_{jj}}\le\max_k m_{kk}\). For \(i\ne j\) the first inequality is strict, because the basis vectors are independent and equality would require dependence. Thus even the largest absolute entry is on the diagonal; in particular the largest signed entry is.
pitfall: A large negative off-diagonal entry might be missed by a signed comparison; the absolute-value bound proves the stronger statement.

subject: linear algebra
title: Normality and commuting Hermitian parts
prompt: Prove a complex matrix \(T\) is normal iff \(T=H+iK\) for commuting Hermitian matrices \(H\) and \(K\).
hints: Recover \(H\) and \(K\) from \(T\) and its adjoint.
Expand both products in the definition of normality.
solution:
Every \(T\) has the unique decomposition
\[
 H=(T+T^*)/2,\qquad K=(T-T^*)/(2i),\qquad T=H+iK,
\]
with \(H^*=H\), \(K^*=K\). Expanding gives
\[
 TT^*=H^2+K^2+i(KH-HK),\qquad
 T^*T=H^2+K^2+i(HK-KH).
\]
Thus \(TT^*=T^*T\) iff \(2i(KH-HK)=0\), precisely \(HK=KH\). Conversely, the same calculation proves normality for any decomposition with commuting Hermitian parts.
pitfall: Hermitian parts always exist; their commutation is the additional condition.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: A Gram matrix is positive definite precisely for invertible \(M\)
prompt: Show \(M^*M\) is positive semidefinite, and is positive definite iff the square matrix \(M\) is invertible.
hints: Compute its quadratic form.
Identify which vectors make that form vanish.
solution:
First \((M^*M)^*=M^*M\), so the matrix is Hermitian. For every \(x\),
\[
 x^*M^*Mx=\|Mx\|^2\ge0.
\]
The form vanishes exactly when \(Mx=0\). It is strictly positive on nonzero vectors iff \(\ker M=\{0\}\), which for a square finite-dimensional matrix is equivalent to invertibility. This proves both assertions. For a rectangular \(M\) the same reasoning gives positive definiteness iff \(M\) has full column rank.
pitfall: Nonnegative quadratic forms establish semidefiniteness, not automatically definiteness.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Bilinear characterization of the Euclidean operator norm
prompt:
For a real matrix \(A\), prove 
\[
\|A\|_2=\max\{x^TAy:\|x\|_2=\|y\|_2=1\}.
\]
hints: For fixed \(y\) maximize over \(x\) first.
Use the direction of Ay to attain Cauchy–Schwarz.
solution: For unit \(x\),\(y\), Cauchy--Schwarz gives \(x^TAy\le\|Ay\|_2\le\|A\|_2\). The continuous function \(y\mapsto\|Ay\|_2\) attains its maximum on the unit sphere; let \(y_0\) be a maximizer. If \(A\) is nonzero then \(Ay_0\ne0\), and choosing \(x_0=Ay_0/\|Ay_0\|_2\) yields \(x_0^TAy_0=\|Ay_0\|_2=\|A\|_2\). If \(A\) is zero, every value is zero. Hence the stated maximum equals the operator norm in all cases.
pitfall: No absolute value is needed in this maximum because \(x\) can be replaced by its negative.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Matrix exponentials: noncommutation and unitarity
prompt: (a) Decide whether \(e^{A+B}=e^Ae^B\) always holds. (b) Prove \(A^*=-A\) implies \(e^A\) is unitary.
hints: For (a) use a nilpotent matrix and a diagonal matrix.
For (b) take the adjoint of the exponential series.
solution:
(a) The identity is false without commutation. Set
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then \(A^2=0\), \(C=A+B\) satisfies \(C^2=C\), and
\[
 e^{A+B}=I+(e-1)C=\begin{pmatrix}1&e-1\\0&e\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 e^Ae^B=\begin{pmatrix}1&e\\0&e\end{pmatrix}.
\]
If \(A\) and \(B\) commute, the binomial formula and absolute convergence of the series do prove the identity.

(b) Absolute convergence allows taking adjoints term by term, giving \((e^A)^*=e^{A^*}=e^{-A}\). Since \(A\) and \(-A\) commute, \(e^{-A}e^A=I\). Thus \((e^A)^*e^A=I\), which is unitarity.
pitfall: The scalar exponential rule requires commuting matrices.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Strict increase of the smallest eigenvalue
prompt:
If \(A\) is Hermitian and \(B\) positive definite, prove 
\[
\lambda_{\min}(A+B)>\lambda_{\min}(A).
\]
hints: Use the Rayleigh quotient.
Positive definiteness supplies a uniform positive lower bound.
solution:
The spectral theorem gives \(x^*Ax\ge\lambda_{\min}(A)\|x\|^2\) and \(x^*Bx\ge\lambda_{\min}(B)\|x\|^2\), with \(\lambda_{\min}(B)>0\). Consequently, for every unit \(x\),
\[
 x^*(A+B)x\ge\lambda_{\min}(A)+\lambda_{\min}(B).
\]
Minimizing over the unit sphere proves
\[
 \lambda_{\min}(A+B)\ge\lambda_{\min}(A)+\lambda_{\min}(B)>\lambda_{\min}(A).
\]
This argument does not require \(A\) and \(B\) to commute.
pitfall: Pointwise strict positivity alone should be converted into the uniform eigenvalue bound before minimizing.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Principal minor inequality and the diagonal exception
prompt: (a) For a positive definite complex \(2\times2\) matrix prove \(a_{11}a_{22}>|a_{12}|^2\). (b) The printed extension asks \(a_{ii}a_{jj}>|a_{ij}|^2\) for all \(i\),\(j\). Analyze and correct it.
hints: Test a vector that cancels the first coordinate of the quadratic form.
For the extension restrict to two distinct coordinate directions.
solution:
(a) Write
\[
 A=\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\\overline b&d\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Positive definiteness gives \(a>0\). With \(x=(-b/a,1)^T\), direct calculation gives \(x^*Ax=d-|b|^2/a>0\). Multiplying by a proves \(ad>|b|^2\).

(b) The strict assertion is false when \(i=j\): since \(a_{ii}>0\) is real, it would read \(a_{ii}^2>a_{ii}^2\). For \(i\ne j\), restrict the positive quadratic form to \(\operatorname{span}\{e_i,e_j\}\). Its \(2\times2\) principal matrix is positive definite, so (a) proves \(a_{ii}a_{jj}>|a_{ij}|^2\). For all indices the valid statement is the non-strict inequality, with equality on the diagonal.
pitfall: Always check coincident indices in a claimed strict inequality.
note: SOURCE ERROR: the strict all-indices inequality fails for \(i=j\). The correct strict claim is for distinct indices. Canonical number 6 is Part \(I\) problem 6.

subject: linear algebra
title: Eigenvalues of a product of commuting matrices
prompt: For commuting real matrices \(A\),\(B\), prove every eigenvalue of \(AB\) is a product of an eigenvalue of \(A\) and one of \(B\).
hints: Work over the complex numbers.
Construct a common invariant flag.
solution:
Interpret eigenvalues over \(\mathbb C\), as required for arbitrary real matrices. Commuting complex matrices can be simultaneously upper triangularized. Here is a proof: choose an eigenvalue \(\alpha\) of \(A\). Its nonzero eigenspace is \(B\)-invariant because \(A(Bv)=B(Av)=\alpha Bv\). The restriction of \(B\) has an eigenvector there, providing a common invariant line. On the quotient by that line the induced operators still commute. Induction on dimension constructs a common invariant flag and hence a basis making both matrices upper triangular.

Their diagonal entries \(\alpha_i,\beta_i\) are their respective eigenvalues, including multiplicities. The product is upper triangular with diagonal \(\alpha_i\beta_i\). Every eigenvalue of \(AB\) is therefore such a product.

If the word eigenvalue is restricted to real eigenvalues, the assertion is false: take \(A=B\) to be rotation through \(\pi/2\) in the plane. Neither has real eigenvalues, whereas \(AB=-I\) does.
pitfall: Separate triangularizing bases do not imply that the eigenvalues pair coordinate by coordinate.
note: Eigenvalues must be taken over \(C\). Canonical number 7 is Part \(I\) problem 7.

subject: linear algebra
title: Symmetric eigenvalues and an explicit orthogonal diagonalization
prompt:
(a) Prove real symmetric \(A\) has real eigenvalues. (b) If \(A\) is also orthogonal, identify its eigenvalues. (c) Orthogonally diagonalize 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
hints: Evaluate the quadratic form on a complex eigenvector.
Use the eigenvectors \((1,1)\) and \((1,-1)\) for the example.
solution:
(a) Regard A as a Hermitian complex matrix. If \(Av=\lambda v\), \(v\ne0\), then \(\lambda=(v^*Av)/(v^*v)\) is real because \(v^*Av\) equals its complex conjugate.

(b) Orthogonality implies \(\|Av\|=\|v\|\) even for complex \(v\), so \(|\lambda|=1\). Together with (a), this gives \(\lambda\in\{1,-1\}\).

(c) Unit eigenvectors \(q_1=(1,1)^T/\sqrt2\), \(q_2=(1,-1)^T/\sqrt2\) have eigenvalues 1 and 3. Thus
\[
 Q=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Q^TAQ=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix},\qquad A=Q\operatorname{diag}(1,3)Q^T.
\]
pitfall: An orthogonal matrix alone need not have real eigenvalues; symmetry provides reality.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Similarity to the transpose
prompt: (a) For A in Jordan form, find \(P\) with \(P^2=I\) and \(PAP=A^T\). (b) Prove every complex matrix is similar to its transpose.
hints: Reverse the basis in each Jordan block.
Transfer the block argument through a similarity.
solution:
(a) For a Jordan block \(J_k(\lambda)\), let \(R_k\) be the permutation matrix reversing the order of the \(k\) coordinates. Then \(R_k^2=I\), and reversal moves the superdiagonal ones to the subdiagonal:
\[
 R_kJ_k(\lambda)R_k=J_k(\lambda)^T.
\]
If \(A\) is a direct sum of blocks, take \(P\) to be the direct sum of their reversal matrices. Then \(P^2=I\) and \(PAP=A^T\).

(b) Write \(A=SJS^{-1}\). By (a), \(PJP=J^T\). The invertible matrix \(T=(S^{-1})^TPS^{-1}\) satisfies
\[
 TAT^{-1}=(S^{-1})^TPJP S^T=(S^{-1})^TJ^TS^T=A^T.
\]
So \(A\) and its transpose are similar.
pitfall: Transposing a similarity reverses the order of its factors.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Six similarity and diagonalizability claims
prompt: Decide, with proof or counterexample: (a) a row interchange preserves similarity; (b) a triangular matrix similar to a diagonal matrix is diagonal; (c) products of diagonalizable matrices are diagonalizable; (d) invertible matrices are diagonalizable; (e) \(A\) is never similar to \(A-I\); (f) eigenvalues of A determine those of \(A^TA\).
hints: For false claims look for 2 by 2 examples.
For (e) use a similarity invariant.
solution:
(a) False. Interchanging the rows of \(I_2\) gives \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Their traces are 2 and 0, so they are not similar.

(b) False. \(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\) is triangular and not diagonal, but its distinct eigenvalues imply diagonalizability.

(c) False. Let \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}\). Each has distinct eigenvalues and is diagonalizable, but \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) is a nontrivial Jordan block.

(d) False. The same nontrivial Jordan block at eigenvalue 1 is invertible and not diagonalizable.

(e) True for positive dimension over \(\mathbb R\) or \(\mathbb C\). Similarity preserves trace, whereas \(\operatorname{tr}(A-I)=\operatorname{tr}A-n\ne\operatorname{tr}A\).

(f) False. Both \(A=0\) and \(A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\) have eigenvalues 0,0. Their respective \(A^TA\) have eigenvalues 0,0 and 0,1.
pitfall: Eigenvalues of a nonsymmetric matrix do not determine its singular values.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Independence of distinct-eigenvalue eigenvectors
prompt: Prove eigenvectors belonging to distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
hints: Assume a shortest nontrivial dependence.
Apply A minus one of the eigenvalues times \(I\).
solution:
Let \(Av_j=\lambda_jv_j\), with nonzero \(v_j\) and pairwise distinct \(\lambda_j\). Suppose a nontrivial dependence exists. Choose one involving the least number \(k\) of vectors and relabel it as \(\sum_{j=1}^k c_jv_j=0\), where all \(c_j\ne0\). Since one nonzero vector cannot be dependent, \(k\ge2\). Applying \(A-\lambda_kI\) gives
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{k-1}c_j(\lambda_j-\lambda_k)v_j=0.
\]
Every coefficient here is nonzero, so this is a dependence with fewer vectors, contradicting minimality. Hence no nontrivial dependence exists.
pitfall: The eigenvalues must be distinct; independent vectors within a repeated eigenspace require a separate choice.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: A dual basis and coordinate evaluation
prompt: For \(v_1=(1,1,1)\), \(v_2=(1,1,-1)\), \(v_3=(1,-1,-1)\), find the dual basis via Euclidean inner products and its values at \(x=(0,1,0)\).
hints: Solve the dot-product equations defining the dual basis.
The dual values are the coordinates of \(x\) in the given basis.
solution:
The vectors form a basis (their column matrix has determinant \(-4\)). The Euclidean representatives of its dual functionals are
\[
 y_1=(1/2,0,1/2),\quad
 y_2=(0,1/2,-1/2),\quad
 y_3=(1/2,-1/2,0).
\]
Direct dot products give \(\langle v_i,y_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}\). Thus \(f_j(z)=\langle z,y_j\rangle\) is the dual basis. At \(x=(0,1,0)\),
\[
 f_1(x)=0,\qquad f_2(x)=1/2,\qquad f_3(x)=-1/2.
\]
Indeed \(x=\tfrac12v_2-\tfrac12v_3\), confirming the coordinate interpretation.
pitfall: A nonorthonormal basis is generally not its own dual basis.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Dimension formula for a sum of subspaces
prompt:
Prove 
\[
\dim(V_1+V_2)=\dim V_1+\dim V_2-\dim(V_1\cap V_2)
\]
 for finite-dimensional subspaces.
hints: Map the external direct sum onto the ordinary sum.
Identify its kernel.
solution:
Define the surjective linear map
\[
 T:V_1\oplus V_2\longrightarrow V_1+V_2,\qquad T(u,v)=u+v.
\]
Its kernel consists exactly of pairs \((w,-w)\) with \(w\in V_1\cap V_2\). The map \(w\mapsto(w,-w)\) is an isomorphism onto this kernel, so \(\dim\ker T=\dim(V_1\cap V_2)\). Rank--nullity now gives
\[
 \dim V_1+\dim V_2=\dim(V_1+V_2)+\dim(V_1\cap V_2),
\]
which is the desired formula.
pitfall: The external direct sum consists of pairs even when the subspaces intersect.
note: Canonical numbers 1–8 are Part \(I\); 9–13 are Part II problems 1–5.

subject: linear algebra
title: Transpose as a diagonalizable operator
prompt: For \(T:M_n(\mathbb R)\to M_n(\mathbb R)\), \(T(A)=A^T\), identify the eigenspaces and show \(T\) is diagonalizable.
hints: Split every matrix into symmetric and skew-symmetric parts.
Write bases for those two spaces.
solution:
For every \(A\),
\[
 A=\tfrac12(A+A^T)+\tfrac12(A-A^T).
\]
The first summand is symmetric and satisfies \(T(S)=S\); the second is skew-symmetric and satisfies \(T(K)=-K\). Their intersection is zero, so
\[
 M_n(\mathbb R)=E_1\oplus E_{-1}.
\]
A basis of \(E_1\) is \(E_{ii}\) for \(1\le i\le n\), together with \(E_{ij}+E_{ji}\) for \(i<j\); its dimension is \(n(n+1)/2\). A basis of \(E_{-1}\) is \(E_{ij}-E_{ji}\) for \(i<j\); its dimension is \(n(n-1)/2\). Joining these bases diagonalizes \(T\). For \(n\ge2\) both 1 and -1 occur. For \(n=1\) the skew-symmetric space is zero and 1 is the only eigenvalue.
pitfall: The assertion of exactly two eigenvalues requires \(n\) at least two.
note: The \(n=1\) case has only eigenvalue +1.

subject: linear algebra
title: Evaluating a polynomial on a defective matrix
prompt:
For 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}3&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}
\]
 and any polynomial \(P\), express \(P(A)\) using \(P(2)\) and \(P'(2)\).
hints: Subtract the repeated eigenvalue.
The resulting nilpotent part has square zero.
solution:
Write \(A=2I+N\), where
\[
 N=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad N^2=0.
\]
Polynomial division, or Taylor's formula for a polynomial, gives
\(P(t)=P(2)+P'(2)(t-2)+(t-2)^2Q(t)\).
Substitution yields
\[
 P(A)=P(2)I+P'(2)N
 =\begin{pmatrix}P(2)+P'(2)&P'(2)\\-P'(2)&P(2)-P'(2)\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The derivative term is necessary because \(A\) is a nontrivial Jordan block up to similarity, rather than a scalar matrix.
pitfall: A repeated eigenvalue alone does not justify replacing A by that scalar.

subject: linear algebra
title: Differentiation is not diagonalizable on positive-degree polynomials
prompt: On the polynomials of degree at most \(n\), show differentiation is not diagonalizable.
hints: Repeated differentiation is nilpotent.
A diagonalizable nilpotent operator must vanish.
solution:
Let \(D\) be differentiation on \(\mathcal P_n\). Since degree drops at each differentiation, \(D^{n+1}=0\), so every eigenvalue is zero: if \(Dp=\lambda p\) with \(p\ne0\), then \(0=D^{n+1}p=\lambda^{n+1}p\), forcing \(\lambda=0\). If \(D\) were diagonalizable, a diagonal matrix similar to it would have every diagonal entry zero; hence \(D\) itself would be zero. For \(n\ge1\), however, \(D(t)=1\ne0\), a contradiction.

The necessary exception is \(n=0\): differentiation is the zero operator on constants and is diagonalizable.
pitfall: Nilpotence rules out diagonalizability only for a nonzero operator.
note: The printed claim requires \(n\ge 1\); for \(n=0\) it is false.

subject: linear algebra
title: Representing a real linear functional by an inner product
prompt: For a linear functional \(f\) on a finite-dimensional real inner product space \(V\), prove there is a unique \(v_0\in V\) with \(f(v)=\langle v,v_0\rangle\) for all \(v\).
hints: Use an orthonormal basis.
For uniqueness test the difference of two representatives against itself.
solution:
Choose an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\), and set \(v_0=\sum_jf(e_j)e_j\). If \(v=\sum_jc_je_j\), linearity and orthonormality give
\[
 f(v)=\sum_jc_jf(e_j)=\langle v,v_0\rangle.
\]
This proves existence. If \(w\) is another representative, then \(\langle v,v_0-w\rangle=0\) for every \(v\). Taking \(v=v_0-w\) gives \(\|v_0-w\|^2=0\), hence \(w\) equals \(v_0\). The zero-dimensional case follows with the empty sum.
pitfall: In a complex space the conjugation convention must also be specified; this problem is real.

subject: linear algebra
title: Eigenvalue square sum and normality
prompt:
For a complex matrix \(A\) with eigenvalues \(\lambda_i\) counted with algebraic multiplicity, prove 
\[
\sum_i|\lambda_i|^2\le\operatorname{tr}(A^*A),
\]
 with equality iff \(A\) is normal.
hints: Use unitary triangularization.
The trace on the right is the squared Frobenius norm.
solution:
By Schur triangularization, \(A=UTU^*\), with \(U\) unitary and \(T\) upper triangular. This theorem follows inductively by taking a unit eigenvector as the first basis vector, extending it orthonormally, and triangularizing the remaining compression. The diagonal entries of \(T\) are the eigenvalues, including algebraic multiplicities. Unitary invariance of trace gives
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(A^*A)=\operatorname{tr}(T^*T)
 =\sum_{i,j}|t_{ij}|^2
 =\sum_i|\lambda_i|^2+\sum_{i<j}|t_{ij}|^2.
\]
This proves the inequality. Equality means every strictly upper triangular entry of \(T\) vanishes, so \(A\) is unitarily diagonalizable and therefore normal. Conversely, the spectral theorem unitarily diagonalizes any normal \(A\); in that basis the last off-diagonal sum is zero, giving equality.
pitfall: The trace here is a sum of squared absolute entries, not a sum of squared entries without conjugation.

subject: linear algebra
title: Two variational formulas for the largest Hermitian eigenvalue
prompt:
For Hermitian \(A\), (a) prove \(\lambda_{\max}=\max_{\|x\|=1}x^*Ax\); (b) if \(A\) has a positive eigenvalue, prove 
\[
\lambda_{\max}=\max_{x^*Ax=1}\frac{1}{x^*x}.
\]
hints: Expand in an orthonormal eigenbasis.
Scale a top eigenvector to satisfy the second constraint.
solution:
(a) If \(x=\sum_jc_je_j\) in an orthonormal eigenbasis, then \(x^*Ax=\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2\). For unit \(x\) these coefficients sum to one, so the value is at most \(\lambda_{\max}\). A unit eigenvector for \(\lambda_{\max}\) attains it.

(b) The positive-eigenvalue hypothesis gives \(\lambda_{\max}>0\). For any \(x\) satisfying \(x^*Ax=1\), the bound from (a), applied after normalization, gives
\[
 1\le\lambda_{\max}x^*x,\qquad 1/(x^*x)\le\lambda_{\max}.
\]
If \(u\) is a unit top eigenvector, \(x=u/\sqrt{\lambda_{\max}}\) satisfies the constraint and attains equality. Thus a maximum exists even though the constraint set need not be compact. \(A\) need not be positive definite for this formula.
pitfall: Do not assume the second constraint surface is compact when \(A\) is indefinite.

subject: linear algebra
title: Multiplication and differentiation in a polynomial inner product
prompt:
On \(\mathcal P_n(\mathbb C)\) with 
\[
\langle p,q\rangle=\int_0^1p(t)\overline{q(t)}\,dt,
\]
 consider (a) \(Tp(t)=tp(t)\), claimed self-adjoint, and (b) \(Dp=p'\), claimed not self-adjoint.
hints: First check that each formula maps the stated space to itself.
For differentiation test \(p=t\) and \(q=1\).
solution:
(a) As written, \(T\) is not an operator from \(\mathcal P_n\) to itself: \(T(t^n)=t^{n+1}\notin\mathcal P_n\). Thus self-adjointness on that finite-dimensional space is not defined. The formal identity
\[
 \int_0^1tp(t)\overline{q(t)}\,dt
 =\int_0^1p(t)\overline{tq(t)}\,dt
\]
is valid, but does not repair the domain defect. On \(L^2[0,1]\), multiplication by \(t\) is a bounded self-adjoint operator. Alternatively, on \(\mathcal P_n\), the orthogonal compression \(S=\Pi_n T|_{\mathcal P_n}\) is self-adjoint: for \(p\),\(q\) in the subspace, \(\langle Sp,q\rangle=\langle Tp,q\rangle=\langle p,Tq\rangle=\langle p,Sq\rangle\).

(b) Differentiation does map \(\mathcal P_n\) to itself. For \(n\ge1\), take \(p=t,q=1\). Then \(\langle Dp,q\rangle=1\), whereas \(\langle p,Dq\rangle=0\), proving it is not self-adjoint. For \(n=0\), \(D\) is zero and is self-adjoint.
pitfall: An integral symmetry identity does not establish self-adjointness until the operator's domain and codomain are correct.
note: SOURCE ERROR: multiplication by \(t\) does not preserve \(P_n\); differentiation's non-self-adjointness also requires \(n\ge 1\).

subject: linear algebra
title: Orientation-preserving orthogonal maps are rotations in dimensions two and three
prompt: Show a real orthogonal matrix with determinant one is (a) a rotation in dimension two and (b) a rotation about an axis in dimension three.
hints: In dimension two use orthonormal columns and orientation.
In dimension three find an eigenvector for eigenvalue one.
solution:
(a) Write the first column as \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)^T\). The second column must be a perpendicular unit vector, and determinant one selects \((-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)^T\). Thus the matrix is the usual plane rotation.

(b) The complex eigenvalues of a real orthogonal matrix have modulus one, with nonreal eigenvalues paired with their conjugates. Every such pair has product one. The real eigenvalues are therefore +1 or -1. In odd dimension at least one eigenvalue is real. Since the product of all eigenvalues is one, a three-dimensional matrix must have an eigenvalue +1: if a nonreal pair occurs, the remaining real eigenvalue is +1; if all are real, three -1 values would have product -1.

Choose a unit real vector \(e\) fixed by \(O\). Since \(O^{-1}e=e\), also \(O^Te=e\), and \(e^\perp\) is invariant: \(\langle Ox,e\rangle=\langle x,O^Te\rangle=0\) for \(x\) perpendicular to \(e\). In an orthonormal basis starting with \(e\), the matrix is \(1\oplus R\), with \(R\) orthogonal and determinant one. Part (a) shows \(R\) is a plane rotation. Thus \(O\) is rotation around the line spanned by \(e\). The identity is the zero-angle case with any axis.
pitfall: A fixed axis is needed before restricting to its perpendicular plane.

subject: analysis
title: A directional obstruction to continuity
prompt: Decide continuity at zero of \(f(x,y)=e^{-\frac{xy}{x^2+y^2}}\) off zero and \(f(0,0)=1\).
hints: Compare a coordinate axis with the diagonal.
A single path with a different limit disproves continuity.
solution:
Along the \(x\)-axis, \(f(t,0)=1\) for \(t\ne0\). Along \(y=x=t\ne0\),
\[
 f(t,t)=e^{-t^2/(2t^2)}=e^{-1/2}\ne1.
\]
In particular \(f(t,t)\) does not tend to the value at the origin. Thus the function is not continuous there, and indeed its limit at zero does not exist.
pitfall: Checking only the coordinate axes misses the mixed term in the exponent.

subject: analysis
title: A higher-order bound gives zero derivative
prompt: For open \(A\ni0\) and \(f:A\to\mathbb R^m\), assume \(\|f(x)\|\le\|x\|^p\) with an integer \(p>1\). Prove differentiability at zero and compute \(Df(0)\).
hints: The bound first determines the value at zero.
Divide by the increment norm.
solution:
The inequality at zero gives \(f(0)=0\). Since \(A\) is open, sufficiently small increments \(h\) lie in \(A\). For nonzero such \(h\),
\[
 \frac{\|f(h)-f(0)-0h\|}{\|h\|}
 \le\|h\|^{p-1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus \(f\) is Fréchet differentiable at zero and \(Df(0)\) is the zero linear map. No differentiability elsewhere or continuity hypothesis is required.
pitfall: The result is local at zero; it does not force \(f\) to be constant elsewhere.

subject: analysis
title: A contraction condition for a nonlinear integral equation
prompt:
For 
\[
Tu(t)=\int_0^1K(s,t)f(s,u(s))\,ds
\]
 on \(C([0,1],[0,1])\), with continuous \(K,f\) and continuous \(f_u\), derive sufficient conditions for a solution of \(u=Tu+\varepsilon\), \(\varepsilon\ne0\).
hints: Check both invariance of the range interval and a contraction estimate.
Use a uniform bound on the derivative in the second argument.
solution:
Equip \(X=C([0,1],[0,1])\) with the uniform distance. It is a closed subset of the complete space \(C([0,1],\mathbb R)\), hence complete. Write \(\Phi u=Tu+\varepsilon\). Continuity of the integrand on a compact set, and uniform continuity of \(K\) in \(t\), imply that \(\Phi u\) is continuous.

For \(s,t\in[0,1]\), define
\[
 \ell(s,t)=\min_{0\le v\le1}K(s,t)f(s,v),\qquad
 h(s,t)=\max_{0\le v\le1}K(s,t)f(s,v).
\]
If for every \(t\)
\[
 0\le\varepsilon+\int_0^1\ell(s,t)\,ds,\qquad
 \varepsilon+\int_0^1h(s,t)\,ds\le1,
\]
then \(0\le\Phi u(t)\le1\), so \(\Phi\) maps \(X\) into itself. These are sufficient, not asserted necessary, conditions for invariance.

Let \(L(s)=\max_{0\le v\le1}|f_u(s,v)|\). The mean value theorem gives
\[
 \|\Phi u-\Phi v\|_\infty
 \le q\|u-v\|_\infty,\qquad
 q=\max_t\int_0^1|K(s,t)|L(s)\,ds.
\]
If \(q<1\), Banach's contraction theorem gives a unique fixed point in \(X\), hence a solution of the required equation.

A simpler checkable sufficient version is \(0<\varepsilon<1\), \(\kappa M\le\min(\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon)\), and \(\kappa L<1\), where \(\kappa=\max_t\int|K(s,t)|\,ds\), \(M=\max|f|\), and \(L=\max|f_u|\). The first inequality ensures invariance even without sign assumptions, and the second ensures contraction. For other nonzero \(\varepsilon\), the general invariance inequalities may still apply.
pitfall: A contraction estimate alone is insufficient on \(C([0,1],[0,1])\); the operator must keep its values in the interval.

subject: analysis
title: When a continuous weight defines a complete norm
prompt: On \(C([0,1],\mathbb R)\), set \(\|f\|_r=\sup_t|f(t)r(t)|\) with continuous \(r\). (a) Characterize when this is a norm. (b) For \(r(t)=e^{-at}\), \(a>0\), prove completeness.
hints: A continuous function is detected by a weight whose nonzero set is dense.
The exponential weight has a positive lower bound.
solution:
Homogeneity and the triangle inequality always hold. Definiteness holds exactly when the zero set of \(r\) has empty relative interior in \([0,1]\), or equivalently when \(\{r\ne0\}\) is dense. Indeed, if \(\|f\|_r=0\), then \(f=0\) on this dense nonzero set, hence everywhere by continuity. Conversely, if \(r=0\) on a nonempty relative open interval, choose a nonzero continuous bump supported inside that interval. Its weighted norm is zero, so definiteness fails. Endpoint intervals admit one-sided bumps as well.

For \(r(t)=e^{-at}\),
\[
 e^{-a}\|f\|_\infty\le\|f\|_r\le\|f\|_\infty.
\]
A weighted-norm Cauchy sequence is therefore uniformly Cauchy, so converges uniformly to a continuous \(f\). The upper inequality then gives convergence in the weighted norm too. Thus the space is complete. A nowhere-zero weight is sufficient for a norm, but not necessary: the isolated zeros of, for example, \(r(t)=t\) do not destroy definiteness.
pitfall: Do not require pointwise nonvanishing in (a); continuous functions cannot be supported at an isolated zero.

subject: analysis
title: Integrating a uniformly convergent trigonometric series
prompt:
Evaluate 
\[
\int_0^{2\pi}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\cos^2(nx)}{n^2+n}\,dx.
\]
hints: Bound every term by a telescoping scalar majorant.
Each squared cosine has the same integral over this interval.
solution:
Since \(0\le\cos^2(nx)/(n^2+n)\le1/(n(n+1))\) and the majorant sums to one, the series converges uniformly by the Weierstrass test. Uniform convergence on the finite interval permits termwise integration. The identity \(\cos^2(nx)=(1+\cos(2nx))/2\) gives integral \(\pi\) for each \(n\ge1\). Hence
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\cos^2(nx)}{n(n+1)}\,dx
 =\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty\left(\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right)=\boxed\pi.
\]
pitfall: Justify exchanging the sum and integral; the uniform majorant is immediate here.

subject: analysis
title: Relative openness and compact complements
prompt: (a) If \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\) is closed and \(B\subset A\) is relatively open, prove \(A\setminus B\) is closed. (b) If continuous injective \(f\) maps compact \(A\) into a metric space and \(f(B)\) is open in the target, prove \(f(A\setminus B)\) is compact.
hints: Write a relatively open set as an ambient open set intersected with \(A\).
Injectivity identifies the preimage of the image of \(B\).
solution:
(a) Relative openness gives \(B=A\cap U\) for an open \(U\subset\mathbb R^n\). Then \(A\setminus B=A\cap(\mathbb R^n\setminus U)\), an intersection of two closed sets.

(b) Since \(f\) is injective, \(f^{-1}(f(B))=B\). Continuity and openness of \(f(B)\) make \(B\) relatively open in \(A\), so \(A\setminus B\) is relatively closed in compact \(A\), hence compact. Its continuous image \(f(A\setminus B)\) is compact in the target. Alternatively, injectivity gives \(f(A\setminus B)=f(A)\setminus f(B)\), a closed subset of the compact set \(f(A)\).
pitfall: Without injectivity, the preimage of \(f(B)\) may contain points outside \(B\).

subject: analysis
title: Uniform convergence of a spreading Gaussian profile
prompt:
For real \(p\), determine when 
\[
f_n(x)=\frac{x e^{-\frac{x^2}{n^2}}}{n^p}
\]
 converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R\).
hints: Find the pointwise candidates first.
Maximize the absolute value using \(x\) divided by \(n\).
solution:
For fixed \(x\), the exponential factor tends to one. If \(p>0\), the pointwise limit is zero; if \(p=0\), it is \(x\); if \(p<0\), the sequence diverges at every nonzero \(x\), so uniform convergence is impossible.

For \(p>0\), set \(t=|x|/n\). Then
\[
 \|f_n\|_\infty=n^{1-p}\sup_{t\ge0}t e^{-t^2}
 =\frac{n^{1-p}}{\sqrt{2e}},
\]
because the maximum occurs at \(t=1/\sqrt2\). This tends to zero exactly when \(p>1\). For \(0<p\le1\) it does not, so convergence is not uniform.

For \(p=0\), each \(f_n\) is bounded while the pointwise limit \(x\) is unbounded; in fact \(\sup_x|f_n(x)-x|=\infty\). Thus uniform convergence fails there as well. The full answer is \(\boxed{p>1}\).
pitfall: The moving maximum lies at a point of order \(n\), invisible to fixed-\(x\) pointwise limits.

subject: analysis
title: Area from Green's theorem and an arc-length bound
prompt:
Let \(T_1\) be \((x-2)^2+y^2=4,\ y\le0\), and \(T_2\) the graph on \([0,4]\) of nonnegative \(f\) with \(f(0)=f(4)=0\), 
\[
\int_0^4f=\frac{1}{2}.
\]
 (a) Parametrize \(T_1\) counterclockwise. (b) Integrate \(F=(x^2,x-y^2)\) around the region between them counterclockwise. (c) Prove an increasing differentiable graph on \([0,L]\) has length at most \(L+g(L)-g(0)\).
hints: The lower semicircle is traversed left to right for this orientation.
The curl is constant; the length estimate follows already for each polygonal approximation.
solution:
(a) A parametrization is
\[
 \gamma(\theta)=(2+2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta),\qquad \pi\le\theta\le2\pi.
\]
It moves from \((0,0)\) to \((4,0)\) through the lower half-plane, counterclockwise around the circle and with the region on its left.

(b) Under the customary regularity of the graph needed for a classical line integral and Green's theorem, the scalar curl is
\[
 \partial_x(x-y^2)-\partial_y(x^2)=1.
\]
The region's area is the lower semicircle area \(2\pi\) plus the area under \(f\), \(1/2\). Thus the integral is \(\boxed{2\pi+1/2}\). One may also note \(x^2\,dx-y^2\,dy\) is exact, leaving \(\oint x\,dy\) as the area integral. The printed data alone do not explicitly impose graph regularity; a discontinuous or nonrectifiable graph would require additional interpretation.

(c) The condition \(g'>0\) implies monotonic increase by the mean value theorem. For any partition \(0=x_0<\cdots<x_k=L\), the sum of successive chord lengths is bounded by
\[
 \sum_i\sqrt{(x_i-x_{i-1})^2+(g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1}))^2}
 \le\sum_i[(x_i-x_{i-1})+(g(x_i)-g(x_{i-1}))]
 =L+g(L)-g(0).
\]
Taking the supremum over partitions proves rectifiability and the asserted bound without assuming continuity of \(g'\).
pitfall: Keep the boundary orientation consistent, and avoid assuming a differentiable graph has a continuous derivative.
note: Classical line integration in (b) implicitly needs a regular graph boundary.

subject: analysis
title: Removing the critical set in change of variables
prompt: Let \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open, bounded and have volume, and let \(g:A\to\mathbb R^n\) be injective and \(C^1\), with \(g(A)\) also having volume. For bounded Riemann integrable \(f\) on \(g(A)\), the change-of-variables formula is granted on noncritical subsets. Put \(B=\{Jg=0\}\). (a) Prove null sets in \(g(C)\) have null preimages when \(0<m_1\le|Jg|\le m_2\) on noncritical \(C\subset A\). (b) Assuming \(A\setminus B\) has volume and using the granted fact that \(g(B)\) is null, extend the formula across \(B\).
hints: Use covers of a null set, not its possibly nonintegrable indicator.
The critical set contributes zero on the domain and a null image on the target.
solution:
Write volume as \(|\cdot|\) and Jacobian determinant as \(Jg\). Here a set having volume means Jordan measurable in the bounded Riemann setting.

(a) For an admissible subset \(E\subset C\), the granted substitution formula applied to the constant function one gives
\[
 |g(E)|=\int_E|Jg|\ge m_1|E|.
\]
Consequently inverse images of small target regions have volume at most their target volume divided by \(m_1\). Cover a null set \(S\) by open boxes of arbitrarily small total volume and apply this bound to their preimages, using outer approximations if a preimage does not itself have Jordan volume. This gives outer measure at most \(\delta/m_1\) for \(g^{-1}(S)\), for every \(\delta>0\), hence zero.

For completeness, the passage to null preimages does not require an unproved global regularity claim about those sets. At any noncritical point, the inverse function theorem supplies a \(C^1\) local inverse. On a sufficiently small closed target ball its derivative is bounded; the segment mean value estimate makes it Lipschitz there. A Lipschitz map takes a null set to a null set: cover by sufficiently small cubes, whose images lie in cubes with volumes bounded by a fixed constant times the original volumes. Countably many such inverse charts cover the image of the noncritical locus, by the countable basis of Euclidean space. Countable unions of null sets are null. This proves the claim even without global Jacobian bounds. It also justifies the local outer approximations in the volume argument. One must not assume that the indicator of an arbitrary dense null set is Riemann integrable.

(b) Put \(U=A\setminus B=\{Jg\ne0\}\). This is open. The local inverse theorem makes \(g(U)\) open, and
\[
 \partial g(U)\subset\partial g(A)\cup g(B).
\]
Indeed any boundary point lying in \(g(A)\) cannot belong to the open subset \(g(U)\), and must therefore be in \(g(B)\); boundary points outside \(g(A)\) lie in its boundary. Thus \(g(U)\) has volume when \(g(A)\) does, because \(g(B)\) is null. Restrict a bounded integrable \(f\) on \(g(A)\) to \(g(U)\). Its zero extension changes discontinuities only on the null boundary and critical image, so it remains integrable and
\[
 \int_{g(A)}f=\int_{g(U)}f.
\]
The granted noncritical substitution formula yields
\[
 \int_{g(U)}f=\int_U f(g(x))|Jg(x)|\,dx.
\]
The integrand is identically zero on \(B\). Since \(U\) has volume by assumption, extending the integral from \(U\) to \(A\) does not change it, giving the requested formula.

There is a necessary convention concerning this last step. The printed assumptions \(C^1\) on an open bounded set alone do not ensure a bounded transformed integrand. For example \(A=(0,1)\), \(g(x)=\sqrt{x}\), and \(f=1\) give \(Jg=1/(2\sqrt{x})\), which is unbounded and not properly Riemann integrable, although its improper integral is one. The exam's granted noncritical formula must therefore be read with improper integrals where necessary, or with additional boundedness of the transformed integrand. In the bounded Riemann version, the zero-extension argument above is legitimate by the Jordan measurability of \(U\); a sufficient added condition is bounded \(Dg\). In the generalized version, apply the same argument to positive and negative parts via exhaustion: their integrals are finite, bounded by \(\|f\|_\infty|g(A)|\), and the zero critical contribution remains zero.
pitfall: Do not use a dense null set's indicator as a Riemann integrand. Also distinguish a proper bounded Riemann integral from an improper transformed integral.
note: The printed C1-on-open-set assumptions do not guarantee a bounded transformed integrand; the granted formula requires an improper-integral convention or extra boundedness.

subject: analysis
title: Pointwise limits and an incomplete integral norm
prompt:
On compact \(K\subset\mathbb R\): (a) give a discontinuous pointwise limit of continuous functions; (b) give an example of incompleteness under 
\[
\|f\|=\int_K|f|;
\]
 (c) prove a uniform limit is uniformly continuous.
hints: For (a) use powers on the unit interval.
For (b) approximate a jump by a narrow continuous ramp.
solution:
(a) Take \(K=[0,1]\) and \(f_n(x)=x^n\). The pointwise limit is zero for \(x<1\) and one at \(1\), hence discontinuous.

(b) On \(K=[0,1]\), for \(n\ge2\), let \(f_n\) be zero on \([0,1/2]\), equal to \(n(x-1/2)\) on \([1/2,1/2+1/n]\), and one afterwards. Each \(f_n\) is continuous. Let \(s\) be the step function zero below \(1/2\) and one above it, with any value at the midpoint. Direct integration gives \(\int|f_n-s|=1/(2n)\), so the triangle inequality makes \((f_n)\) Cauchy in the integral norm. If it converged to a continuous \(h\) in that norm, the same triangle inequality would give \(\int|h-s|=0\). Continuity forces \(h=0\) on \((0,1/2)\) and \(h=1\) on \((1/2,1)\), since any nonzero difference there persists on an interval. Such an \(h\) cannot be continuous at \(1/2\). Thus the space is incomplete. For a general compact \(K\), the displayed integral may even be only a seminorm (for instance if \(K\) is null); the interval example supplies an actual norm and proves the requested failure.

(c) Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\) with \(\|f-f_N\|_\infty<\varepsilon/3\). The continuous \(f_N\) is uniformly continuous on compact \(K\), so for some \(\delta>0\), nearby points have \(f_N\)-values differing by less than \(\varepsilon/3\). Adding the two uniform approximation errors gives \(|f(x)-f(y)|<\varepsilon\).
pitfall: An integral-norm limit need not be continuous. On arbitrary compact sets, first check that the integral is a genuine norm.

subject: analysis
title: Boundary crossing and Euclidean connectedness
prompt: (a) Prove a clopen \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\) has empty boundary. (b) Prove a segment from a point of bounded nonempty \(A\) to a point outside \(A\) meets its boundary. (c) Prove the only clopen subsets are empty and all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
hints: The boundary is closure minus interior.
The first time the path leaves the interior is a boundary point.
solution:
(a) Since \(A\) is closed, \(\overline A=A\); since it is open, \(A^\circ=A\). Therefore \(\partial A=\overline A\setminus A^\circ=\varnothing\).

(b) Let \(\phi(t)=(1-t)x+ty\) with \(x\in A\), \(y\notin A\). If \(x\in\partial A\), take \(t^*=0\). Otherwise \(x\in A^\circ\). The set \(Z=\{t\in[0,1]:\phi(t)\notin A^\circ\}\) is closed and nonempty (it contains \(1\)), so has a least element \(t^*>0\). For every \(t<t^*\), \(\phi(t)\in A^\circ\). Continuity gives \(\phi(t^*)\in\overline A\); membership in \(Z\) gives \(\phi(t^*)\notin A^\circ\). Thus it belongs to \(\partial A\). This proof does not need boundedness.

(c) If a clopen \(A\) were nonempty and proper, choose \(x\in A\), \(y\notin A\). The strengthened version of (b), valid also for unbounded sets, gives a boundary point, contradicting (a). Hence \(A\) is empty or all of Euclidean space. The stronger observation is needed because the literal bounded version of (b) alone would not cover unbounded proper clopen sets.
pitfall: The boundary-crossing proof works for arbitrary subsets; boundedness is an unnecessary printed hypothesis in (b).

subject: analysis
title: Riemann integrability and dense zeros
prompt:
(a) Prove \(|f|\) is Riemann integrable if bounded \(f\) is. (b) If bounded Riemann integrable \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) has a zero in every nonempty open subinterval, prove 
\[
\int_0^1f=0.
\]
hints: Absolute value does not increase oscillation.
Every lower sum of the nonnegative absolute value is zero.
solution:
(a) On every subinterval \(I\), the inequality \(||f(x)|-|f(y)||\le|f(x)-f(y)|\) gives \(\operatorname{osc}_I|f|\le\operatorname{osc}_I f\). Therefore for every partition, the upper-minus-lower Darboux sum for \(|f|\) is at most that for \(f\). The Darboux criterion proves integrability.

(b) By (a), \(|f|\) is integrable. Every nondegenerate partition subinterval contains a zero in its interior, so the infimum of \(|f|\) there is zero. All lower sums are therefore zero, and the integral of \(|f|\) is zero. It follows that \(|\int f|\le\int|f|=0\). The quantified intervals are understood to have endpoints \(a<b\); otherwise the request for a point in \((a,b)\) would be impossible.
pitfall: Dense zeros alone do not force a function to vanish; Riemann integrability is what makes their zero lower sums determine the integral.

subject: analysis
title: A series uniform on a bounded interval but not on a half-line
prompt:
Determine pointwise and uniform convergence of 
\[
\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{x^2}{n(n+x^2)}
\]
 on (a) \((0,1)\), (b) \((1,\infty)\).
hints: For a fixed bounded \(x\) compare with one over \(n^2\).
For large \(x\), a long finite block approaches a harmonic block.
solution:
For every fixed real \(x\), the terms are nonnegative and at most \(x^2/n^2\), so the series converges pointwise.

(a) On \((0,1)\), every term is at most \(1/n^2\). The Weierstrass test gives uniform convergence.

(b) On \((1,\infty)\), suppose the uniform Cauchy criterion held. Choose any \(N\ge1\). For the finite tail block,
\[
 \lim_{x\to\infty}\sum_{n=N+1}^{2N}\frac{x^2}{n(n+x^2)}
 =\sum_{n=N+1}^{2N}\frac1n\ge\frac12.
\]
Hence its supremum over \(x>1\) is at least \(1/2\), for every \(N\). Taking, for example, the uniform Cauchy tolerance \(1/4\) gives a contradiction. Thus the series is pointwise convergent but not uniformly convergent on the half-line.
pitfall: The individual term suprema tend to zero, which is necessary but not sufficient for uniform series convergence. Use a full tail block.

subject: analysis
title: Differentiability thresholds for two powers
prompt:
Find all real \(\alpha\) for which 
\[
f(x,y)=\frac{|x|^{3\alpha}+|y|^{7-\alpha}}{x^2+y^2},
\]
 with value zero at zero, is differentiable there.
hints: The function is even, so any derivative at zero must be zero.
Compare both numerator powers with the third power of the radius.
solution:
Whenever the expression defines a real function on a neighborhood of zero, it is even under \((x,y)\mapsto(-x,-y)\). If a derivative \(L\) existed, the two differentiability expansions would imply \(Lh=-Lh\), hence \(L=0\). Thus differentiability requires \(f(h)=o(|h|)\).

Along \(x=y=t>0\), with \(r=\sqrt2t\),
\[
 \frac{f(t,t)}r=\frac1{2\sqrt2}\left(t^{3\alpha-3}+t^{4-\alpha}\right).
\]
The terms are nonnegative. This can tend to zero only if \(3\alpha-3>0\) and \(4-\alpha>0\), that is \(1<\alpha<4\). Outside the natural domain of positive exponents, the formula can additionally fail to be defined on the axes; in any event it cannot yield differentiability.

Conversely, if \(1<\alpha<4\), both numerator exponents are positive. For \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}>0\),
\[
 \frac{|f(x,y)|}{r}\le r^{3\alpha-3}+r^{4-\alpha}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore \(f\) is differentiable with zero derivative. The answer is \(\boxed{1<\alpha<4}\); equality at either endpoint gives a nonzero radial-size term and fails.
pitfall: Differentiability needs an error small relative to \(r\), not merely a function tending to zero. The borderline absolute-value powers do not produce a linear derivative.

subject: analysis
title: Justified integration of a conditionally convergent series
prompt:
(a) Prove 
\[
\int_0^\infty\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^{n+1}e^{-nx}\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n}.
\]
 (b) Deduce that the sum is \(\log2\).
hints: Sum the finite geometric series and estimate its integrated remainder.
The infinite geometric sum is one over one plus \(e\) to the \(x\).
solution:
For \(x>0\), the geometric series sums to \(g(x)=e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})=1/(1+e^x)\). Its partial sum \(g_N\) satisfies
\[
 g_N(x)=\frac{e^{-x}(1-(-e^{-x})^N)}{1+e^{-x}},\qquad
 |g(x)-g_N(x)|\le e^{-(N+1)x}.
\]
Thus
\[
 \int_0^\infty|g-g_N|\,dx\le\frac1{N+1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Each finite sum can be integrated termwise, giving \(\int g_N=\sum_{n=1}^N(-1)^{n+1}/n\). The integrated remainder proves (a), without an unjustified interchange of a conditionally convergent series.

At \(x=0\), the displayed infinite series is the divergent alternating string of ones. Its integral is understood over \(x>0\), or with the summed function assigned the continuous endpoint value \(g(0)=1/2\). Changing one endpoint value has no effect on the integral.

For (b), the substitution \(u=e^{-x}\) gives
\[
 \int_0^\infty\frac{e^{-x}}{1+e^{-x}}\,dx=\int_0^1\frac{du}{1+u}=\log2.
\]
Together with (a) this establishes the alternating harmonic sum.
pitfall: The series of integrals is not absolutely convergent, and the integrand series is undefined at the endpoint zero. The explicit remainder handles both issues.

subject: linear algebra
title: Polynomial row and column operations
prompt:
For 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}x-1&1\\0&x-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
 find invertible polynomial-entry \(P,Q\) making \(PAQ\) diagonal.
hints: Move the constant entry to the top left.
Clear its column and row with polynomial operations.
solution:
Put \(a=x-1\). Swap the columns, then subtract \(a\) times the first row from the second, and finally subtract \(a\) times the first column from the second. Explicitly,
\[
 P=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-a&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&-a\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Their determinants are \(1,-1\), so they are invertible for every \(x\) and have polynomial inverses. Direct multiplication gives
\[
 AQ=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\a&-a^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 PAQ=\operatorname{diag}(1,-(x-1)^2).
\]
The resulting diagonal matrix may be singular at \(x=1\); only \(P,Q\) were required invertible.
pitfall: This is left-right equivalence, not similarity; different changes are allowed on the two sides.

subject: linear algebra
title: Products in opposite order share their eigenvalues
prompt: Prove \(AB\) and \(BA\), for square matrices over a field, have the same set of eigenvalues.
hints: For a nonzero eigenvalue, transfer an eigenvector by \(B\).
Handle zero using determinants.
solution:
Suppose \(ABv=\lambda v\) with \(v\ne0\) and \(\lambda\ne0\). Then \(Bv\ne0\), since otherwise \(ABv=0\). Moreover \(BA(Bv)=B(ABv)=\lambda Bv\), so \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(BA\). Exchanging \(A,B\) gives the reverse implication. For zero, \(AB\) is singular exactly when
\[
 \det(AB)=\det A\det B=\det(BA)=0.
\]
Singularity of a square matrix over a field is equivalent to a nontrivial kernel, hence to zero being an eigenvalue. This proves equality of the sets, either over the original field or after extending scalars.
pitfall: The transferred vector can vanish when the eigenvalue is zero, so that case needs a separate argument.

subject: linear algebra
title: Testing four matrices for unitary diagonalization
prompt:
Which of 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&i\\-i&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},
\]
 
\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&2\end{pmatrix}
\]
 are unitarily similar to diagonal matrices?
hints: Unitary diagonalizability is equivalent to normality.
Hermitian is sufficient but not necessary.
solution:
The first matrix is Hermitian, so the spectral theorem gives unitary diagonalization. The second is \(I+K\), with \(K=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(K^*=-K\). Direct multiplication gives \(HH^*=H^*H=2I\), so it is normal and unitarily diagonalizable over \(\mathbb C\), with eigenvalues \(1\pm i\).

The third matrix \(N\) is nonzero and \(N^2=0\). A diagonalizable nilpotent matrix would have only zeros on its diagonal and hence be zero, so \(N\) is not even diagonalizable.

For the fourth matrix \(T\),
\[
 TT^*=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 T^*T=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&5\end{pmatrix}.
\]
These differ, so \(T\) is not normal and cannot be unitarily diagonalized, despite having distinct eigenvalues and being diagonalizable by an unrestricted similarity.
pitfall: Distinct eigenvalues imply diagonalizability but do not imply unitary diagonalizability.

subject: linear algebra
title: Cauchy--Schwarz directly from a quadratic form
prompt:
For symmetric positive definite real \(A\), define \(\langle x,y\rangle=x^TAy\) and directly prove 
\[
|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle\langle y,y\rangle}.
\]
hints: Expand positivity on \(x\) minus a scalar multiple of \(y\).
Choose the scalar minimizing the quadratic.
solution:
If \(y=0\), the assertion is immediate. Otherwise positive definiteness gives \(b=\langle y,y\rangle>0\). Symmetry and bilinearity imply for all real \(t\)
\[
 0\le\langle x-ty,x-ty\rangle
 =\langle x,x\rangle-2t\langle x,y\rangle+t^2b.
\]
Take \(t=\langle x,y\rangle/b\). The result is
\[
 0\le\langle x,x\rangle-\frac{\langle x,y\rangle^2}{b},
\]
which proves the squared inequality and then the asserted one. Equality holds precisely when \(x-ty=0\), including zero-vector cases; hence precisely for linearly dependent \(x,y\). This stronger absolute-value form implies the printed one-sided inequality as well.
pitfall: The cross terms combine because \(A\) is symmetric. Positivity without symmetry would not define this inner product.

subject: linear algebra
title: Eigenvalues of differentiation and commutator operators
prompt: Solve both offered alternatives: (a) on real polynomials of degree at most three, \(Tp=p''+2p'+p\); (b) on \(M_2(\mathbb C)\), \(TB=AB-BA\) for \(A=\operatorname{diag}(1,4)\). Find eigenvalues with multiplicities.
hints: Differentiation lowers degree.
For a diagonal \(A\), each matrix unit is an eigenvector of its commutator action.
solution:
(a) In the basis \(1,t,t^2,t^3\), differentiation is strictly upper triangular. Thus \(T=I+2D+D^2\) has upper triangular matrix
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}1&2&2&0\\0&1&4&6\\0&0&1&6\\0&0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Its only eigenvalue is \(1\), with algebraic multiplicity four. To give the geometric multiplicity too, \(T-I=D(2I+D)\), where \(2I+D\) is invertible and commutes with \(D\); thus its kernel equals \(\ker D\), the constants, and has dimension one.

(b) For matrix units \(E_{ij}\), \(AE_{ij}-E_{ij}A=(a_i-a_j)E_{ij}\), where \(a_1=1,a_2=4\). Hence \(E_{11},E_{22}\) have eigenvalue \(0\), \(E_{12}\) has eigenvalue \(-3\), and \(E_{21}\) has eigenvalue \(3\). These four units form a basis, so \(0\) has multiplicity two, \(-3,3\) multiplicity one each, and this operator is diagonalizable.
pitfall: Multiplicity for a polynomial operator is counted in the dimension of the polynomial space, not the degree of one chosen input.

subject: linear algebra
title: Eigenvalue existence and absence of generalized chains
prompt:
Solve both alternatives: (a) prove an endomorphism of a nontrivial finite-dimensional complex vector space has an eigenpair; (b) if 
\[
\ker(\lambda I-A)\cap\operatorname{range}(\lambda I-A)=\{0\}
\]
 for all complex \(\lambda\), prove \(A\) has an eigenbasis.
hints: Use a root of the characteristic polynomial.
For (b), split off one eigenspace using rank--nullity and induct.
solution:
(a) If \(d=\dim V>0\), the monic characteristic polynomial has degree \(d\), hence a complex root \(\lambda\) by the fundamental theorem of algebra. Then \(\lambda I-A\) is singular and has a nonzero kernel vector, giving an eigenpair. The operator may itself be zero; only the space needs positive dimension.

(b) We induct on \(d\), with the zero-dimensional case trivial. Choose an eigenvalue \(\lambda\), and put \(K=\ker(\lambda I-A)\), \(R=\operatorname{range}(\lambda I-A)\). The hypothesis and rank--nullity give \(V=K\oplus R\). Both are \(A\)-invariant, because \(A\) commutes with \(\lambda I-A\). On \(K\), \(A=\lambda I\), so any basis is an eigenbasis. Since \(K\ne0\), \(\dim R<d\). For every \(\mu\), the kernel and range of \(\mu I-A|_R\) are contained in the respective full-space kernel and range, so their intersection is zero. The induction hypothesis supplies an eigenbasis of \(R\). Joining the two bases gives an eigenbasis of \(V\).

Equivalently, a Jordan block of size at least two produces an eigenvector that is also the image of a generalized eigenvector, violating the intersection hypothesis.
pitfall: Part (a) requires a nontrivial space, not a nonzero operator. The range complement in (b) is invariant and must inherit the hypothesis.

subject: linear algebra
title: Primary decomposition, compressions, and a cyclic commutant
prompt:
Solve all three offered alternatives: (a) if \(\chi_A=p_1p_2\) with coprime real factors, prove 
\[
\mathbb R^n=\ker p_1(A)\oplus\ker p_2(A);
\]
 (b) for polynomial spaces \(E_k\) of degree at most \(k\) with inner product 
\[
\int_0^1pq,
\]
 multiplication \(Ap=tp\), and orthogonal projection \(P_n:E_{n+1}\to E_n\), prove \(P_nA\) self-adjoint on \(E_n\) but \(AP_n\) not self-adjoint on \(E_{n+1}\); (c) for 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&1\\1&0&0&0\\0&1&0&-2\\0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
 prove a cyclic basis, \(A^4=I-2A^2\), and that its commutant consists of polynomials in \(A\).
hints: Use Bezout's identity in (a).
For (b), test the top-degree orthogonal polynomial.
For (c), one cyclic vector determines every commuting map.
solution:
(a) Choose polynomials \(u,v\) with \(up_1+vp_2=1\). Cayley--Hamilton gives \(p_1(A)p_2(A)=0\). For every \(x\),
\[
 x=u(A)p_1(A)x+v(A)p_2(A)x.
\]
The first summand is in \(\ker p_2(A)\), the second in \(\ker p_1(A)\), because polynomial matrices commute. If \(x\) belongs to both kernels, the Bezout identity gives \(x=0\). This proves the direct sum.

(b)(i) For \(p,q\in E_n\), orthogonal projection and real multiplication by \(t\) give
\[
 \langle P_nAp,q\rangle=\langle tp,q\rangle
 =\langle p,tq\rangle=\langle p,P_nAq\rangle.
\]
Thus the compression is self-adjoint on \(E_n\).

(ii) Choose a nonzero \(r\in E_{n+1}\cap E_n^\perp\). Its degree is \(n+1\); otherwise orthogonality to itself would force zero. Take \(q=t^n\). Then \(AP_nr=0\), while \(AP_nq=t^{n+1}\), and \(\langle t^{n+1},r\rangle\ne0\): subtract a suitable nonzero multiple of \(r\) from \(t^{n+1}\) to obtain an element of \(E_n\). Hence \(\langle AP_nq,r\rangle\ne\langle q,AP_nr\rangle\), disproving self-adjointness.

(c)(i) Take \(\xi=e_1\). Then \(\xi,A\xi,A^2\xi,A^3\xi=e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4\), a basis over any field.

(ii) \(A^4\xi=Ae_4=e_1-2e_3=\xi-2A^2\xi\). The operator \(A^4-I+2A^2\) commutes with \(A\) and vanishes on \(\xi\), hence on every vector of the cyclic basis. Thus \(A^4=I-2A^2\), including in characteristic two.

(iii) If \(B\) commutes with \(A\), expand \(B\xi=\sum_{j=0}^3c_jA^j\xi\) and put \(p(t)=\sum c_jt^j\). For each \(k=0,1,2,3\),
\[
 BA^k\xi=A^kB\xi=A^kp(A)\xi=p(A)A^k\xi.
\]
Equality on the basis gives \(B=p(A)\). Conversely every polynomial in \(A\) commutes with \(A\).
pitfall: Compression \(P_nA\) and the reversed product \(AP_n\) act on different spaces here; do not apply the same self-adjointness calculation to both.

subject: linear algebra
title: A large power of a unipotent matrix
prompt:
Compute \(A^{100}\) for 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}5&-4\\4&-3\end{pmatrix}.
\]
hints: Subtract the identity.
The resulting nilpotent matrix squares to zero.
solution:
Write \(A=I+N\), where \(N=\begin{pmatrix}4&-4\\4&-4\end{pmatrix}\). Direct multiplication gives \(N^2=0\). The binomial theorem applies to the commuting matrices \(I,N\), so
\[
 (I+N)^{100}=I+100N
 =\boxed{\begin{pmatrix}401&-400\\400&-399\end{pmatrix}}.
\]
All binomial terms of order at least two vanish.
pitfall: Do not try to diagonalize this nonidentity unipotent matrix; its nilpotent part is the efficient route.

subject: linear algebra
title: Simultaneous diagonalization of two real quadratic forms
prompt: Find a linear change \((z,w)=(ax+by,cx+dy)\) preserving \(x^2+y^2=z^2+w^2\) and giving \(x^2+2xy-3y^2=\lambda z^2-\mu w^2\).
hints: Diagonalize the symmetric coefficient matrix orthogonally.
Normalize an eigenvector and its perpendicular.
solution:
The second form has symmetric matrix \(H=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-3\end{pmatrix}\), with characteristic polynomial \(t^2+2t-4\). Its eigenvalues are \(-1+\sqrt5\) and \(-1-\sqrt5\). Put \(r=\sqrt5-2\) and \(s=\sqrt{1+r^2}\). The unit eigenvectors \((1,r)/s\) and \((-r,1)/s\) correspond to these eigenvalues and form an orthonormal basis. Therefore take
\[
 z=\frac{x+ry}{s},\qquad w=\frac{-rx+y}{s}.
\]
The coordinate transformation is orthogonal, giving \(z^2+w^2=x^2+y^2\), while the spectral diagonalization gives
\[
 x^2+2xy-3y^2=(\sqrt5-1)z^2-(\sqrt5+1)w^2.
\]
Thus \(\lambda=\sqrt5-1\), \(\mu=\sqrt5+1\).
pitfall: Preserving the first quadratic form requires an orthogonal change, not an arbitrary completion of squares.

subject: linear algebra
title: The block determinant and Schur complement
prompt:
For invertible square \(A\), prove 
\[
\det\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}=\det A\,\det(D-CA^{-1}B).
\]
hints: Eliminate the lower-left block by a determinant-one triangular multiplier.
Then use the determinant of a block triangular matrix.
solution:
Multiply on the left by
\[
 E=\begin{pmatrix}I&0\\-CA^{-1}&I\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det E=1.
\]
Block multiplication gives
\[
 E\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\0&D-CA^{-1}B\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The determinant of this block upper triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal block determinants, giving the claimed formula because multiplication by \(E\) does not change the determinant. No invertibility assumption on \(D\) or on its Schur complement is required.
pitfall: Block matrix order matters; the Schur complement is \(D-CA^{-1}B\).

subject: linear algebra
title: Equal kernels of linear functionals
prompt: If linear functionals \(f,g:V\to F\) have equal kernels, prove \(f=cg\) for some nonzero scalar \(c\).
hints: Handle the zero-functional case first.
Normalize a vector on which \(g\) is nonzero and subtract its component.
solution:
If \(g=0\), its kernel is \(V\); equality of kernels gives \(f=0\), and any nonzero \(c\) (for example \(1\)) works. Otherwise choose \(v\) with \(g(v)\ne0\) and replace it by \(v/g(v)\), so \(g(v)=1\). The common kernel implies \(f(v)\ne0\). For every \(x\),
\[
 g(x-g(x)v)=0,\quad\text{so}\quad f(x-g(x)v)=0.
\]
Thus \(f(x)=f(v)g(x)\). Taking \(c=f(v)\ne0\) proves the result over every field, with no finite-dimensional assumption.
pitfall: Equal kernels include the case where both functionals are zero; do not divide by a nonexistent nonzero value in that case.

subject: linear algebra
title: An integer companion matrix and a finite-order example
prompt:
Solve both alternatives: (a) find integers a,\(b\),\(c\),\(d\) making the companion matrix 
\[
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&a\\1&0&0&b\\0&1&0&c\\0&0&1&d\end{pmatrix}
\]
 similar over \(\mathbb Q\) to 
\[
A=\operatorname{diag}(\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix});
\]
 (b) give an integer matrix of order four, with its odd power not the identity.
hints: The minimal polynomial of \(A\) is the product of its coprime block polynomials.
A quarter-turn rotation has integer entries.
solution:
(a) The two block minimal polynomials are \((t-1)^2\) and \(t^2+1\), which are relatively prime over \(\mathbb Q\). Thus the minimal polynomial of \(A\), equal here to its characteristic polynomial, is
\[
 p(t)=(t-1)^2(t^2+1)=t^4-2t^3+2t^2-2t+1.
\]
Take \(v=(0,1,1,0)^T\), cyclic in each block. If a polynomial annihilates \(v\), its first block must be divisible by \((t-1)^2\) and its second by \(t^2+1\). Their coprimeness means no nonzero polynomial of degree at most three annihilates \(v\). Hence \(S=[v,Av,A^2v,A^3v]\) is an invertible rational matrix. The identity \(p(A)=0\) gives \(A^4v=-v+2Av-2A^2v+2A^3v\). In this cyclic basis the matrix is \(B\) with
\[
 \boxed{a=-1,\quad b=2,\quad c=-2,\quad d=2}.
\]
This supplies the similarity, not just equality of characteristic polynomials.

(b) Take \(R=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Its integer entries give \(R^2=-I\), \(R^3=-R\ne I\), and \(R^4=I\). More generally every odd power is \(R\) or \(-R\), and is not \(I\); in particular \(R^9=R\ne I\). Thus the example has exact order four and satisfies the printed power requirements (whose small superscripts are faint in the scan).
pitfall: Equal characteristic polynomials alone do not establish similarity; the cyclic basis does.
note: The scanned superscripts in part (b) are faint; the explicit exact-order-four example includes both cube and ninth-power nonidentity checks.

subject: linear algebra
title: A commutator's kernel and a triangular polynomial operator
prompt:
Solve both alternatives: (a) find kernel and range bases for \(TB=AB-BA\) on \(M_2(\mathbb C)\), 
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix};
\]
 (b) find eigenvalues and multiplicities on \(E_2\) for 
\[
Tp(t)=t^2p''(t)+tp'(0)+\int_0^1p(s)\,ds.
\]
hints: Expand the commutator of a general two-by-two matrix.
In (b), apply the operator to 1, \(t\), and \(t^2\).
solution:
(a) For \(B=\begin{pmatrix}p&q\\r&s\end{pmatrix}\),
\[
 TB=\begin{pmatrix}2r-3q&2s-2p-3q\\3p+3r-3s&3q-2r\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Setting this to zero gives \(r=3q/2\), \(s=p+3q/2\). Thus the kernel is two-dimensional and has basis \(\{I,A\}\): take the coefficient of \(A\) to be \(q/2\) and of \(I\) to be \(p-q/2\). Rank--nullity gives range dimension two. The independent outputs
\[
 T(E_{11})=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\3&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 T(E_{12})=\begin{pmatrix}-3&-3\\0&3\end{pmatrix}
\]
therefore form a range basis.

(b) With \(p=a+bt+ct^2\),
\[
 Tp=(a+b/2+c/3)+bt+2ct^2.
\]
Its matrix in \(1,t,t^2\) is
\[
 \begin{pmatrix}1&1/2&1/3\\0&1&0\\0&0&2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The eigenvalues are \(1\) of algebraic multiplicity two and \(2\) of algebraic multiplicity one. The eigenspace at \(1\) consists of constants and is one-dimensional, so this polynomial operator is not diagonalizable.
pitfall: The derivative term in (b) is \(t^2p''(t)\), while the first derivative is evaluated at zero.

subject: linear algebra
title: Quadratic minimization and finite-dimensional orthogonal projection
prompt: Solve both alternatives: (a) for symmetric positive definite \(A\), prove \(Az=b\) iff \(z\) minimizes \(\phi(x)=x^TAx-2b^Tx\); (b) for the integral inner product on \(C([0,1])\), prove each \(f\) has a unique moment-matching \(f_n\in E_n\), and the map \(P_nf=f_n\) is an orthogonal projection.
hints: Complete the square about a solution in (a).
Choose an orthonormal basis of the finite-dimensional polynomial subspace in (b).
solution:
(a) Since \(A>0\), it is invertible. Put \(z=A^{-1}b\). For any \(h\),
\[
 \phi(z+h)-\phi(z)=2h^T(Az-b)+h^TAh=h^TAh\ge0,
\]
with equality only for \(h=0\). Thus \(z\) is the unique global minimizer. Conversely, if \(z\) minimizes \(\phi\), then for every real \(t\) and vector \(h\),
\[
 0\le\phi(z+th)-\phi(z)=2t h^T(Az-b)+t^2h^TAh.
\]
A nonzero linear coefficient would make this negative for sufficiently small \(t\) of the opposite sign. Thus \(h^T(Az-b)=0\) for every \(h\), implying \(Az=b\).

(b) The integral is an inner product on continuous functions: a nonzero continuous function has positive squared integral. Gram--Schmidt gives an orthonormal basis \(q_0,\ldots,q_n\) of \(E_n\). Define
\[
 f_n=\sum_{j=0}^n\langle f,q_j\rangle q_j.
\]
Expanding any \(q\in E_n\) proves \(\langle f-f_n,q\rangle=0\), the required moment matching. If two polynomial choices worked, their difference would be in \(E_n\) and orthogonal to itself, hence zero. The formula shows linearity, range \(E_n\), and \(P_nq=q\) for \(q\in E_n\), hence \(P_n^2=P_n\). The error \(f-P_nf\) is orthogonal to the range. These are precisely the orthogonal projection properties. No completeness of the full continuous-function space in this integral norm is needed, because the target subspace is finite dimensional.
pitfall: Completeness of the ambient space is unnecessary for projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace.

subject: linear algebra
title: An orthonormal eigenbasis and a common eigenvector
prompt: Solve both alternatives: (a) if \(\ker(\lambda I-A)\perp\operatorname{range}(\lambda I-A)\) for every complex \(\lambda\), prove an orthonormal eigenbasis exists; (b) prove any finite commuting family on a nontrivial finite dimensional complex vector space shares a common eigenvector.
hints: In (a), the orthogonal complement of an eigenvector is invariant.
In (b), successively restrict to a nonzero eigenspace while preserving commutation.
solution:
(a) Induct on dimension. In positive dimension choose a unit eigenvector \(e\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\). The hypothesis gives \(\langle e,(\lambda I-A)y\rangle=0\) for all \(y\), so for \(y\perp e\) one has \(\langle e,Ay\rangle=0\). Thus \(e^\perp\) is \(A\)-invariant. The restriction inherits the kernel--range orthogonality: a kernel vector of the restriction lies in the full kernel, and a range vector of the restriction lies in the full range. Induction therefore gives an orthonormal eigenbasis of \(e^\perp\). Adjoining \(e\) yields the desired basis. The zero-dimensional case has the empty basis.

(b) Start with \(V_0=V\). Choose an eigenvalue \(\lambda_1\) of \(A_1\) and let \(V_1=\ker(A_1-\lambda_1I)\ne0\). Every \(A_j\) preserves \(V_1\) because it commutes with \(A_1\). Choose an eigenvalue of \(A_2|_{V_1}\), and take its nonzero eigenspace \(V_2\subset V_1\). Commutation again makes \(V_2\) invariant under all remaining operators. Continue through the finite family. At each stage the nonzero finite dimensional complex restriction has an eigenvalue, so the final space \(V_m\ne0\). Any nonzero vector in it is an eigenvector of each \(A_j\) with its selected eigenvalue.
pitfall: A common eigenvector is guaranteed, but a common eigenbasis requires further assumptions such as diagonalizability.

subject: analysis
title: A superlinear Hölder bound forces constancy
prompt: If \(\|f(y)-f(x)\|\le M\|y-x\|^\alpha\) for all \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\), with \(\alpha>1\), prove differentiability, \(Df=0\), and constancy.
hints: Divide the increment bound by the length of the increment.
Restrict to a line segment to deduce constancy.
solution:
For every \(x\) and nonzero increment \(h\),
\[
 \frac{\|f(x+h)-f(x)-0h\|}{\|h\|}\le M\|h\|^{\alpha-1}\longrightarrow0.
\]
This is Fréchet differentiability with zero linear derivative at every \(x\). For \(x,y\), the function \(g(t)=f(x+t(y-x))\), \(0\le t\le1\), has derivative \(Df(x+t(y-x))(y-x)=0\). Applying the scalar mean value theorem to each coordinate gives \(g(1)=g(0)\), hence \(f(y)=f(x)\). Alternatively split the segment into \(k\) equal pieces and sum the original bound to get \(\|f(y)-f(x)\|\le M\|y-x\|^\alpha k^{1-\alpha}\), which tends to zero.
pitfall: The strict inequality \(\alpha>1\) is essential; Lipschitz functions need not be constant.

subject: analysis
title: Taylor's integral remainder along a segment
prompt:
A \(C^2\) function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) has a local minimum at zero and \(f(0)=0\). Prove 
\[
f(x)=\int_0^1(1-t)x^TD^2f(tx)x\,dt.
\]
hints: At an interior local minimum the first derivative is zero.
Apply integration by parts to the restriction to the segment.
solution:
Fermat's theorem, applied to every directional restriction, gives \(Df(0)=0\). For fixed \(x\), set \(g(t)=f(tx)\). Then \(g(0)=0\), \(g'(0)=Df(0)x=0\), and \(g''(t)=x^TD^2f(tx)x\). Integration by parts gives
\[
 \int_0^1(1-t)g''(t)\,dt
 =[(1-t)g'(t)]_0^1+\int_0^1g'(t)\,dt
 =-g'(0)+g(1)-g(0)=f(x).
\]
This proves the identity for every \(x\), including \(x=0\). The local minimum is used only to eliminate the linear term.
pitfall: A local minimum does not imply a globally nonnegative Hessian; no such assertion is needed.

subject: analysis
title: Uniform continuity prevents persistent integrable spikes
prompt: If nonnegative \(f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\) is integrable and uniformly continuous, prove \(f(x)\to0\).
hints: A value bounded away from zero forces a whole interval with positive height.
Choose a separated subsequence of such intervals.
solution: If the limit were not zero, there would be \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(x_k\to\infty\) with \(f(x_k)\ge\varepsilon\). Uniform continuity provides \(\delta>0\) such that \(|s-t|<\delta\) implies \(|f(s)-f(t)|<\varepsilon/2\). Pass to a subsequence with \(x_k>\delta\) and pairwise separation greater than \(2\delta\). On the disjoint intervals \([x_k-\delta/2,x_k+\delta/2]\), \(f\ge\varepsilon/2\). Integrating over the first \(K\) such intervals gives at least \(K\delta\varepsilon/2\), contradicting finiteness of the nonnegative integral. Thus \(f(x)\to0\). The argument works for either a finite improper Riemann integral or a Lebesgue integral.
pitfall: Integrability alone allows arbitrarily narrow spikes; uniform continuity supplies one common width.

subject: analysis
title: Local inverse preserves the Cauchy--Riemann equations
prompt: Suppose smooth \(f=(f_1,f_2)\) satisfies \(f_{1x}=f_{2y}\), \(f_{1y}=-f_{2x}\). If \(Df\ne0\) at a point, prove local invertibility and the same equations for its inverse.
hints: The derivative has only two independent entries.
Invert that special matrix explicitly.
solution:
At the point write \(a=f_{1x}=f_{2y}\) and \(b=f_{2x}=-f_{1y}\). Then
\[
 Df=\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{pmatrix},\qquad\det Df=a^2+b^2.
\]
The hypothesis that the matrix is nonzero gives \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\), so its determinant is positive. The inverse function theorem gives a smooth local inverse \(g\). On the inverse neighborhoods, after shrinking if needed, the derivative remains invertible and
\[
 Dg=\frac1{a^2+b^2}\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(a,b\) are evaluated at \(g\)'s argument pulled back by \(g\). Its entries give \(g_{1u}=g_{2v}\) and \(g_{1v}=-g_{2u}\), proving the inverse equations.
pitfall: A nonzero matrix is usually not enough for invertibility; the special Cauchy--Riemann form makes it enough here.

subject: analysis
title: The Gaussian integral
prompt:
Evaluate 
\[
\iint_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-x^2-y^2}\,dx\,dy
\]
 and prove 
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.
\]
hints: First integrate over disks in polar coordinates.
Compare disks with squares to identify the square of the one-dimensional integral.
solution:
For the disk of radius \(R\), polar coordinates give
\[
 \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta
 =\pi(1-e^{-R^2})\longrightarrow\pi.
\]
Let \(I_R=\int_{-R}^R e^{-t^2}\,dt\). On the square \([-R,R]^2\), the double integral is \(I_R^2\) by iterated integration of the continuous product. The disk of radius \(R\) is contained in this square, which is contained in the disk of radius \(\sqrt2R\). Nonnegativity therefore bounds \(I_R^2\) between \(\pi(1-e^{-R^2})\) and \(\pi(1-e^{-2R^2})\). Both tend to \(\pi\), so \(I_R\to\sqrt\pi\). This establishes convergence of the improper one-dimensional integral and of the double integral, with respective values \(\sqrt\pi\) and \(\pi\).
pitfall: Use finite regions first so that the argument does not assume convergence of the Gaussian integral it is proving.

subject: analysis
title: Green's second identity
prompt:
For a bounded smooth region \(\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3\), prove 
\[
\int_\Omega(u\Delta v-v\Delta u)=\int_{\partial\Omega}(u\nabla v-v\nabla u)\cdot n.
\]
hints: Apply divergence to the vector field displayed on the boundary.
The mixed gradient terms cancel.
solution:
With the customary boundary regularity assumption \(u,v\in C^2(\overline\Omega)\) (or defined \(C^2\) on a neighborhood of the closure), set \(F=u
abla v-v
abla u\). The product rule gives
\[
 \operatorname{div}F=
abla u\cdot
abla v+u\Delta v-
abla v\cdot
abla u-v\Delta u
 =u\Delta v-v\Delta u.
\]
The divergence theorem, with the outward normal, yields the stated identity. If \(C^2\) is assumed only in the open region, boundary values and the boundary integral need not even exist. For instance \(u=1/(1-|x|^2)\) on the unit ball is smooth inside but diverges at the boundary. Thus the usual extension to the boundary, or suitable trace/integrability conditions, is implicit in the exam statement.
pitfall: The boundary expression requires boundary regularity; being smooth only in the interior does not supply it.
note: Boundary regularity is implicit in the printed statement.

subject: analysis
title: Simple zeros cannot accumulate in a compact interval
prompt: If differentiable \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(f'\) have no common zeros, prove \(f\) has finitely many zeros in \([0,1]\).
hints: An infinite set of zeros has an accumulation point.
Take difference quotients through the distinct zeros.
solution:
Suppose infinitely many distinct zeros lie in \([0,1]\). By compactness choose distinct zeros \(x_k\to c\in[0,1]\), discarding a possible term equal to \(c\). Continuity of \(f\) gives \(f(c)=0\). Differentiability at \(c\), including the endpoints because \(f\) is defined on all of \(\mathbb R\), gives
\[
 f'(c)=\lim_k\frac{f(x_k)-f(c)}{x_k-c}=0.
\]
This contradicts the no-common-zero hypothesis. No continuity of \(f'\) is needed.
pitfall: Do not use continuity of the derivative, which is not assumed; the difference quotient supplies its value at the accumulation point.

subject: analysis
title: A stationary point on the half-line
prompt: Let \(f\) be continuous on \([0,\infty)\), differentiable inside, with \(f(0)=0\) and \(f(x)\to0\). Prove \(f'(c)=0\) for some \(c>0\).
hints: If the function is nonzero somewhere, its signed extremum is achieved on a large finite interval.
Choose the distant endpoint to have smaller absolute value.
solution: If \(f\equiv0\), any positive \(c\) works. Otherwise take \(t>0\) with \(f(t)\ne0\). Choose \(R>t\) such that \(|f(R)|<|f(t)|\). If \(f(t)>0\), the continuous function on \([0,R]\) attains a maximum at a point \(c\); its value is at least \(f(t)\), strictly greater than both endpoint values. Hence \(c\in(0,R)\), and Fermat's theorem gives \(f'(c)=0\). If \(f(t)<0\), use an interior minimum instead.
pitfall: Rolle's theorem cannot be applied directly with an endpoint at infinity; first find an interior extremum on a finite interval.

subject: analysis
title: Continuity of a factorial series
prompt:
Prove 
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(\frac{x^n}{n!})^2
\]
 is continuous on \(\mathbb R\).
hints: Use the maximum absolute value of \(x\) on a compact interval.
The majorant series has ratio tending to zero.
solution:
Fix \(R>0\). On \([-R,R]\),
\[
 \left|\left(\frac{x^n}{n!}\right)^2\right|\le\frac{R^{2n}}{(n!)^2}.
\]
The ratio of successive majorants is \(R^2/(n+1)^2\to0\), so the scalar majorant series converges. The Weierstrass test gives uniform convergence on \([-R,R]\). Each summand is a polynomial and therefore continuous, so the sum is continuous there. Every real point lies in such an interval, proving continuity on \(\mathbb R\).
pitfall: Local uniform convergence is enough; uniform convergence on the whole real line is not asserted.

subject: analysis
title: Vanishing moments force a continuous function to vanish
prompt:
If continuous real \(f\) on \([0,1]\) satisfies 
\[
\int_0^1f(x)x^n\,dx=0
\]
 for every \(n\ge0\), prove \(f=0\).
hints: The moment conditions imply orthogonality to every polynomial.
Approximate the function itself uniformly by polynomials.
solution:
Linearity gives \(\int_0^1fp=0\) for every real polynomial \(p\). By Weierstrass approximation choose polynomials \(p_k\) with \(\|p_k-f\|_\infty\to0\). Then
\[
 0\le\int_0^1 f^2=\int_0^1f(f-p_k)
 \le\left|\int_0^1f(f-p_k)\right|
 \le \|f-p_k\|_\infty\int_0^1|f|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus \(\int_0^1f^2=0\). If \(f\) were nonzero at some point, continuity would give a subinterval of positive length on which \(f^2\) is bounded below by a positive number, contradicting the zero integral. This includes nonzero endpoint values by a one-sided interval.
pitfall: Zero integral of \(f\) alone allows cancellation; the polynomial approximation yields the nonnegative integral of its square.

subject: analysis
title: Strict distance decrease on a compact set
prompt: For nonempty compact \(E\subset\mathbb R^n\), let continuous \(T:E\to E\) strictly decrease every distance between distinct points. Prove existence of a fixed point.
hints: Minimize the displacement function.
A nonzero minimum is reduced by applying \(T\).
solution:
The continuous function \(d(x)=|T(x)-x|\) attains its minimum at some \(x_0\in E\), using nonempty compactness. If \(T(x_0)\ne x_0\), strict distance decrease gives
\[
 d(Tx_0)=|T(Tx_0)-T(x_0)|<|Tx_0-x_0|=d(x_0),
\]
contradicting minimality since \(Tx_0\in E\). Thus \(Tx_0=x_0\). Two distinct fixed points would contradict strict distance decrease, so the fixed point is also unique. Nonemptiness is essential: the empty set, technically compact, has no fixed point. This is not the usual Banach theorem since no uniform contraction constant less than one is supplied.
pitfall: Strict decrease for each pair need not provide a common contraction factor. Compactness allows a different proof.
note: Nonemptiness of \(E\) is implicit and necessary.

subject: analysis
title: An exponential weighted limit
prompt:
If \(a_n\to g\), prove 
\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}e^{-x}\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{a_n x^n}{n!}=g.
\]
hints: The weights are nonnegative and sum to one for \(x\) at least zero.
