pitfall: Keep \(i\) fixed while passing to the limit in the approximating sequence; only afterward send \(i\) to infinity.

subject: analysis
title: The location of a mean-value point
prompt:
Let \(n\ge3\), \(f\in C^n(\mathbb R)\), \(f^{(k)}(0)=0\) for \(2\le k<n\), and \(f^{(n)}(0)\ne0\). If \(0<\theta(h)<h\) satisfies \(f(h)-f(0)=hf'(\theta(h))\), prove 
\[
\frac{\theta(h)}{h}\to n^{-\frac{1}{n-1}}
\]
 as \(h\downarrow0\).
hints: Expand \(f\) at \(h\) and \(f'\) at the mean-value point.
The bound on the mean-value point controls its remainder after dividing by a power of \(h\).
solution:
Write \(c=f^{(n)}(0)\ne0\). Taylor expansion and the vanishing intermediate derivatives give
\[
\frac{f(h)-f(0)}h=f'(0)+\frac{c}{n!}h^{n-1}+o(h^{n-1}),
\]
and
\[
f'(\theta)=f'(0)+\frac{c}{(n-1)!}\theta^{n-1}+o(\theta^{n-1}).
\]
Equating these expressions, subtracting \(f'(0)\), and dividing by \(h^{n-1}\) gives
\[
\frac c{n!}+o(1)=\frac c{(n-1)!}\left(\frac{\theta(h)}h\right)^{n-1}+o(1).
\]
The second remainder is indeed \(o(1)\): write it as \(\varepsilon(\theta)\theta^{n-1}/h^{n-1}\), where \(\varepsilon(\theta)\to0\), and use \(0<\theta/h<1\) and \(\theta\to0\). Therefore \((\theta/h)^{n-1}\to1/n\). Positivity and continuity of the positive root function yield the stated limit. This holds for any choice of mean-value point, with no uniqueness or continuity of that choice assumed.
pitfall: Do not assume the mean-value point is a continuous function of \(h\); only its location between zero and \(h\) is needed.

subject: analysis
title: A Gaussian-weighted growing integral
prompt:
Prove 
\[
\lim_{x\to+\infty}e^{-x^2}\int_0^x e^{t^2}\,dt=0.
\]
hints: Write the expression as the integral of the exponential of \(t^2\) minus \(x^2\).
Split at \(x\) over two and estimate the two regions separately.
solution:
For \(x>0\), the expression is nonnegative and equals \(\int_0^x e^{t^2-x^2}\,dt\). On \([0,x/2]\), \(t^2-x^2\le-3x^2/4\), so that part is at most \((x/2)e^{-3x^2/4}\). On \([x/2,x]\), \(x^2-t^2=(x-t)(x+t)\ge x(x-t)\). Hence
\[
0\le e^{-x^2}\int_0^x e^{t^2}\,dt
\le\frac x2e^{-3x^2/4}+\int_{x/2}^x e^{-x(x-t)}\,dt
\le\frac x2e^{-3x^2/4}+\frac1x.
\]
Both upper-bound terms tend to zero, so the squeeze theorem proves the limit. Alternatively, applying \(l\)'Hôpital's rule to the quotient of the integral by \(e^{x^2}\) gives derivative quotient \(1/(2x)\to0\).
pitfall: The crude bound of the integrand by its endpoint value only gives a bound of \(x\), which does not resolve the limit.

subject: analysis
title: A global diffeomorphism close to the identity
prompt: If \(f\in C^1(\mathbb R)\), \(|f'|\le\frac{1}{2}\), and \(g(x,y)=(x+f(y),y+f(x))\), prove global diffeomorphism onto \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(|g([0,1]^2)|\in[\frac{3}{4},\frac{5}{4}]\).
hints: For any target point, solve the inverse equations as a contraction on the plane.
The Jacobian is positive and bounded; its integral even gives a sharper area bound.
solution:
The mean value theorem makes \(f\) Lipschitz with constant \(1/2\). For any target \((u,v)\), define
\[
T_{u,v}(x,y)=(u-f(y),\,v-f(x)).
\]
In the Euclidean norm, the sum of the two squared coordinate differences shows \(T_{u,v}\) is a contraction with constant \(1/2\). Since \(\mathbb R^2\) is complete, it has a unique fixed point. The fixed-point equations are precisely \(g(x,y)=(u,v)\). Thus \(g\) is bijective onto \(\mathbb R^2\).

Its derivative is
\[
Dg(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix}1&f'(y)\\f'(x)&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det Dg=1-f'(x)f'(y)\in[3/4,5/4].
\]
The inverse function theorem gives a \(C^1\) inverse locally at every point. These local inverses agree with the global inverse by bijectivity, so the latter is \(C^1\). Hence \(g\) is a global \(C^1\) diffeomorphism.

Change of variables gives the area as the integral of this positive Jacobian over the unit square, immediately between \(3/4\) and \(5/4\). In fact Fubini and the fundamental theorem of calculus give the exact expression
\[
|g([0,1]^2)|=1-\left(\int_0^1 f'(t)\,dt\right)^2
=1-(f(1)-f(0))^2\in[3/4,1].
\]
The sharper bound follows from \(|f(1)-f(0)|\le1/2\).
pitfall: An everywhere-invertible derivative proves only local invertibility; the contraction argument proves both global existence and uniqueness of inverse images.

subject: linear algebra
title: Reflection across a specified plane
prompt: Find the standard matrix of reflection in the plane \(3x+2y+z=0\) in \(\mathbb R^3\).
hints: Reflection fixes the plane and reverses its normal direction.
Subtract twice the orthogonal projection onto the normal line.
solution:
A normal vector is \(u=(3,2,1)^T\), with \(u^Tu=14\). The orthogonal projection onto its line is \(P=uu^T/14\). Every vector splits into its planar and normal components, and reflection preserves the former while negating the latter. Therefore
\[
T=I-2P=I-\frac17
\begin{pmatrix}9&6&3\\6&4&2\\3&2&1\end{pmatrix}
=\frac17\begin{pmatrix}-2&-6&-3\\-6&3&-2\\-3&-2&6\end{pmatrix}.
\]
As a check, \(Tu=-u\), and if \(u^Tx=0\), then \(Tx=x\), exactly the two defining properties of the reflection.
pitfall: Reflection in a plane negates its normal component, not its planar component.

subject: linear algebra
title: The Hermitian part of a nonzero nilpotent matrix
prompt: If \(A\ne0\) is a complex nilpotent matrix, prove \(A+A^*\) is not nilpotent.
hints: A nilpotent matrix and all its positive powers have zero trace.
The trace of the square of A plus \(A^*\) is twice the positive squared Hilbert–Schmidt norm of \(A\).
solution:
Let \(H=A+A^*\). Nilpotence of \(A\) implies \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)=0\), since all eigenvalues of its powers are zero. Likewise \(\operatorname{tr}((A^*)^2)=\overline{\operatorname{tr}(A^2)}=0\). Expanding and using trace cyclicity gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}(H^2)=\operatorname{tr}(A^2)+\operatorname{tr}((A^*)^2)+
\operatorname{tr}(AA^*)+\operatorname{tr}(A^*A)
=2\operatorname{tr}(A^*A)=2\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^2>0.
\]
If \(H\) were nilpotent, \(H^2\) would have trace zero, a contradiction. This establishes the claim without assuming the nilpotent \(A\) is diagonalizable.
pitfall: Nilpotent matrices have zero eigenvalues but can have nonzero entries; their positive Hilbert–Schmidt norm detects this here.

subject: linear algebra
title: Jordan form from two polynomials
prompt: Find the complex Jordan canonical forms with characteristic polynomial \((t+1)^2(t-1)^3(t^2+1)^2\) and minimal polynomial \((t+1)(t-1)^2(t^2+1)\).
hints: Characteristic multiplicities give the total size for each eigenvalue.
The minimal-polynomial exponent gives the largest block size for that eigenvalue.
solution:
Over \(\mathbb C\), the eigenvalues are \(-1,1,i,-i\), with algebraic multiplicities \(2,3,2,2\), respectively. The minimal polynomial has exponents \(1,2,1,1\) at those roots. Thus the blocks for \(-1\) must be two size-one blocks; those for \(1\) must partition three with largest size two, forcing sizes two and one; and those for each of \(i,-i\) must be two size-one blocks. Therefore there is a unique Jordan form up to block order:
\[
J_1(-1)\oplus J_1(-1)\oplus J_2(1)\oplus J_1(1)
\oplus J_1(i)\oplus J_1(i)\oplus J_1(-i)\oplus J_1(-i).
\]
Its total size is nine. These blocks have exactly the stated characteristic polynomial and minimal polynomial, verifying sufficiency as well as necessity.
pitfall: The exponent in the minimal polynomial bounds the largest block, whereas the characteristic exponent counts the sum of block sizes.

subject: linear algebra
title: A basis adapted to a complete flag
prompt:
For a strict flag 
\[
0\subsetneq F_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq F_n=\mathbb C^n
\]
 preserved by \(T\), construct a basis whose first \(k\) vectors span \(F_k\), and prove the matrix of \(T\) is upper triangular.
hints: There are \(n\) strict dimension increases in dimension \(n\), so each increase is exactly one.
Choose each new vector in the next subspace but outside the previous one.
solution:
The \(n\) strict inclusions from zero to an \(n\)-dimensional space force \(\dim F_k=k\): every step increases dimension by at least one, and the sum of the increases is exactly \(n\). Choose \(b_1\ne0\) in \(F_1\). Inductively, having a basis \(b_1,\ldots,b_{k-1}\) of \(F_{k-1}\), choose \(b_k\in F_k\setminus F_{k-1}\). It is independent of the previous vectors; the resulting \(k\) independent vectors in the \(k\)-dimensional \(F_k\) form its basis. At \(k=n\) this gives the desired basis of \(\mathbb C^n\).

Because \(b_j\in F_j\) and \(T(F_j)=F_j\), \(Tb_j\) lies in \(\operatorname{span}(b_1,\ldots,b_j)\). Therefore column \(j\) of the matrix has zero entries in every row \(i>j\). This is precisely upper triangularity. Inclusion \(T(F_j)\subset F_j\) would already suffice for the triangular conclusion; the stated equality also implies invertibility of \(T\).
pitfall: Use column \(j\) for the coordinates of the image of the \(j\)-th basis vector; otherwise upper and lower triangular conventions can be reversed.

subject: linear algebra
title: The adjoint action on trace-zero two by two matrices
prompt:
(a) Prove \(\mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb C)\) has dimension three and is closed under \([A,B]=AB-BA\). (b) Prove \(\operatorname{ad}(M):A\mapsto[M,A]\) linear. (c) For 
\[
E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
 find the eigenvalues and Jordan form of \(\operatorname{ad}(E)\).
hints: Use the usual diagonal and off-diagonal trace-zero basis.
Calculate three commutators to expose one nilpotent chain of length three.
solution:
(a) Every trace-zero \(2\times2\) matrix is uniquely \(aH+bE+cF\), where
\[
H=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad
E=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad
F=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\1&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
These matrices are independent, so the dimension is three. Trace cyclicity gives \(\operatorname{tr}(AB-BA)=0\), proving closure.

(b) For fixed \(M\), distributivity gives \([M,\alpha A+\beta B]=\alpha[M,A]+\beta[M,B]\), establishing linearity.

(c) Direct multiplication gives
\[
[E,E]=0,\qquad [E,H]=-2E,\qquad [E,F]=H.
\]
In the ordered basis \((E,H,F)\), the matrix is
\[
\begin{pmatrix}0&-2&0\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It has cube zero, but its square maps \(F\) to \(-2E\ne0\). Its only eigenvalue is zero, with eigenspace \(\operatorname{span}(E)\), and it has one Jordan block \(J_3(0)\). Explicitly, the chain \(E,-H/2,-F/2\) is a basis in which the matrix is exactly that block.
pitfall: The adjoint action is an operator on the three-dimensional matrix space; its matrix is not the original two by two \(E\).

subject: linear algebra
title: Interlacing for a principal compression
prompt:
For Hermitian \(3\times3\) \(A\), let its eigenvalues be \(\gamma_1\le\gamma_2\le\gamma_3\), and those of its upper-left \(2\times2\) corner be \(\mu_1\le\mu_2\). Use min–max to prove 
\[
\gamma_1\le\mu_1\le\gamma_2\le\mu_2\le\gamma_3.
\]
hints: View the smaller matrix as the quadratic form restricted to the coordinate plane.
Use both min–max formulas for the middle eigenvalue of \(A\).
solution:
Let \(W=\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)\subset\mathbb C^3\), and write \(R(x)=x^*Ax/\|x\|^2\). On \(W\), this is the Rayleigh quotient of the principal corner \(B\). Therefore \(\mu_1=\min_{x\in W\setminus0}R(x)\) and \(\mu_2=\max_{x\in W\setminus0}R(x)\).

The minimum over all nonzero vectors is \(\gamma_1\), so \(\gamma_1\le\mu_1\); the maximum over all is \(\gamma_3\), so \(\mu_2\le\gamma_3\). For the middle eigenvalue, the two Courant--Fischer formulas are
\[
\gamma_2=\max_{\dim L=2}\min_{x\in L\setminus0}R(x),\qquad
\gamma_2=\min_{\dim L=2}\max_{x\in L\setminus0}R(x).
\]
Testing both at \(L=W\) gives \(\gamma_2\ge\mu_1\) and \(\gamma_2\le\mu_2\). Combining these four inequalities proves the asserted interlacing.
pitfall: The compression need not preserve the coordinate plane as an operator; equality of the restricted quadratic forms is sufficient.

subject: linear algebra
title: Extending an independent set to a basis
prompt: Prove that every linearly independent set in a finite-dimensional vector space extends to a basis.
hints: If the current independent set does not span, choose a vector outside its span.
Each such addition increases the dimension of its span, so the procedure terminates.
solution:
Let \(\dim V=n\). Any linearly independent set has at most \(n\) members, so list the given set as \(v_1,\ldots,v_k\), allowing \(k=0\). If it spans \(V\), it is already a basis. Otherwise choose \(w\notin\operatorname{span}(v_1,\ldots,v_k)\). The enlarged set is independent: a relation with nonzero coefficient of \(w\) would express \(w\) as a combination of the others, and a relation with that coefficient zero reduces to independence of the original set.

Repeat whenever the enlarged set fails to span. Each addition increases the span dimension by one, and independence prevents more than \(n\) vectors. After at most \(n-k\) steps, the set spans \(V\) and is independent, hence is a basis containing the original set.
pitfall: Choose outside the current span, not merely a vector different from the ones already chosen.

subject: linear algebra
title: A determinant identity under one commutation relation
prompt: If \(AB=BA\), prove \(\det(A+BC)=\det(A+CB)\) for square matrices of the same size.
hints: If \(B\) is invertible, the two sums are similar.
Perturb \(B\) by a scalar multiple of the identity; this preserves its commutation with \(A\).
solution:
If \(B\) is invertible, commutation gives
\[
B^{-1}(A+BC)B=A+CB,
\]
so the determinants are equal. For arbitrary \(B\), put \(B_t=B+tI\). This still commutes with \(A\), and it is invertible for all but finitely many \(t\), since \(\det(B+tI)\) is a monic nonzero polynomial. Choose real \(t_j\to0\) avoiding its roots. The invertible case gives
\[
\det(A+B_{t_j}C)=\det(A+CB_{t_j}).
\]
Continuity of determinant as \(j\to\infty\) yields the desired equality. This works over both the real and complex fields and makes no assumption that \(A\) or \(B\) itself is invertible.
pitfall: Only \(A\) and \(B\) commute; do not assume \(C\) commutes with either. The scalar-identity perturbation preserves the actual hypothesis.

subject: linear algebra
title: Trace bounded by dimension times the squared operator norm
prompt:
For a complex \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), prove 
\[
|\operatorname{tr}(A^*A)|\le n\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2.
\]
hints: Compute the trace in an orthonormal basis.
Each column norm is bounded by the operator norm.
solution:
For the standard orthonormal basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_n\),
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^*A)=\sum_{j=1}^n e_j^*A^*Ae_j
=\sum_{j=1}^n\|Ae_j\|^2.
\]
This is real and nonnegative, so the absolute value does not change it. Each \(e_j\) is a unit vector and the operator norm gives \(\|Ae_j\|\le\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). Summing the squared bounds yields \(\operatorname{tr}(A^*A)\le n\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2\).
pitfall: The Hilbert–Schmidt squared norm is the trace on the left; the norm on the right is the operator norm.

subject: linear algebra
title: The forward-difference operator on cubic polynomials
prompt: On real polynomials of degree at most three, let \(Tp(t)=p(t+1)-p(t)\). Find all eigenvalues/eigenspaces and its Jordan canonical form.
hints: A forward difference lowers the degree of every nonconstant polynomial.
Use falling-factorial polynomials to obtain a normalized Jordan chain.
solution:
For a polynomial of positive degree \(d\) with leading coefficient \(a\), its forward difference has degree \(d-1\) and leading coefficient \(ad\). Thus \(T^4=0\) on this four-dimensional space, while \(T^3(t^3)=6\ne0\). The only eigenvalue is zero, and \(\ker T\) consists exactly of the constant polynomials, since a nonconstant polynomial has a nonzero difference. Its eigenvectors are the nonzero constants.

An explicit Jordan chain is
\[
b_0=1,\quad b_1=t,\quad b_2=\frac{t(t-1)}2,\quad
b_3=\frac{t(t-1)(t-2)}6.
\]
The polynomial identity for successive binomial coefficients, also verified by direct expansion, gives \(Tb_0=0\) and \(Tb_j=b_{j-1}\) for \(j=1,2,3\). Their distinct degrees make them a basis. In this basis the operator is \(J_4(0)\). In particular its characteristic and minimal polynomials are both \(t^4\).
pitfall: Finite difference is not differentiation, though both lower degree here; falling-factorial polynomials normalize the difference chain.

subject: linear algebra
title: The product rule for a matrix square
prompt: For differentiable matrix-valued \(A(t)\), is \(\frac d{dt}A(t)^2=2A(t)A'(t)\) always true? Prove or give a counterexample.
hints: Apply the product rule without changing the order of the factors.
Choose an idempotent matrix path whose derivative does not commute with it.
solution:
Entrywise differentiation and the ordinary product rule give
\[
\frac d{dt}A(t)^2=A'(t)A(t)+A(t)A'(t).
\]
This equals \(2A(t)A'(t)\) exactly when \(A'(t)A(t)=A(t)A'(t)\). That commutation need not hold. For example, let
\[
A(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A'(t)=N=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Here \(A(t)^2=A(t)\), so the derivative of the square is \(N\). But \(A(t)N=N\) and \(NA(t)=0\), giving \(2A(t)A'(t)=2N\ne N\). This differentiable path disproves the asserted general formula.
pitfall: The product rule keeps the two factor orders; scalar simplifications are valid only with the corresponding matrix commutation.

subject: linear algebra
title: Integer inverses and determinant one
prompt: For an invertible integer \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), prove \(A^{-1}\) has integer entries iff \(\det A=\pm1\).
hints: An integer inverse would have an integer determinant reciprocal to that of \(A\).
Use the adjugate formula for the converse.
solution:
If \(A^{-1}\) has integer entries, both \(\det A\) and \(\det A^{-1}\) are integers, and their product is one. The only integers with an integer reciprocal are \(1,-1\), so \(\det A=\pm1\).

Conversely, the adjugate matrix of an integer matrix has integer entries, because each entry is a signed determinant of an integer submatrix. If \(\det A=\pm1\), the inverse formula
\[
A^{-1}=\frac{\operatorname{adj}(A)}{\det A}
\]
therefore gives integer entries. This proves both directions.
pitfall: An integer nonzero determinant ensures invertibility over the rationals, but an integer inverse requires that determinant to be a unit in the integers.

subject: analysis
title: A factorially weighted limit
prompt:
If real \(a_n\to g\), prove 
\[
\lim_{x\to+\infty}e^{-x}\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{a_n x^n}{n!}=g.
\]
hints: The nonnegative weights for positive \(x\) add to one.
Split off finitely many early terms, whose weights vanish as \(x\) grows.
solution:
The convergent sequence is bounded, so the series converges absolutely for every real \(x\), by comparison with a constant times \(\sum |x|^n/n!\). For \(x\ge0\), define \(w_n(x)=e^{-x}x^n/n!\). Then \(w_n(x)\ge0\) and \(\sum_n w_n(x)=1\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\) such that \(|a_n-g|<\varepsilon\) for \(n\ge N\). Therefore
\[
\left|e^{-x}\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\frac{x^n}{n!}-g\right|
\le\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}|a_n-g|e^{-x}\frac{x^n}{n!}+\varepsilon\sum_{n=N}^\infty w_n(x)
\le e^{-x}P(x)+\varepsilon,
\]
where \(P\) is a fixed polynomial with nonnegative coefficients. Exponential decay dominates each polynomial term, so the first term tends to zero as \(x\to+\infty\). The upper limit of the error is at most every positive \(\varepsilon\), proving the result.
pitfall: The normalization makes the total weight one; boundedness alone would not determine the limiting weighted average.
theorems: Tail estimate for a convergent sequence

subject: analysis
title: An exact Taylor identity forces a cubic
prompt:
Suppose \(f\in C^4(\mathbb R)\) and 
\[
f(x+h)=f(x)+f'(x)h+\frac12f''(x+\frac{h}{3})h^2
\]
 for all real \(x,h\). Prove \(f^{(4)}=0\).
hints: Expand both sides to fourth order in \(h\) at a fixed \(x\).
The cubic coefficients agree but the fourth-order coefficients differ.
solution:
Fix \(x\). Taylor's theorem with a Peano remainder gives
\[
f(x+h)=f(x)+f'(x)h+\tfrac12f''(x)h^2+\tfrac16f'''(x)h^3+
\tfrac1{24}f^{(4)}(x)h^4+o(h^4).
\]
Apply second-order Taylor expansion to the \(C^2\) function \(f''\):
\[
f''(x+h/3)=f''(x)+\tfrac h3f'''(x)+\tfrac{h^2}{18}f^{(4)}(x)+o(h^2).
\]
Substituting this into the given right side yields the same terms through degree three, but fourth-order coefficient \(f^{(4)}(x)/36\). Equality of the two expressions therefore implies
\[
\left(\tfrac1{24}-\tfrac1{36}\right)f^{(4)}(x)h^4+o(h^4)=0.
\]
Divide by \(h^4\) for \(h\ne0\) and let \(h\to0\). The nonzero coefficient \(1/72\) forces \(f^{(4)}(x)=0\). As \(x\) was arbitrary, this holds everywhere. In fact the functions satisfying the identity are exactly the polynomials of degree at most three.
pitfall: Differentiating the right side four times in \(h\) would require more regularity of \(f\) than C4; Taylor remainders avoid that issue.

subject: analysis
title: Compactness of the union of convergent images
prompt: Let continuous \(f_n:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m\) converge uniformly to \(f\) on compact \(K\). Prove \(S=f(K)\cup\bigcup_{n\ge1}f_n(K)\) is compact.
hints: A sequence of image points either uses a fixed map infinitely often or has map indices tending to infinity.
For the latter case, uniform convergence controls the image points while compactness controls their preimages.
solution:
The uniform limit \(f|_K\) is continuous. If \(K=\varnothing\), then \(S=\varnothing\) is compact. Otherwise take a sequence \(y_j\in S\). For each term choose \(x_j\in K\) and an index \(n_j\ge0\) such that \(y_j=f_{n_j}(x_j)\), where \(f_0=f|_K\).

If some index occurs infinitely often, pass to that subsequence. The corresponding image \(f_n(K)\) is compact by continuity, so there is a convergent subsequence whose limit belongs to \(S\). If no index occurs infinitely often, pass to a subsequence with \(n_j\to\infty\). Compactness of \(K\) supplies a further subsequence with \(x_j\to x\in K\). Then
\[
|y_j-f(x)|\le\sup_{z\in K}|f_{n_j}(z)-f(z)|+|f(x_j)-f(x)|\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus the limit is \(f(x)\in S\). Every sequence in \(S\) has a subsequence converging within \(S\), so \(S\) is compact by the metric-space compactness criterion.
pitfall: An infinite union of compact sets need not be compact. Uniform convergence and inclusion of the limit image close the possible gaps.
theorems: Continuous image of a compact set

subject: analysis
title: Comparison for an exponential Laplace equation
prompt: On the open unit disk, let \(f,g\in C^2\), with \(g\) bounded, \(f(x,y)\to+\infty\) as \(x^2+y^2\to1\), \(\Delta f=e^f\), and \(\Delta g\ge e^g\). Prove \(f\ge g\).
hints: A positive maximum of \(g\) minus \(f\) must occur in the interior.
Compare the Laplacian at that maximum with the increasing exponential nonlinearity.
solution:
Let \(h=g-f\). Boundedness of \(g\) and divergence of \(f\) to positive infinity imply \(h<0\) sufficiently close to the disk boundary. Suppose \(h(a)>0\) at some interior point. Choose \(r<1\) large enough that \(a\) is in the disk of radius \(r\) and \(h<0\) for all points with radius at least \(r\). Continuity on the closed disk of radius \(r\) gives a positive maximum of \(h\) at some interior point \(b\).

At an interior maximum, both second directional derivatives in the coordinate directions are nonpositive, so \(\Delta h(b)\le0\). But \(h(b)>0\) means \(g(b)>f(b)\), and the differential inequalities yield
\[
\Delta h(b)=\Delta g(b)-\Delta f(b)\ge e^{g(b)}-e^{f(b)}>0,
\]
a contradiction. Consequently \(h\le0\) throughout the disk, or \(f\ge g\).
pitfall: Boundary blow-up is used to force the hypothetical positive maximum into a compact interior region; the open disk itself is not compact.

subject: analysis
title: Three implicit branches and their derivatives
prompt:
Let 
\[
F(x,y)=e^x y^3+2x^2y^2-y\cos x+2\sin x.
\]
 Find smooth branches \(f<g<h\) near zero with \(F(x,f(x))=F(x,g(x))=F(x,h(x))=0\), and compute their derivatives at zero.
hints: At \(x\) zero the three roots are minus one, zero, and one.
Check the \(y\) derivative at each root and use implicit differentiation.
solution:
At \(x=0\), \(F(0,y)=y^3-y\), whose roots are \(-1,0,1\). We have
\[
F_y=3e^xy^2+4x^2y-\cos x,\qquad
F_x=e^xy^3+4xy^2+y\sin x+2\cos x.
\]
At the three roots \(F_y(0,y)=3y^2-1\) equals \(2,-1,2\), respectively, and is nonzero in every case. Since \(F\) is smooth, the implicit function theorem gives three smooth functions on a common sufficiently small open interval \(U\) around zero, with \(f(0)=-1\), \(g(0)=0\), \(h(0)=1\), solving the equation. Shrinking \(U\) if needed, continuity keeps their values in disjoint ordered intervals about those three initial values, so \(f(x)<g(x)<h(x)\) throughout \(U\).

Implicit differentiation gives \(y'(0)=-F_x(0,y(0))/F_y(0,y(0))\). Since \(F_x(0,y)=y^3+2\),
\[
f'(0)=-\tfrac12,\qquad g'(0)=2,\qquad h'(0)=-\tfrac32.
\]
pitfall: The three branches come from three different base points; choose a common neighborhood and preserve their ordering by continuity.

subject: analysis
title: A global triangular diffeomorphism and its volume factor
prompt:
Let smooth \(f_k:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R\), \(1\le k\le9\), define \(\Phi_1(x)=x_1\) and 
\[
\Phi_i(x)=ix_i+f_{i-1}(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1}),
\]
 \(2\le i\le10\). Prove \(\Phi\) is a diffeomorphism onto an open set and compute \(|\Phi((-1,1)^{10})|\).
hints: Solve the coordinates in order to construct a global inverse.
The derivative is triangular with constant diagonal entries.
solution:
For any \(y\in\mathbb R^{10}\), solve \(\Phi(x)=y\) recursively:
\[
x_1=y_1,\qquad
x_i=\frac{y_i-f_{i-1}(x_1,\ldots,x_{i-1})}{i},\quad 2\le i\le10.
\]
This gives a unique \(x\) for every \(y\). Each coordinate is a smooth function of \(y\), by induction and composition of smooth functions. Hence \(\Phi\) is a global smooth diffeomorphism, in fact onto all of \(\mathbb R^{10}\), stronger than the requested open-image assertion.

Its Jacobian is lower triangular, since the \(i\)-th output depends only on the first \(i\) coordinates, and its diagonal is \(1,2,\ldots,10\). Thus \(\det D\Phi=10!\) everywhere. Change of variables gives
\[
|\Phi((-1,1)^{10})|
=\int_{(-1,1)^{10}}|\det D\Phi(x)|\,dx
=2^{10}\,10!=3{,}715{,}891{,}200.
\]
pitfall: A nonzero Jacobian only proves local invertibility; the recursive coordinate solution proves global bijectivity here.

subject: analysis
title: A monotone nonlinear iteration
prompt: For \(x_0>0\), let \(x_n=3(\sqrt{x_{n-1}+1}-1)\). Prove convergence and find the limit.
hints: Find the fixed points and compare the iteration with the identity.
The update is increasing and fixes three, so an iterate cannot cross that fixed point.
solution:
Let \(G(x)=3(\sqrt{x+1}-1)\), \(x\ge0\). Rationalizing gives
\[
G(x)=\frac{3x}{\sqrt{x+1}+1}.
\]
The fixed points are \(0\) and \(3\): for a positive fixed point the denominator must equal three. The map is strictly increasing. If \(0<x<3\), the denominator is less than three, so \(x<G(x)<G(3)=3\). If \(x>3\), it is greater than three, so \(3=G(3)<G(x)<x\).

Thus an initial value below three generates an increasing sequence bounded above by three; one above three generates a decreasing sequence bounded below by three; and \(x_0=3\) gives a constant sequence. In each case there is a limit \(L\). Continuity gives \(L=G(L)\), and \(L>0\) because the increasing case stays at least \(x_0>0\) and the other cases stay at least three. The zero fixed point is excluded, so \(L=3\).
pitfall: Finding fixed points alone does not prove convergence; establish monotonicity and boundedness for each initial-value range.

subject: analysis
title: One subsequence for every sine multiple
prompt: Find an increasing integer sequence \(a_1<a_2<\cdots\) such that \(\sin(ka_j)\) converges for every positive integer \(k\).
hints: Each bounded sine sequence has a convergent subsequence.
Use nested subsequences for successive \(k\) and take a diagonal.
solution:
Start with the increasing sequence of positive integers. Since \(\sin m\in[-1,1]\), Bolzano--Weierstrass gives an increasing subsequence \(S_1\) along which \(\sin m\) converges. Extract from \(S_1\) an increasing subsequence \(S_2\) along which \(\sin(2m)\) converges, then continue to obtain nested sequences \(S_k\). For every \(r\le k\), \(\sin(rm)\) converges along \(S_k\), since it is a subsequence of \(S_r\).

Let \(a_j\) be the \(j\)-th entry of \(S_j\). Because \(S_{j+1}\) is a subsequence of \(S_j\), its \((j+1)\)-st entry is larger than the \(j\)-th entry of \(S_j\); hence \(a_{j+1}>a_j\). For fixed \(k\), all entries \(a_j\) with \(j\ge k\) belong to \(S_k\), in increasing order. The tail therefore forms a subsequence of \(S_k\), so \(\sin(ka_j)\) converges. This handles all countably many \(k\) with one sequence.
pitfall: Choosing separate subsequences for each \(k\) does not give a common one; nested extraction and the diagonal are both needed.

subject: analysis
title: A continuous positive series with divergent improper integral
prompt:
For \(n\ge2\), let \(f_n(x)=nx\) on \([0,\frac{1}{n}]\) and \(f_n(x)=\frac n{n-1}(1-x)\) on \([\frac{1}{n},1]\). Prove 
\[
\sum_{n=2}^\infty f_n(x)^n
\]
 converges pointwise on \([0,1]\) to a function continuous on \((0,1]\), whose improper integral at zero diverges.
hints: Away from zero, the tail has a common geometric bound.
Each powered tent function has integral one over \(n\) plus one; compare with finite partial sums before taking the improper limit.
solution:
The two formulas for \(f_n\) agree at \(1/n\), so each \(f_n^n\) is continuous and nonnegative. At \(x=0\) or \(x=1\) all terms are zero. Fix \(0<\delta<1\). For \(n\ge1/\delta\) and \(x\in[\delta,1]\), the second branch applies, and
\[
f_n(x)^n=\left(\frac n{n-1}\right)^n(1-x)^n
\le e^2(1-\delta)^n,
\]
using \(n\log(1+1/(n-1))\le n/(n-1)\le2\). This geometric majorant gives uniform convergence on \([\delta,1]\). It proves pointwise convergence for all positive \(x\), and continuity of the sum \(f\) on \((0,1]\).

Compute the integral of one term directly:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 f_n(x)^n\,dx
&=\int_0^{1/n}(nx)^n\,dx+
\int_{1/n}^1\left(\frac n{n-1}(1-x)\right)^n\,dx\\
&=\frac1{n(n+1)}+\frac{n-1}{n(n+1)}=\frac1{n+1}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For any fixed \(N\), the nonnegative sum satisfies \(f\ge\sum_{n=2}^Nf_n^n\). Integrate on \([\delta,1]\) and let \(\delta\downarrow0\). The improper integral of \(f\) exists as an extended value by positivity and obeys
\[
\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx\ge\sum_{n=2}^N\frac1{n+1}.
\]
The right side is unbounded as \(N\to\infty\), so the improper integral is positive infinity. This argument uses only finite sums inside the improper-limit comparison, with no unjustified termwise integration at zero.
pitfall: The series is uniformly convergent on intervals away from zero, but its peaks accumulate near zero and obstruct a finite integral there.

subject: analysis
title: Extending a Lipschitz map into a complete metric space
prompt: If \(A\subset\mathbb R^n\) is dense, \(X\) is complete, and \(d(f(x),f(y))\le|x-y|\) on \(A\), prove there is a \(1\)-Lipschitz extension \(F:\mathbb R^n\to X\). Give a counterexample without completeness.
hints: Images of a Cauchy approximating sequence are Cauchy.
Use the rationals as an incomplete target for the counterexample.
solution:
(a) For \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), choose \(a_j\in A\) with \(a_j\to x\). The Lipschitz bound makes \(f(a_j)\) a Cauchy sequence, and completeness gives a limit in \(X\). If \(b_j\to x\) is another such sequence, \(d(f(a_j),f(b_j))\le|a_j-b_j|\to0\), so the limits agree. Define \(F(x)=\lim_j f(a_j)\). For \(x\in A\), the constant sequence proves \(F(x)=f(x)\). For arbitrary \(x,y\), take approximating sequences for both and pass to the limit in the metric inequality:
\[
d(F(x),F(y))\le|x-y|.
\]
This proves the required extension, and also its uniqueness by continuity and density.

(b) Let \(A=\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb R\), let \(X=\mathbb Q\) with its usual metric, and let \(f(q)=q\). This is \(1\)-Lipschitz, but \(X\) is incomplete. If an extension with the asserted bound existed, for an irrational \(x\) and rationals \(q_j\to x\) we would have
\[
|F(x)-q_j|\le|x-q_j|\longrightarrow0.
\]
This forces the rational number \(F(x)\) to equal the irrational number \(x\), a contradiction.
pitfall: The approximating image sequence may have a limit only in the completion of \(X\); the hypothesis ensures that limit belongs to \(X\) itself.

subject: analysis
title: A Hessian bound controls the disk integral
prompt:
Suppose \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^2)\), \(f(0)=f_x(0)=f_y(0)=0\), and \(f_{xx}^2+2f_{xy}^2+f_{yy}^2\le M\) on the closed unit disk \(D\). Prove 
\[
|\int_D f|\le\frac{\pi\sqrt M}{4}.
\]
hints: The hypothesis bounds the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the Hessian.
Apply the integral Taylor formula along each radial segment and then integrate the squared radius.
solution:
The symmetric Hessian \(H=D^2f\) has \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{HS}}\le\sqrt M\) on \(D\). For \(v\in D\), let \(g(t)=f(tv)\). The initial conditions give \(g(0)=g'(0)=0\), so twice using the fundamental theorem of calculus yields
\[
f(v)=g(1)=\int_0^1(1-t)g''(t)\,dt
=\int_0^1(1-t)v^TH(tv)v\,dt.
\]
Hilbert--Schmidt Cauchy--Schwarz and \(\|vv^T\|_{\mathrm{HS}}=|v|^2\) imply \(|v^TH(tv)v|\le\sqrt M\,|v|^2\). Thus
\[
|f(v)|\le\tfrac12\sqrt M\,|v|^2.
\]
Polar coordinates now give
\[
\left|\int_D f\right|\le\int_D|f|
\le\frac{\sqrt M}{2}\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1r^2r\,dr\,d\theta
=\frac{\pi\sqrt M}{4}.
\]
pitfall: The mixed derivative occurs twice in the squared Hessian norm; this is precisely the factor in the printed bound.

subject: analysis
title: Local coordinates from an orthonormal moving frame
prompt:
Let smooth \(\gamma:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n\) and \(v_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n\), \(1\le i<n\), satisfy that \(\gamma'(t),v_1(t),\ldots,v_{n-1}(t)\) are orthonormal. Define 
\[
\Phi(x)=\gamma(x_n)+\sum_{i<n}x_iv_i(x_n).
\]
 Find \(D\Phi\), prove local diffeomorphism near each axis point, and find 
\[
\lim_{r\downarrow0}\frac{|\Phi(B^n(0,r))|}{|B^n(0,r)|}.
\]
hints: The first \(n\) minus one derivative columns are the frame vectors.
At an axis point the last column is the unit tangent, so the absolute Jacobian is one.
solution:
With \(t=x_n\), the derivative has columns
\[
D\Phi(x)=\left[v_1(t)\ \cdots\ v_{n-1}(t)\quad
\gamma'(t)+\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}x_iv_i'(t)\right].
\]
Equivalently, on an increment \(h\) it acts as \(\sum_{i<n}h_iv_i(t)+h_n(\gamma'(t)+\sum_{i<n}x_iv_i'(t))\). At \(x=(0,\ldots,0,t)\), the columns form an orthonormal basis, only permuted from the given one. The derivative is invertible with absolute determinant one. The inverse function theorem gives a diffeomorphism on a neighborhood of every such point.

In particular there is a neighborhood of zero on which \(\Phi\) is injective with smooth inverse. For sufficiently small \(r\), the ball \(B^n(0,r)\) lies in it, so change of variables gives
\[
\frac{|\Phi(B^n(0,r))|}{|B^n(0,r)|}
=\frac1{|B^n(0,r)|}\int_{B^n(0,r)}|\det D\Phi(x)|\,dx.
\]
Continuity of the derivative and \(|\det D\Phi(0)|=1\) bound the difference of this average from one by \(\sup_{|x|\le r}\big||\det D\Phi(x)|-1\big|\to0\). The requested limit is one.
pitfall: The moving-frame map need not be globally injective; apply change of variables only on the local diffeomorphism neighborhood containing the shrinking balls.

subject: linear algebra
title: Products in opposite orders: characteristic versus minimal polynomial
prompt: Prove that \(AB\) and \(BA\) have the same characteristic polynomial for arbitrary complex \(n\times n\) matrices. Must they have the same minimal polynomial?
hints: Use the determinant identity for \(I\) minus two products.
Find singular factors for which one product is zero and the other a nonzero square-zero matrix.
solution:
The determinant identity \(\det(I-CD)=\det(I-DC)\) holds without invertibility assumptions: evaluate the determinant of \(\begin{pmatrix}I&C\\D&I\end{pmatrix}\) by block elimination, first subtracting \(D\) times the top block row from the bottom to get the lower-right block \(I-DC\), or subtracting \(C\) times the bottom block row from the top to get the upper-left block \(I-CD\). Each eliminating multiplier has determinant one.

For \(t\ne0\), apply this identity to \(C=A,D=t^{-1}B\):
\[
\det(tI-AB)=t^n\det(I-t^{-1}AB)
=t^n\det(I-t^{-1}BA)=\det(tI-BA).
\]
The two polynomials agree for all nonzero \(t\), so they agree identically.

Minimal polynomials need not agree. Take
\[
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
B=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Then \(AB=B\ne0\), \((AB)^2=0\), so its minimal polynomial is \(t^2\), whereas \(BA=0\) has minimal polynomial \(t\). Both characteristic polynomials are \(t^2\). When \(A\) is invertible, the products are similar via \(A^{-1}(AB)A=BA\), but this argument does not extend to singular \(A\).
pitfall: Equality of characteristic polynomials does not imply equality of minimal polynomials, especially at the zero eigenvalue.

subject: linear algebra
title: Complementary ranges from a rank equality
prompt:
If real \(n\times n\) matrices satisfy \(A+B=I\) and 
\[
\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B=n,
\]
 prove 
\[
\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{ran}B=\{0\}.
\]
hints: The identity decomposition shows the two ranges span the whole space.
Use the dimension formula for a sum of subspaces.
solution:
For every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \(x=Ax+Bx\), so \(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B=\mathbb R^n\). Therefore
\[
n=\dim(\operatorname{ran}A+\operatorname{ran}B)
=\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B-
\dim(\operatorname{ran}A\cap\operatorname{ran}B).
\]
The assumed rank sum is \(n\), hence the intersection has dimension zero and consists only of zero. This establishes a direct sum of the two ranges.
pitfall: The sum-to-identity hypothesis proves spanning; the rank condition then rules out overlap.
theorems: Dimension formula for a sum of subspaces

subject: linear algebra
title: A unitary square root
prompt: Prove every complex unitary matrix \(Q\) has a unitary square root \(R\).
hints: Use a unitary eigenbasis for \(Q\).
Choose one unit-modulus square root of each eigenvalue.
solution:
A unitary matrix is normal, so the complex spectral theorem gives
\[
Q=P\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)P^*
\]
with \(P\) unitary. Its eigenvalues have modulus one: if \(Qv=\lambda v\ne0\), norm preservation implies \(|\lambda|=1\). Choose \(\mu_j\) with \(\mu_j^2=\lambda_j\); necessarily \(|\mu_j|=1\). For example choose \(\lambda_j=e^{i\theta_j}\) and \(\mu_j=e^{i\theta_j/2}\). Let \(R=P\operatorname{diag}(\mu_j)P^*\). Then \(R^*R=I\) and \(R^2=Q\). Thus the desired square root is unitary.
pitfall: Use the complex unitary spectral theorem; a real orthogonal square root is a different requirement.
note: Archive label is April 2016; the PDF header says May 2016. Records follow the archive label.

subject: linear algebra
title: A complex outer product with transpose
prompt: For nonzero \(v\in\mathbb C^n\), let \(M=vv^T\), using transpose without conjugation. Find its eigenvalues/eigenvectors, characteristic and minimal polynomials, and determine diagonalizability.
hints: Compute \(M^2\) and the kernel of the functional \(v^T\).
Over the complex field, the scalar \(v^T\) \(v\) can vanish even for nonzero \(v\).
solution:
Put \(\alpha=v^Tv=\sum_jv_j^2\). The matrix is rank one, since \(Mx=v(v^Tx)\), with nonzero vector \(v\) and nonzero functional \(v^T\). Thus
\[
M^2=\alpha M,\qquad \ker M=\{x:v^Tx=0\},\qquad \dim\ker M=n-1.
\]

If \(\alpha\ne0\), \(Mv=\alpha v\), and the eigenspaces are \(E_\alpha=\operatorname{span}(v)\) and \(E_0=\ker(v^T)\), with the latter absent when \(n=1\). They intersect trivially and their dimensions sum to \(n\), so \(M\) is diagonalizable. Its characteristic polynomial is \(t^{n-1}(t-\alpha)\). For \(n\ge2\) both eigenvalues occur, so \(m_M(t)=t(t-\alpha)\); for \(n=1\), \(m_M(t)=t-\alpha\). Eigenvectors are exactly the nonzero vectors in the indicated eigenspaces.

If \(\alpha=0\), which can occur only when \(n\ge2\), then \(M\ne0\) but \(M^2=0\). Its only eigenvalue is zero, its eigenvectors are the nonzero vectors in \(\ker(v^T)\), its characteristic polynomial is \(t^n\), and its minimal polynomial is \(t^2\). It is not diagonalizable: a diagonalizable matrix with only zero eigenvalues would be zero. Its Jordan form has one size-two zero block and \(n-2\) size-one zero blocks. For example \(v=(1,i)^T\) has \(v^Tv=0\) and exhibits this case.
pitfall: The source uses transpose, not conjugate transpose. Replacing it by \(v\) \(v\)-star would lose the nonzero nilpotent case.
note: Archive label is April 2016; the PDF header says May 2016. Records follow the archive label.

subject: linear algebra
title: A full nilpotent chain is a basis
prompt: If \(A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) has minimal polynomial \(t^n\), prove some \(v\) makes \(v,Av,\ldots,A^{n-1}v\) a basis.
hints: Choose \(v\) not killed by A to the power \(n\) minus one.
In a supposed dependence, isolate the smallest nonzero coefficient by applying a power of \(A\).
solution:
The minimal polynomial hypothesis gives \(A^n=0\) and \(A^{n-1}
e0\). Choose \(v\) with \(A^{n-1}v
e0\). Suppose \(\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jA^jv=0\) and not all coefficients vanish. Let \(r\) be the smallest index with \(c_r
e0\). Apply \(A^{n-1-r}\). The terms with index less than \(r\) have zero coefficients, while those with greater index contain a power at least \(n\) and vanish. Thus \(c_rA^{n-1}v=0\), contrary to both factors being nonzero. The \(n\) vectors are independent in an \(n\)-dimensional space, hence a basis. This also covers \(n=1\), where \(A=0\) and any nonzero \(v\) suffices.
pitfall: Nilpotence alone does not guarantee a single full-length chain; the nilpotency index must equal the dimension.

subject: linear algebra
title: Determinant inequalities on the positive cone
prompt: (a) For Hermitian positive semidefinite \(A,B\), prove \(\det(A+B)\ge\det A+\det B\). (b) Prove that positive definite matrices with determinant greater than one form a convex set.
hints: For an invertible positive \(A\), reduce by congruence to \(I\) plus a positive matrix.
For convexity, prove log-determinant concavity using scalar log concavity on the eigenvalues of a relative positive matrix.
solution:
(a) First suppose \(A>0\), and put \(C=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}\ge0\), with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\ge0\). Then
\[
\det(A+B)=\det A\prod_{j=1}^n(1+\lambda_j)
\ge\det A\left(1+\prod_{j=1}^n\lambda_j\right)
=\det A+\det B.
\]
The inequality follows by expanding the product: all omitted terms are nonnegative (for \(n=1\) it is equality). If \(A\) is merely semidefinite, apply the result to \(A+\varepsilon I>0\) and \(B\), then let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), using continuity of determinant.

(b) Let \(A,B>0\) with \(\det A,\det B>1\), and \(0\le t\le1\). Their convex combination \(H=tA+(1-t)B\) is positive definite by its quadratic form. Now \(C=A^{-1/2}BA^{-1/2}>0\), with eigenvalues \(\lambda_j>0\), and
\[
\log\det H=\log\det A+\sum_j\log(t+(1-t)\lambda_j).
\]
The scalar logarithm is concave, since its second derivative is \(-1/x^2<0\); hence each summand is at least \((1-t)\log\lambda_j\). Consequently
\[
\log\det H\ge t\log\det A+(1-t)\log\det B>0.
\]
Thus \(\det H>1\), proving convexity. The argument also establishes the general log-concavity of determinant on the positive definite cone.
pitfall: The additive determinant inequality in part (a), after scaling, does not by itself give the needed convexity bound; use log-concavity.

subject: linear algebra
title: The transpose operator
prompt: For \(T:M_n(\mathbb R)\to M_n(\mathbb R)\), \(T(A)=A^T\), find the characteristic/minimal polynomials and Jordan form.
hints: Split matrix space into symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices.
The operator is respectively plus and minus the identity on these subspaces.
solution:
Every matrix decomposes uniquely as \(A=(A+A^T)/2+(A-A^T)/2\). The symmetric subspace has dimension \(s=n(n+1)/2\) and eigenvalue \(1\) under \(T\); the skew-symmetric subspace has dimension \(a=n(n-1)/2\) and eigenvalue \(-1\). Bases are \(E_{ii},E_{ij}+E_{ji}\) for the former and \(E_{ij}-E_{ji}\), \(i<j\), for the latter. Their union is an eigenbasis, so
\[
\chi_T(t)=(t-1)^s(t+1)^a,\qquad
T\sim\operatorname{diag}(I_s,-I_a).
\]
All Jordan blocks have size one. For \(n\ge2\), both eigenspaces are nonzero, giving \(m_T(t)=(t-1)(t+1)=t^2-1\). For \(n=1\), \(T=I\) and the minimal polynomial is only \(t-1\).
pitfall: The identity \(T^2\) equals \(I\) gives an annihilating polynomial; the one-dimensional case lacks the minus-one eigenspace.

subject: linear algebra
title: Stabilization of kernels
prompt: If \(\ker A=\ker A^2\) on a finite-dimensional vector space, show \(\ker A^m=\ker A\) for every integer \(m>0\).
hints: A vector killed by a higher power can be moved two steps from zero.
Use the assumed kernel equality repeatedly to reduce the exponent.
solution: The inclusion \(\ker A\subset\ker A^m\) is immediate. Conversely, if \(A^mx=0\) with \(m\ge2\), let \(y=A^{m-2}x\). Then \(A^2y=0\), so the assumption gives \(Ay=0\), or \(A^{m-1}x=0\). Repeating this reduction yields \(Ax=0\). Thus every vector in \(\ker A^m\) is in \(\ker A\), proving equality. For \(m=1\) there is nothing to show. The proof in fact does not need finite dimensionality.
pitfall: Apply the kernel hypothesis to an intermediate iterate, not directly to a vector only known to be killed by a much higher power.

subject: linear algebra
title: Integer bases and unit lattice volume
prompt: For integer vectors \(v_1,v_2,v_3\in\mathbb Z^3\), prove they generate every integer vector with integer coefficients iff their parallelepiped has Euclidean volume one.
hints: Form the integer matrix whose columns are the given vectors.
An integer inverse exists exactly when its integer determinant is plus or minus one.
solution:
Let \(V=[v_1\ v_2\ v_3]\). The parallelepiped volume is \(|\det V|\). If every integer vector is an integer combination of the columns, apply this to each standard basis vector \(e_j\). There is an integer matrix \(C\) with \(VC=I\). Taking determinants gives \(\det V\det C=1\). Both determinants are integers, so \(\det V=\pm1\), and the volume is one.

Conversely, volume one means \(\det V=\pm1\). The adjugate formula gives \(V^{-1}=\operatorname{adj}(V)/\det V\), whose entries are integers because all cofactors are integer determinants. For \(w\in\mathbb Z^3\), the coefficient vector \(V^{-1}w\) is therefore integral, and \(w\) is an integer combination of the \(v_j\).
pitfall: Nonzero volume proves a real basis, but generation of the entire integer lattice requires determinant plus or minus one.

subject: linear algebra
title: Density of complex diagonalizable matrices
prompt: Prove every complex \(n\times n\) matrix is a limit of diagonalizable complex matrices.
hints: Triangularize the matrix and perturb only the diagonal.
Avoid the finitely many perturbation values at which two diagonal entries coincide.
solution:
Unitary Schur triangularization gives \(A=QTQ^*\), with \(T\) upper triangular and diagonal entries \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\). Set \(D=\operatorname{diag}(1,2,\ldots,n)\). The diagonal entries of \(T+\varepsilon D\) are \(\lambda_i+\varepsilon i\). Two of them coincide only if \(\varepsilon=(\lambda_j-\lambda_i)/(i-j)\), for some \(i\ne j\). There are finitely many forbidden values. Choose positive real \(\varepsilon_k\to0\) avoiding them.

Then \(T+\varepsilon_kD\) has \(n\) distinct complex eigenvalues, since the eigenvalues of an upper triangular matrix are its diagonal entries. Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent, so each such matrix is diagonalizable. Let \(A_k=Q(T+\varepsilon_kD)Q^*\). These are diagonalizable and \(A_k\to A\), since \(A_k-A=\varepsilon_kQDQ^*\to0\).
pitfall: The proof uses complex eigenvalues. Density of matrices diagonalizable over the real field is a different, generally false assertion for real matrices.
theorems: Independence of eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues

subject: linear algebra
title: Positivity of principal minors
prompt: If \(A\) is complex Hermitian positive definite, show the determinant of every principal submatrix is a positive real number.
hints: Embed a vector on the selected coordinates into the full space with zeros elsewhere.
The principal submatrix is Hermitian positive definite and therefore has positive eigenvalues.
solution:
For a nonempty index set \(I=\{i_1,\ldots,i_k\}\), let \(C=(a_{i_pi_q})_{p,q=1}^k\). Hermitian symmetry of \(A\) implies \(C^*=C\). Given nonzero \(z\in\mathbb C^k\), define \(x\in\mathbb C^n\) with entries \(x_{i_p}=z_p\) and zero elsewhere. Then \(x\ne0\) and
\[
z^*Cz=x^*Ax>0.
\]
Thus \(C\) is positive definite. By the Hermitian spectral theorem, all its eigenvalues are positive real numbers, so their product \(\det C\) is positive and real. If the empty principal submatrix is included, its determinant is one by convention.
pitfall: The same row and column index set is essential; an arbitrary submatrix of a positive matrix need not be Hermitian or have positive determinant.

subject: linear algebra
title: Recovering nilpotent Jordan blocks from nullities
prompt: For complex nilpotent matrices \(A,B\), prove they are similar iff \(\dim\ker A^k=\dim\ker B^k\) for every positive integer \(k\).
hints: A nilpotent block of size \(s\) contributes the minimum of \(k\) and \(s\) to the \(k\)-th nullity.
Successive nullity differences count blocks of at least a given size.
solution:
If \(B=PAP^{-1}\), then \(B^k=PA^kP^{-1}\), so the kernels have equal dimensions for every \(k\).

Conversely, for a nilpotent matrix \(M\) with Jordan block sizes \(s_1,\ldots,s_r\), let \(n_k=\dim\ker M^k\) and \(n_0=0\). A block of size \(s\) has \(k\)-th power kernel dimension \(\min(k,s)\); therefore
\[
n_k=\sum_{\ell=1}^r\min(k,s_\ell),\qquad
d_k:=n_k-n_{k-1}=\#\{\ell:s_\ell\ge k\}.
\]
The number of blocks of size exactly \(k\) is
\[
d_k-d_{k+1}=2n_k-n_{k-1}-n_{k+1}.
\]
For \(k\) at least the nilpotency index, \(n_k=n\) and later differences are zero, so these formulas recover the entire finite multiset of block sizes. Equal nullity sequences for \(A,B\) thus give identical nilpotent Jordan forms, which means the matrices are similar.
pitfall: Nilpotence is essential: the nullities of powers alone give no information about nonzero eigenvalues.

subject: analysis
title: A logarithmically normalized improper integral
prompt:
Suppose \(f\) is Riemann integrable on every \([1,A]\) and \(xf(x)\to1\). Prove 
\[
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac1t\int_1^{e^t}f(x)\,dx=1.
\]
hints: Compare \(f\) with one over \(x\) beyond a fixed large point.
The initial finite integral disappears after division by \(t\).
solution:
Fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Choose \(R>1\) such that for \(x\ge R\),
\[
\frac{1-\varepsilon}{x}\le f(x)\le\frac{1+\varepsilon}{x}.
\]
For \(t\ge\log R\), write \(C_R=\int_1^R f(x)\,dx\). Integrating the inequalities gives
\[
C_R+(1-\varepsilon)(t-\log R)
\le\int_1^{e^t}f(x)\,dx
\le C_R+(1+\varepsilon)(t-\log R).
\]
Divide by \(t\) and take lower and upper limits to get \(1-\varepsilon\le\liminf\le\limsup\le1+\varepsilon\). Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves the limit. No convergence of the unnormalized improper integral is asserted; it grows like \(t\).
pitfall: The integral generally diverges; estimate its growth rather than trying to assign it a finite improper-integral value.
note: Archive label is April 2017; the PDF header says May 4, 2017. Records follow the archive label.

subject: analysis
title: A common Lipschitz bound upgrades convergence
prompt:
(1) If all \(f_n:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) have the same Lipschitz constant \(K>0\), prove pointwise convergence is equivalent to uniform convergence. (2) Prove 
\[
\int_0^1 n\log(1+\frac{x}{n})\,dx\to\frac{1}{2}.
\]
hints: The pointwise limit retains the Lipschitz bound; control the interval using a finite fine net.
For the logarithmic functions, bound the derivatives and find the pointwise limit.
solution:
(1) Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence. Conversely assume \(f_n(x)\to f(x)\) at every point. Passing to the limit in the Lipschitz inequality gives \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le K|x-y|\). Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose finitely many mesh points such that each \(x\in[0,1]\) is within \(\delta<\varepsilon/(3K)\) of one of them. Pointwise convergence at these finitely many points gives a common \(N\) after which the error at every mesh point is less than \(\varepsilon/3\). For a nearby mesh point \(y\),
\[
|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le K|x-y|+|f_n(y)-f(y)|+K|y-x|<\varepsilon.
\]
Thus convergence is uniform.

(2) Put \(g_n(x)=n\log(1+x/n)\). Then \(g_n'(x)=1/(1+x/n)\), so the functions have a common Lipschitz constant one. The elementary limit \(\log(1+u)/u\to1\) gives \(g_n(x)\to x\), with the value zero at \(x=0\). Part (1) gives uniform convergence, and therefore
\[
\left|\int_0^1g_n(x)\,dx-\int_0^1x\,dx\right|\le\|g_n-x\|_\infty\to0.
\]
The limit is \(1/2\).
pitfall: Pointwise convergence on a compact set is not generally uniform; the shared modulus of continuity is the crucial additional hypothesis.
note: Archive label is April 2017; the PDF header says May 4, 2017. Records follow the archive label.

subject: analysis
title: Compactness of the Hilbert cube in the supremum metric
prompt: Prove compactness of \(H=\{(x_n):0\le x_n\le2^{-n}\}\) for \(d(x,y)=\sup_n|x_n-y_n|\).
hints: Diagonalize so that every fixed coordinate converges.
The uniform decay of the coordinate bounds controls all the remaining coordinates at once.
solution:
Take any sequence \(x^{(j)}\in H\). Coordinate one lies in the compact interval \([0,2^{-1}]\), so pass to a subsequence on which it converges. Successively extract subsequences for coordinates two, three, and so on, then take diagonal indices. On the resulting subsequence, every coordinate converges, say \(x_n^{(j_k)}\to x_n\). The closed coordinate intervals imply \(x=(x_n)\in H\).

Given \(\varepsilon>0\), choose \(N\) with \(2^{-(N+1)}<\varepsilon\). For \(n>N\), both coordinate values are in \([0,2^{-n}]\), so \(|x_n^{(j_k)}-x_n|\le2^{-n}<\varepsilon\), independently of \(k\). For the finitely many coordinates \(n\le N\), choose \(k\) large enough that all their differences are less than \(\varepsilon\). Then \(d(x^{(j_k)},x)<\varepsilon\). Every sequence has a convergent subsequence in \(H\), so \(H\) is compact by the equivalence of sequential compactness and compactness for metric spaces.
pitfall: Coordinatewise convergence alone need not be convergence in the supremum metric; the decaying tail bounds make it so here.
note: Archive label is April 2017; the PDF header says May 4, 2017. Records follow the archive label.

subject: analysis
title: Uniform convergence away from a singular limiting point
prompt:
For 
\[
f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{nx}{1+n^4x^2},
\]
 prove uniform convergence on \([a,\infty)\) for \(a>0\). For a positive perfect square \(N\), prove 
\[
f(\frac{1}{N})\ge(\frac{N}{2})\sum_{n\ge\sqrt N}n^{-3}\ge\frac{1}{4},
\]
 and deduce failure of uniform convergence on \(\mathbb R\).
hints: Use a summable bound when \(x\) is bounded below.
At \(x\) equal to one over \(N\), compare the large-index terms from below; the sum is discontinuous at zero.
solution:
The \(n=0\) term is identically zero. For \(n\ge1\) and \(x\ge a>0\),
\[
0\le\frac{nx}{1+n^4x^2}\le\frac1{n^3x}\le\frac1{a n^3}.
\]
The Weierstrass \(M\)-test proves uniform convergence on \([a,\infty)\).

Let \(N=m^2\), \(m\ge1\). For \(n\ge m\), \(n^4/N^2\ge1\), so
\[
\frac{n/N}{1+n^4/N^2}\ge\frac{n/N}{2n^4/N^2}=\frac{N}{2n^3}.
\]
All terms at \(1/N\) are nonnegative. Since \(x^{-3}\) decreases,
\[
f(1/N)\ge\frac N2\sum_{n=m}^\infty n^{-3}
\ge\frac N2\int_m^\infty x^{-3}\,dx=\frac N{4m^2}=\frac14.
\]
For each nonzero real \(x\), absolute convergence follows from the bound \(1/(n^3|x|)\); at zero every term vanishes, so \(f(0)=0\). Taking \(N=m^2\to\infty\), the lower bound shows \(f\) is not continuous at zero. Each partial sum is continuous on \(\mathbb R\). A uniform limit of continuous functions would be continuous, hence this series cannot converge uniformly on \(\mathbb R\).
pitfall: The lower bound concerns a tail whose starting index grows with \(N\); keep the perfect-square condition when comparing the integral.
note: Archive label is April 2017; the PDF header says May 4, 2017. Records follow the archive label.

subject: analysis
title: A positive semidefinite Hessian implies convexity
prompt: Suppose \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice differentiable and \(D^2f_p(v,v)\ge0\) everywhere. Prove \(f((1-t)p+tq)\le(1-t)f(p)+tf(q)\) for \(0\le t\le1\), including a proof of the one-dimensional case.
hints: In one dimension the first derivative is nondecreasing.
Restrict the multivariable function to the line segment joining the two points.
solution:
First let \(g\) be twice differentiable on a real interval and \(g''\ge0\). By the mean value theorem applied to \(g'\), the derivative \(g'\) is nondecreasing. For \(u<v<w\), the mean value theorem on \([u,v]\) and \([v,w]\) gives
\[
\frac{g(v)-g(u)}{v-u}\le\frac{g(w)-g(v)}{w-v},
\]
because the derivative values occur at points in those respective intervals. Rearranging yields
\[
g(v)\le\frac{w-v}{w-u}g(u)+\frac{v-u}{w-u}g(w).
\]
This proves one-dimensional convexity, with the endpoints giving equality.

For arbitrary \(p,q\), let \(g(s)=f(p+s(q-p))\), \(s\in\mathbb R\). The chain rule gives
\[
g''(s)=D^2f_{p+s(q-p)}(q-p,q-p)\ge0.
\]
Apply the one-dimensional result to \(u=0,v=t,w=1\) for \(0<t<1\). It gives \(f(p+t(q-p))\le(1-t)f(p)+tf(q)\). The cases \(t=0,1\), or \(p=q\), are immediate. The proof needs existence of the second derivative, not its continuity.
pitfall: A nonnegative Hessian means its quadratic form is nonnegative in every direction; entrywise nonnegativity is a different condition.
note: Archive label is April 2017; the PDF header says May 4, 2017. Records follow the archive label.

subject: analysis
title: Cubic roots, multiplicity, and a defective uniqueness claim
prompt: For \(f_{p,q}(x)=x^3-px+q\), the source claims that any \(y,z\in\mathbb R\) determine a unique \((p,q)\) with \(f_{p,q}(y)=f_{p,q}(z)=0\), defining a smooth at-most-six-to-one map \(\phi\), locally a diffeomorphism exactly when its fiber has six points. Assess the statement and solve the intended multiplicity-based version.
hints: Check the case in which the two proposed roots coincide.
For distinct roots subtract the equations, extend the resulting formulas smoothly, and calculate the Jacobian.
solution:
The printed uniqueness assertion is false when \(y=z\). For example \(y=z=0\) only forces \(q=0\), and every \(p\in\mathbb R\) works. Thus the map as literally defined does not exist. Moreover a cubic with three distinct real roots has nine ordered pairs of roots if repetitions are allowed, so the unrestricted root-pair relation does not have the claimed bound.

For \(y\ne z\), subtracting the two equations gives
\[
p=\frac{y^3-z^3}{y-z}=y^2+yz+z^2,\qquad q=py-y^3=yz(y+z).
\]
These formulas have a unique smooth continuation to all of \(\mathbb R^2\):
\[
\phi(y,z)=(y^2+yz+z^2,\ yz(y+z)).
\]
They are characterized by the factorization
\[
x^3-px+q=(x-y)(x-z)(x+y+z).
\]
When \(y=z\), this imposes a double root, the missing multiplicity requirement. Equivalently the corrected problem requires divisibility by \((x-y)(x-z)\).

For this corrected map, a fiber consists of ordered choices of two roots from the multiset of three real or complex roots, with multiplicity respected, and both chosen roots real. With three distinct real roots there are exactly six ordered choices. With a double root \(r\ne0\) and simple root \(-2r\), the fiber has exactly \((r,r),(r,-2r),(-2r,r)\). A triple root must be zero and gives only \((0,0)\). A cubic with only one simple real root has no such real pair. In every case the fiber has at most six points, and has six exactly when there are three distinct real roots.

Finally,
\[
D\phi(y,z)=
\begin{pmatrix}2y+z&y+2z\\z(2y+z)&y(y+2z)\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\det D\phi=(y-z)(2y+z)(y+2z).
\]
This determinant is nonzero precisely when the three real roots \(y,z,-y-z\) are distinct, equivalently when the fiber has six points. The inverse function theorem then supplies a local diffeomorphism. Conversely any local \(C^1\) diffeomorphism has invertible derivative by the chain rule for its inverse, proving the necessity. This completes the intended corrected problem; it does not repair the literal uniqueness claim without adding multiplicity.
pitfall: Two equations become the same equation when the two roots coincide. Do not divide by their difference without treating that case.
note: Archive label is April 2017; the PDF header says May 4, 2017. Records follow the archive label. SOURCE ERROR: coincident \(y\),\(z\) do not uniquely determine \(p\),\(q\); the multiplicity-based correction and counterexample are explicit. The final printed neighborhood coordinates also have a naming typo.

subject: analysis
title: Persistence of a zero in a parameter-dependent integral
prompt:
For 
\[
I_y(x)=\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\pi}(e^{-t^2x}\cos(ty)-e^{t^2y}\sin(tx))\,dt,
\]
 prove that for all sufficiently small \(|y|\), some \(x\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(I_y(x)=0\).
hints: At \(y\) zero, compare the signs at \(x\) zero and \(x\) one.
Continuity in the parameter preserves those strict signs.
solution:
At \(y=0\),
\[
I_0(0)=\int_{\pi/2}^\pi1\,dt=\pi/2>0,\qquad
I_0(1)=\int_{\pi/2}^\pi e^{-t^2}\,dt-\int_{\pi/2}^\pi\sin t\,dt.
\]
The second integral is one. Since \(t\ge\pi/2>1\), we have \(e^{-t^2}\le e^{-t}\), and
\[
\int_{\pi/2}^\pi e^{-t^2}\,dt
\le e^{-\pi/2}-e^{-\pi}<1.
\]
Thus \(I_0(1)<0\).

The integrand is jointly continuous in \(x,y,t\). On any compact parameter rectangle it is uniformly continuous, so its integral is continuous in \(x,y\) (bound the difference by the integration length times the uniform difference of the integrands). In particular \(I_y(0)>0\) and \(I_y(1)<0\) for \(|y|<\varepsilon\), after choosing a sufficiently small common \(\varepsilon>0\). For each such \(y\), continuity of \(x\mapsto I_y(x)\) and the intermediate value theorem give a zero strictly between zero and one.
pitfall: A strict sign at both endpoints allows the zero to persist without proving a nonzero derivative at any particular zero.

subject: analysis
title: A countable determining set
prompt: For a closed set \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\), find a countable \(S\subset X\) such that every continuous \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is determined by its values on \(S\).
hints: Use Euclidean balls with rational centers and radii as a countable base.
Choose one point of \(X\) in each base ball that meets \(X\).
solution:
The balls in \(\mathbb R^n\) with rational centers and positive rational radii form a countable base. For each such ball \(B\) meeting \(X\), choose one point \(s_B\in B\cap X\), and let \(S\) be the set of chosen points. It is countable. If \(X=\varnothing\), take \(S=\varnothing\).

Every nonempty relatively open subset of \(X\) contains some \(B\cap X\ne\varnothing\) from this base, and hence contains \(s_B\). Thus \(S\) is dense in \(X\). If continuous functions \(f,g:X\to\mathbb R\) agree on \(S\), then for each \(x\in X\) choose \(s_j\in S\) tending to \(x\); continuity gives \(f(x)=\lim_j f(s_j)=\lim_j g(s_j)=g(x)\). Hence restriction to \(S\) determines a continuous function uniquely. Closedness of \(X\) was not needed; the construction works for every subset of \(\mathbb R^n\).
pitfall: The rational points belonging to \(X\) need not be dense in \(X\); choose points of \(X\) inside rational balls instead.

subject: analysis
title: The Taylor series of log \(x\) divided by \(x\)
prompt:
Find the Taylor coefficients \(h_n\) of \(f(x)=\frac{\log x}{x}\) at \(x=1\). Determine all open intervals on which the series converges uniformly to \(f\). Does 
\[
\sum h_n
\]
 converge to \(\frac{\log2}{2}\)?
hints: Multiply the logarithm and geometric series in \(x\) minus one.
Uniform convergence on an open interval still forces the individual terms to tend uniformly to zero.
solution:
Put \(w=x-1\). For \(|w|<1\), integration of the geometric series gives \(\log(1+w)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty(-1)^{j+1}w^j/j\), while \(1/(1+w)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty(-1)^kw^k\). Both converge absolutely there, so the Cauchy product is
\[
\frac{\log(1+w)}{1+w}=\sum_{n=1}^\infty(-1)^{n+1}H_n w^n,
\qquad H_n=\sum_{j=1}^n\frac1j.
\]
Thus \(h_0=0\) and \(h_n=(-1)^{n+1}H_n\) for \(n\ge1\); these are the Taylor coefficients since a power series can be differentiated inside its radius of convergence.

For any \(0<a<b<2\), \(r=\max(|a-1|,|b-1|)<1\). Since \(H_n\le n\), the terms on \((a,b)\) are dominated by \(n r^n\), a summable series. Therefore convergence to \(f\) is uniform there.

These are all the nonempty open intervals of uniform convergence. At a point with \(|x-1|\ge1\), the terms \(H_n|x-1|^n\) do not even tend to zero. Any interval of pointwise convergence must lie in \((0,2)\). If its infimum is zero or its supremum is two, then
\[
\sup_{x\in I}|h_n(x-1)^n|=H_n,
\]
so the terms do not tend uniformly to zero, contradicting uniform convergence of the series. Thus an interval must stay a positive distance from both endpoints: exactly \(I=(a,b)\) with \(0<a<b<2\).

At \(x=2\), the proposed sum is \(\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}H_n\). Its terms fail to tend to zero, so it diverges and cannot equal \(\log2/2\).
pitfall: An alternating sign is insufficient for convergence when the term magnitudes grow. Uniform convergence on intervals approaching the radius boundary also fails.
theorems: Cauchy product of absolutely convergent series

subject: analysis
title: Polynomial approximation to the floor function
prompt:
Construct polynomials \(p_k\) converging pointwise to \(\lfloor x\rfloor\) on \(\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Z\), and satisfying 
\[
\int_K|\lfloor x\rfloor-p_k(x)|\,dx\to0
\]
 for every compact \(K\subset\mathbb R\).
hints: Replace each jump by a short continuous linear transition.
Approximate the smoothed function on an expanding compact interval, then bound the total lengths of the transition strips.
solution:
Let \(\delta_k=1/(10k^2)\). Construct a continuous function \(g_k\) as follows: outside the disjoint intervals \([m-\delta_k,m+\delta_k]\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\), put \(g_k(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor\). On each such interval interpolate linearly from \(m-1\) at its left endpoint to \(m\) at its right endpoint. The definitions match at the endpoints, so \(g_k\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R\), and \(|g_k-\lfloor x\rfloor|\le1\).

By the Weierstrass approximation theorem, choose a polynomial \(p_k\) with \(\sup_{[-k,k]}|p_k-g_k|<1/k\). For fixed \(x\notin\mathbb Z\), its positive distance from the integers eventually exceeds \(\delta_k\), and eventually \(|x|\le k\). Then \(g_k(x)=\lfloor x\rfloor\), so \(p_k(x)\to\lfloor x\rfloor\).

For a compact \(K\), choose \(R\ge1\) with \(K\subset[-R,R]\), and let \(M_R\) be the finite number of integers in \([-R-1,R+1]\). When \(k\ge R\), the discrepancy \(g_k-\lfloor x\rfloor\) on \([-R,R]\) is supported on strips of total length at most \(2M_R\delta_k\). Thus
\[
\int_K|\lfloor x\rfloor-p_k(x)|\,dx
\le\int_{-R}^R|\lfloor x\rfloor-p_k(x)|\,dx
\le2M_R\delta_k+\frac{2R}{k}\longrightarrow0.
\]
The integral on an arbitrary compact set is interpreted in its usual Lebesgue sense; the displayed bound over an interval also uses only elementary Riemann-integral estimates. Uniform convergence across a jump is neither required nor possible.
pitfall: The approximation interval must grow with \(k\); approximation on one fixed interval does not construct a sequence valid on all of the real line.

subject: analysis
title: Differentiability in a rational-function family
prompt:
Let 
\[
f_k(x,y)=\frac{x^2(x+y^2)}{x^2+y^{2k}}
\]
 away from the origin, with \(f_k(0,0)=0\). Show \(f_1\) is not differentiable there, but \(f_k\) is differentiable there for every integer \(k\ge2\).
hints: The coordinate axes force the only possible derivative to be \(x\).
Subtract \(x\), and bound the two remainder terms by quadratic quantities.
solution:
For every \(k\), \(f_k(x,0)=x\) and \(f_k(0,y)=0\). Thus the partial derivatives at the origin are \(1,0\), and the only possible total derivative is \(L(x,y)=x\).

For \(k=1\), take \(x=y=t>0\). Then \(f_1(t,t)=(t+t^2)/2\), so
\[
\frac{f_1(t,t)-L(t,t)}{\sqrt{t^2+t^2}}
=\frac{-1+t}{2\sqrt2}\longrightarrow-\frac1{2\sqrt2}\ne0.
\]
The required remainder estimate fails.

For \(k\ge2\),
\[
f_k(x,y)-x=\frac{x^2y^2-xy^{2k}}{x^2+y^{2k}}.
\]
The first term has magnitude at most \(y^2\). For the second, \(2|x||y|^k\le x^2+|y|^{2k}\) yields
\[
\frac{|x||y|^{2k}}{x^2+|y|^{2k}}\le\frac12|y|^k.
\]
When \(|y|\le1\), this is at most \(y^2/2\). Therefore, with \(\rho=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\),
\[
|f_k(x,y)-x|\le\tfrac32 y^2\le\tfrac32\rho^2=o(\rho).
\]
This proves differentiability at the origin for \(k\ge2\), with derivative \(L(x,y)=x\).
pitfall: Existence of the two partial derivatives does not imply differentiability; the first member of this family supplies the counterexample.

subject: analysis
title: A contraction for the quaternionic square equation
prompt:
For 
\[
s(x,y,z,w)=(x^2-y^2-z^2-w^2,2xy,2xz,2xw)
\]
 and \(|b|\le\frac{1}{16}\), prove \(s(v)-v+b=0\) has a unique solution with \(|v|\le\frac{1}{8}\).
hints: Prove the norm of the square equals the squared norm of the input.
Estimate the derivative on the closed small ball and apply the contraction theorem.
solution:
Write \(v=(x,u)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\), so \(s(v)=(x^2-|u|^2,2xu)\). Direct calculation gives
\[
|s(v)|^2=(x^2-|u|^2)^2+4x^2|u|^2=(x^2+|u|^2)^2,
\]
hence \(|s(v)|=|v|^2\). For \(h=(h_0,h')\),
\[
Ds(v)[h]=2(xh_0-u\cdot h',\,xh'+h_0u).
\]
Expanding the squared norm cancels the cross terms and gives
\[
\tfrac14|Ds(v)[h]|^2=(x^2+|u|^2)h_0^2+x^2|h'|^2+(u\cdot h')^2
\le |v|^2|h|^2
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz. Thus \(\|Ds(v)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2|v|\).

Let \(X=\overline B(0,1/8)\), a complete metric space, and \(T(v)=s(v)+b\). For \(v\in X\),
\[
|T(v)|\le(1/8)^2+1/16=5/64<1/8,
\]
so \(T\) maps \(X\) into itself. Integrating the derivative along the segment joining two points of this convex ball gives \(|T(v)-T(w)|\le\frac14|v-w|\). The contraction mapping theorem supplies a unique fixed point in \(X\), equivalent to the stated equation. The strict image bound actually puts that solution in the interior, even when \(|b|=1/16\).
pitfall: The ball must be closed to be complete. A small derivative bound alone is insufficient without checking that the map sends the ball into itself.
theorems: Derivative bound on a convex set

subject: linear algebra
title: A rank-one positive semidefinite matrix is an outer product
prompt: If \(A=[a_{jk}]\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) is nonnegative and has rank one, prove \(a_{jk}=v_j\overline{v_k}\) for some nonzero \(v\in\mathbb C^n\).
hints: Diagonalize A using the Hermitian spectral theorem.
There is exactly one positive eigenvalue; absorb its square root into its unit eigenvector.
solution: Nonnegative means Hermitian positive semidefinite, as specified in the exam. By the spectral theorem, \(A\) has an orthonormal eigenbasis and nonnegative eigenvalues. Rank one implies that precisely one eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is nonzero; hence \(\lambda>0\). If \(u\) is a unit eigenvector for \(\lambda\), spectral decomposition gives \(A=\lambda uu^*\). Let \(v=\sqrt\lambda\,u\ne0\). Then \(A=vv^*\), so its entries satisfy \(a_{jk}=v_j\overline{v_k}\), as required.
pitfall: Rank one alone only gives an arbitrary outer product; positive semidefiniteness makes the two vectors conjugate to each other.

subject: linear algebra
title: The span of planar rotations and a two-orthogonal decomposition
prompt:
(a) Find a basis for 
\[
W=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}SO(2).
\]
 (b) Find its Hilbert–Schmidt orthogonal complement in real \(2\times2\) matrices. (c) Show every real \(2\times2\) matrix is \(a_1R_1+a_2R_2\) with \(a_i\ge0\), \(R_i\in O(2)\).
hints: Planar rotations lie in the span of the identity and the quarter-turn.
Split an arbitrary matrix into its rotation-span part and its orthogonal complement; each part is a scalar times an orthogonal matrix.
solution:
(a) Every special orthogonal \(2\times2\) matrix has the form \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\). Thus, with \(J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\),
\[
W=\{aI+bJ:a,b\in\mathbb R\},\qquad \{I,J\}\ \hbox{is a basis}.
\]
Both basis matrices themselves belong to \(SO(2)\).

(b) For \(M=\begin{pmatrix}u&v\\w&t\end{pmatrix}\), the Hilbert--Schmidt products with \(I,J\) are \(u+t\) and \(w-v\). Orthogonality to both therefore gives
\[
W^\perp=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\d&-c\end{pmatrix}:c,d\in\mathbb R\right\},
\]
with basis \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\).

(c) Every \(A\) decomposes uniquely as
\[
A=C+F,\qquad
C=\begin{pmatrix}a&-b\\b&a\end{pmatrix},\quad
F=\begin{pmatrix}c&d\\d&-c\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Explicitly, \(a=(A_{11}+A_{22})/2\), \(b=(A_{21}-A_{12})/2\), \(c=(A_{11}-A_{22})/2\), \(d=(A_{12}+A_{21})/2\). We have \(C^TC=(a^2+b^2)I\) and \(F^TF=(c^2+d^2)I\). Put \(a_1=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), \(a_2=\sqrt{c^2+d^2}\). For a nonzero coefficient define \(R_1=C/a_1\) or \(R_2=F/a_2\); these are orthogonal. If a coefficient vanishes, take the corresponding \(R_i=I\), since that summand is zero. This yields the required decomposition with nonnegative scalars.
pitfall: The complement of the rotation span contains reflections after normalization, so the matrices in part (c) need the full orthogonal group.

subject: linear algebra
title: An eigenvalue sum inequality from min–max
prompt:
For Hermitian \(A,B\), list eigenvalues increasingly. If \(1\le j,k\le n\) and \(j+k>n\), prove 
\[
\lambda_{j+k-n}(A+B)\le\lambda_j(A)+\lambda_k(B)
\]
 using min–max.
hints: Intersect the subspaces spanned by the lowest \(j\) and \(k\) eigenvectors.
The intersection has enough dimension for the increasing-order min–max formula.
solution:
Let \(E\) be the span of eigenvectors for the lowest \(j\) eigenvalues of \(A\), and \(F\) the analogous \(k\)-dimensional subspace for \(B\). The spectral theorem gives
\[
x^*Ax\le\lambda_j(A)\|x\|^2\ (x\in E),\qquad
x^*Bx\le\lambda_k(B)\|x\|^2\ (x\in F).
\]
The dimension formula yields \(\dim(E\cap F)\ge j+k-n=:m\ge1\). Choose an \(m\)-dimensional subspace \(L\subset E\cap F\). Every unit \(x\in L\) satisfies \(x^*(A+B)x\le\lambda_j(A)+\lambda_k(B)\). The Courant--Fischer formula for eigenvalues in increasing order is
\[
\lambda_m(A+B)=\min_{\dim M=m}\ \max_{\substack{x\in M\\\|x\|=1}}x^*(A+B)x.
\]
Testing this minimum at \(L\) proves the inequality.
pitfall: Match the min–max formula to increasing eigenvalue order; the relevant test subspace has dimension \(j+k-n\).

subject: linear algebra
title: Inverting identity minus differentiation
prompt:
On 
\[
V_n=\{p\in\mathbb C[x]:\deg p\le n\},
\]
 let \(Tp=p-p'\). (a) Prove \(T\) invertible and \(T^{-1}\) a polynomial in \(T\). (b) Find the Jordan form of \(T^{-1}\).
hints: Differentiation is nilpotent on this finite-degree space.
The nilpotent part of the inverse has the same maximal chain length as differentiation.
solution:
Let \(D\) be differentiation. Since \(D^{n+1}=0\), \(T=I-D\) has inverse
\[
T^{-1}=I+D+\cdots+D^n=\sum_{r=0}^n(I-T)^r,
\]
which is a polynomial in \(T\). Multiplying by \(I-D\) verifies the inverse by telescoping.

Put \(N=T^{-1}-I=D(I-D)^{-1}\). Differentiation commutes with \((I-D)^{-1}\), so \(N^{n+1}=0\). For \(n\ge1\), \(N^n=D^n(I-D)^{-n}=D^n\), because all positive powers of \(D\) in the latter inverse factor disappear after multiplication by \(D^n\). Since \(D^n(x^n)=n!\ne0\), the nilpotency index of \(N\) is \(n+1\). The entire space has dimension \(n+1\), so its Jordan form must be a single nilpotent block of that size. Thus
\[
T^{-1}\sim J_{n+1}(1).
\]
For \(n=0\), the operator is the identity on constants, giving the same conclusion \(J_1(1)\).
pitfall: The eigenvalue one alone does not determine the Jordan form; establish the size of the nilpotent chain.

subject: linear algebra
title: Normality characterized by a unitary multiplier
prompt: On a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space, prove \(T\) is normal iff \(T^*=UT\) for some unitary operator \(U\). The proof must cover real spaces as well.
hints: For necessity, use the positive square root of \(T\)-star \(T\) and construct a commuting unitary polar factor.
For sufficiency, take the adjoint and multiply the equation to compare \(T\) \(T\)-star with \(T\)-star \(T\).
solution:
First suppose \(T\) is normal, \(T^*T=TT^*\). Let \(H=(T^*T)^{1/2}\), defined by the real symmetric or complex Hermitian spectral theorem. Normality implies \(T(T^*T)=(T^*T)T\), so \(T\) preserves each eigenspace of \(H^2\), and hence of \(H\).

On an eigenspace \(E_\lambda\) of \(H\) with \(\lambda>0\), define \(Q=T/\lambda\). This maps \(E_\lambda\) to itself, and
\[
\|Qv\|^2=\lambda^{-2}\langle T^*Tv,v\rangle=\|v\|^2.
\]
It is an isometry and, in finite dimension, a surjective one. On \(\ker H=\ker T\), define \(Q=I\). The orthogonal direct sum of these definitions is unitary (orthogonal over \(\mathbb R\)), commutes with \(H\), and satisfies \(T=QH\). Therefore \(T^*=HQ^*=Q^*H\). Set \(U=(Q^*)^2\), also unitary; then
\[
UT=(Q^*)^2QH=Q^*H=T^*.
\]
This uses a positive spectral decomposition, valid over both fields, rather than a complex eigenbasis for \(T\).

Conversely, if \(T^*=UT\) with \(U\) unitary, then
\[
TT^*=(T^*)^*T^*=(UT)^*(UT)=T^*U^*UT=T^*T.
\]
Thus \(T\) is normal. The argument includes singular operators and the zero operator.
pitfall: A normal real operator need not be diagonalizable over the real field. Use positive square roots and real orthogonal factors to cover that case.
theorems: Spectral theorem over real and complex inner product spaces

subject: linear algebra
title: Even-dimensional skew symmetry and a rank-one determinant update
prompt: Let \(A^T=-A\), \(B^T=B\) be real \(n\times n\) matrices, with even \(n\). (a) Prove \(\operatorname{cof}(A):B=0\) for the Hilbert–Schmidt inner product. (b) If \(B\) has rank one, prove \(\det(A+B)=\det A\).
hints: The cofactor matrix is also skew-symmetric when \(n\) is even.
Expand the determinant by row multilinearity; terms containing two rank-one update rows vanish.
solution:
(a) Cofactors satisfy \(\operatorname{cof}(A^T)=\operatorname{cof}(A)^T\) and \(\operatorname{cof}(cA)=c^{n-1}\operatorname{cof}(A)\), directly from their \((n-1)\times(n-1)\) determinant definitions. Since \(n\) is even and \(A^T=-A\),
\[
\operatorname{cof}(A)^T=\operatorname{cof}(-A)=-\operatorname{cof}(A).
\]
Thus \(K=\operatorname{cof}(A)\) is skew-symmetric. Its diagonal entries vanish, and the two contributions \(K_{ij}B_{ij}+K_{ji}B_{ji}\) cancel because \(B\) is symmetric. Therefore \(K:B=\sum_{ij}K_{ij}B_{ij}=0\).

(b) Rank one means all rows of \(B\) are multiples of a single row vector. Expand \(\det(A+B)\) using multilinearity in rows. The term with no row from \(B\) is \(\det A\); any term with at least two rows from \(B\) vanishes because those rows are dependent. The sum of the terms with exactly one update row is \(\sum_{ij}B_{ij}\operatorname{cof}(A)_{ij}\). Consequently
\[
\det(A+B)=\det A+\operatorname{cof}(A):B=\det A.
\]
No invertibility of \(A\) is needed.
pitfall: The cofactor matrix and adjugate are transposes of one another; the row-expansion derivative pairs with the cofactor matrix entrywise.
theorems: Orthogonality of symmetric and skew-symmetric matrices

subject: linear algebra
title: Cofactors commute with powers and a planar exponential
prompt:
(a) For \(A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) and integer \(m\ge0\), prove 
\[
\operatorname{cof}(A^m)=\operatorname{cof}(A)^m.
\]
 (b) For \(n=2\), prove 
\[
\operatorname{cof}(e^A)=e^{\operatorname{cof}(A)}.
\]
